The Scraped Arrow
You carve an observation rule instead of a fixed direction.
Carve a current rule
You remove the marker so no crew mistakes it for reliable guidance again.
Remove the board
You pass on what you found and leave the local pilots to decide on a new system.
Leave it to the locals
A final marker carries the symbol intact but no arrow. At its base, several crews carved their own corrections; the sabotage has finally made the marker network useless to everyone.
The Last Board
event.active_paradise_p1_classic_01_saba: The crate falls into the cleared area and nobody is hit.
Cut it over clear ground
Several hands pull together and bring the crate back onto the platform.
Haul it back
A second rope takes the weight and the crate reaches the ground gently.
Lower it by rope
The lift is almost stable, but one crate hangs by a single strap above the cleared market. The operator can cut it loose or try to haul it back onto the platform.
The Hanging Crate
The membrane bursts beneath you and you fall with two baskets into the market.
You also secure the hanging crate before it can fall onto the crowd.
You slow the lift, but one crate comes loose and smashes an empty stall.
You catch the safety line and guide the lift toward a clear trunk.
Catch the safety line
Vendors pull customers out of the area before the membrane bursts.
Clear the market
The baskets descend on ropes and lighten the lift before it fails.
Lower the baskets
A bubble lift loaded with baskets rises between two mangroves when its membrane turns white. A crowd passes underneath, and the operator frantically searches his tools for the safety line.
The Bursting Lift
Workers clear the area so the line can be bled with nobody beneath it.
Clear the walkway
You tighten the wrong valve and a pocket of hot resin splashes your arm.
You isolate the line without shutting down the other vats and avoid stopping the whole yard.
You reduce the leak, but the work area must be evacuated to clean the sticky floor.
You find the cracked joint and cut pressure just upstream.
Isolate the line
The crew Shipwright spots the bypass valve and isolates the line cleanly.
Let the Shipwright handle it
In a coating yard, a resin pipe leaks above a walkway. The floor turns slick, two workers are trapped beyond the valve, and the vat keeps pushing hot mixture through the line.
Resin Under Pressure
A harbor clerk publicly confirms the seller has no authorization.
Fetch a real clerk
You leave before the broker invents another story.
Leave the newcomers
The buyers compare their papers and put their money away.
Point out the bad stamp
A man sells supposedly official berthing papers beneath a tree, but his stamp carries the wrong grove number. Two newly arrived crews are already preparing to pay him an advance.
The Broker Without an Office
A few porters move barriers and create a pedestrian lane around the toll.
Open the side lane
The group hesitates before a line that collectively refuses to move or pay.
Stand with the merchants
The merchants turn back before the jam traps them between both groups.
Turn the carts around
An armed group blocks a narrow passage beneath a root and demands payment from every cart. Merchants pile up behind them while a second route begins filling too.
Passage Under the Root
The crew First Mate organizes the movement and keeps the boats from blocking each other.
Follow the First Mate
You follow the wrong channel and emerge directly into a patrol line you must avoid in a hurry.
You combine root contours and patrol timing to reach the exit without ever crossing their route.
You find a way out, but it costs enough time to miss your passage window.
You read the bubble drift and choose a channel that stays clear between two patrols.
Pick the quiet channel
The boatmen let the patrol pass and then take the main channel.
Wait for the patrol
Among the mangrove roots, several channels meet near a watched sector. Boatmen wait for a patrol to pass, but surface bubbles show a secondary current has just shifted.
Channels Among Roots
event.active_paradise_p1_classic_01_thri: Someone watches the gate while the rest of the group looks for the chain’s owner.
Post a guard
You force the chain and the gate rebounds into you when something pulls from the other side.
You open it just enough to get the trapped travelers out without letting the gate bang in the fog.
The chain gives, but the noise draws movement all around the cemetery.
You find the secondary latch hidden under moss and open the gate without ringing the bars.
Open it quietly
The travelers explain where they entered and wait while you look for another exit.
Talk through the bars
A cemetery gate is chained from the outside while two travelers call from the other side. Shapes move between the stones, and nobody recognizes the chain wrapped around the gate.
The Cemetery Gate
The salvagers leave through the side before the plaster comes down.
Clear the side door
They abandon the haul and gain enough time to clear the entrance.
Drop the chandeliers
You block the entrances after everyone leaves so another salvager does not enter.
Mark the room unsafe
In an abandoned dining hall, salvagers pull down chandeliers when a cable groans overhead. A long crack runs across the ceiling, and the main door is blocked by furniture.
Ceiling for Dinner
You tie scraps of cloth to stones along the real path.
Mark the real path
The remaining travelers return to the paving as soon as the false path disappears.
Snuff the false lamps
You follow a flame that is too steady and step into a pit hidden under leaves.
You find the dark cord linking several false lanterns and reveal where they are being controlled.
You prove one lantern is false, but two travelers have already vanished behind the trees.
You compare the heights and spot hand-placed lamps away from the true path.
Test the lantern line
In the fog, a row of lanterns leads travelers away from the paved path. The flames barely move despite the wind, and recent footprints stop abruptly near the trees.
Lying Lanterns
The chest reaches an open yard before anyone touches the lock.
Drag it outside
The salvagers mark the shed and decide the contents are not worth the risk.
Leave it shut
The knocks follow an irregular rhythm that sounds more like an animal than a person.
Listen before opening
An iron-banded chest pounds from the inside at the back of a shed. Two salvagers want to open it immediately, while a third points to fresh claw marks around the lock.
The Pounding Chest
You strike the wrong fitting; the chain lashes your shoulder before vanishing into the fog.
You reset the chain quietly and spot a mark showing it was moved recently.
You slow the slide, but the anchor catches something below the surface and stays jammed.
You follow the chain's tension and secure the link jumping out of its guide.
Catch the bad link
Bystanders leave the impact area while the barge drifts slowly.
Clear the pilings
An iron bar locks the mechanism until the chain can be hauled back.
Wedge the ratchet
A heavy mooring chain slides on its own along a fogbound quay. The ratchet no longer holds, and every lost meter brings a dark barge closer to a row of pilings.
Chain in the Fog
event.active_paradise_p1_classic_01_wate: The food moves first; mechanics wait for the next slot.
Prioritize the food
The repair parts move first; food sellers protest but keep the next slot.
Prioritize the parts
The crews load from half the pier each and accept a slower pace for everyone.
Split the pier
Two dock crews claim the same pier for urgent cargo. One carries food, the other repair parts, and the harbormaster refuses to choose in front of his own workers.
Pier Number Four
The punt rides up a side ramp before reaching the gate.
Beach the punt
You pull the emergency chain and slow the gate enough to pass.
Grab the chain
The operator stops the gate inches above the gunwale.
Shout to the operator
The punt clears the junction, then a canal gate begins dropping ahead. The mechanism is already halfway down, and the operator has not seen the boat coming.
The Canal Gate
The gondoliers open a lane and the punt eventually reaches an empty quay.
Clear the junction
You jump onto the wrong side and the punt throws you against the quay at the first turn.
You ride a canal wave and bring the punt alongside an empty quay without touching anything.
You slow the punt, but it clips a gondola loaded with crates.
You reach the tiller before the junction and avoid the line of gondolas.
Jump for the tiller
A gondola catches the line and slows the punt before the junction.
Throw a line
A delivery punt slides riderless down a canal after its rope snaps. Ahead, a junction is crowded with gondolas, and the vendor chasing it cannot swim.
The Runaway Punt
The workers clear the bay before any more fasteners shift.
Clear the bay
The crew Shipwright recognizes the brace twist and has the joint reset.
Let the Shipwright read it
You load the brace too quickly; a rivet pops and a plank drops onto the lower deck.
You also spot a batch of defective rivets before they are installed elsewhere.
You steady the scaffold, but the yard must close the bay to replace several fasteners.
You identify the joint taking the load sideways and have it reset correctly.
Trace the bad joint
In a shipyard, scaffolding groans above an open hull. A foreman notices three rivet heads vibrating together while workers keep carrying planks underneath.
Singing Rivets
The block closes immediately without waiting for the argument to be settled.
Follow harbor orders
Goods move to higher shelves while the shutters close.
Move the low crates
You call the wrong hour and several merchants leave their stalls exposed to the first surge.
You find an old forgotten mark that gives the whole block a few extra minutes.
You understand the danger, but too late to save every crate stacked at canal level.
You cross-check the height marks and get shutters closed before the sudden rise.
Read the water marks
A tide siren sounds earlier than expected and merchants argue over the actual surge time. Wet marks on the walls already show the canal is rising.
Marks on the Wall
Buyer and seller pull the same rope and postpone their dispute until after the rescue.
Make both sides pull
The lumber is caught before the bridge and the sale can resume.
Secure the lumber
Boatmen close the passage beneath the bridge before the raft reaches it.
Warn the bridge
A rafted lot of lumber breaks loose during a sale and drifts toward a low bridge. Buyer and seller are still arguing over who is responsible for it.
The Floating Lot
event.active_paradise_p1_classic_01_whis: Half the brawlers stay inside; the street regains enough room to move.
Bar the tavern door
The drivers shove with you and save their cargo from the melee.
Pull the carts clear
Your intervention puts you between two thrown stools; you take the hit and the room erupts.
You turn the two ringleaders against each other verbally, and the crowd laughs instead of swinging.
You separate one pair, but the fight spills toward loaded carts outside the door.
Your voice creates a pause long enough to pull the carts clear.
Shout them down
A tavern brawl spills toward three carts loaded with bottles. The drivers are pinned against a wall while fighters already tear off sideboards to use as clubs.
The Cart Brawl
The courier opens it just enough to show contracts stamped by several ports.
Demand the seal
You slide it under flour sacks until the hunters move on.
Hide the satchel
The courier takes the satchel back and vanishes into a rear yard.
Refuse the package
A breathless courier pushes a sealed satchel toward you and points at three hunters searching the inns. He swears it holds only shipping contracts but refuses to show the inner seal.
The Courier’s Satchel
The crowd points out the drawing’s mistakes and the copyist loses his leverage.
Mock the likeness
You destroy the copy he is waving, but he claims to have more.
Tear up one copy
Denied a scene, the copyist looks for an easier target.
Walk past
A street copyist waves a portrait that vaguely resembles you and promises to sell it to bounty hunters. He demands money to destroy the other copies in front of an amused crowd.
Portrait for Sale
When he drops the chit, you catch it before it slides into the drain.
Cover the gutter
You step back and let the chit’s owner settle the exchange.
Let the captain negotiate
The thief returns the chit for a ladder and vanishes into the crowd.
Offer a way down
The thief reaches an awning with no exit and holds the chit over a gutter. Below, the captain threatens to knock him down unless he returns the paper immediately.
Cornered on the Awning
You step onto a rotten tile that gives way; the thief gains two rooftops.
You force the thief down exactly in front of the owner of the stolen chit.
You follow the trail, but the thief throws the mooring chit into an unreachable gutter.
You cut across a balcony and block the next ledge.
Chase over the roofs
You cover his only safe way down and the thief eventually drops the chit.
Cut toward the gutter
The harbor suspends the ship move while the chase continues.
Warn the harbormaster
A young thief snatches a mooring chit from a captain and climbs onto the awnings. Without it, the ship will be moved before nightfall and its cargo left in the street.
The Chit on the Roofs
You call the wrong token and two groups claim the same berth at once.
You identify the copyist who made the duplicates before he can leave the square.
You see something is wrong, but not quickly enough to stop the swap.
Fresh ink and scraped numbers reveal which tokens were switched.
Compare the tokens
The hostess restarts the distribution under everyone’s eyes.
Return every token
You take a worse berth and avoid an immediate fight.
Trade your berth

Berth Tokens

Your appeal turns the crowd against the guards. You take a hit and the auction ends in chaos.
The guards reopen and return the seized lots. {{npc_active_recruit_lot_runner}} closes the auction and joins your route.
The gate stays shut. {{npc_active_recruit_lot_runner}} loses the lot and part of the crowd.
You secure one final clean sale. {{npc_active_recruit_lot_runner}} wipes away the number and chooses to leave with you.
Get the gate reopened
You leave the market to close. {{npc_active_recruit_lot_runner}} stays to calm sellers and buyers.
Walk away from the crowd
Guards close the market while {{npc_active_recruit_lot_runner}} still holds one last chalk number overhead. Sellers crowd the gate and the buyers begin to shove.
The Gate Before the Last Lot
You pay for timber and a mobile shelter. {{npc_active_recruit_notice_carver}} agrees to rebuild the board while traveling with you.
Fund a new board
You do not oppose the agents. {{npc_active_recruit_notice_carver}} stays to carve the lost names from memory.
Let the board burn
You choke on smoke and save the wrong panel. Several names vanish in the fire.
You save the names and the imprint of the forged order. {{npc_active_recruit_notice_carver}} takes her tools and joins you.
You recover fragments, but too many names are already unreadable.
You reconstruct the list before it burns. {{npc_active_recruit_notice_carver}} decides to travel with you to preserve it.
Save the readable names
Agents tear down {{npc_active_recruit_notice_carver}}’s carved board and throw it into a brazier. Beneath the burning paste, several missing-person notices reappear before the flames reach the names.
Names in the Smoke
You leave the drydock. {{npc_owen}} remains alone with the owner and the broken hoist.
Leave {{npc_owen}} with the claim
You pay to end the claim. {{npc_owen}} retrieves his tools and agrees to leave with you.
Pay for the broken keel
Your demonstration breaks a second brace. You are hurt and the yard doubles its claim.
You prove the yard already knew about the crack. {{npc_owen}} takes his tools and joins your crew.
The marks remain ambiguous. The owner keeps the claim against {{npc_owen}}.
You find the old crack in the hoist. The claim collapses and {{npc_owen}} chooses to leave the yard with you.
Prove the hoist failed
A hoist breaks above a keel and the yard blames {{npc_owen}} for bracing the hull badly. The owner demands compensation before anyone can leave the drydock.
The Hoist That Failed
You pull the last wedges. The ramp collapses into the water and {{npc_owen}} disappears through another exit.
Collapse the slipway together
You hand the plans to the patrol. The slipway is seized and {{npc_owen}} immediately understands who exposed it.
Hand over the plans
You abandon the slipway before the soldiers arrive. {{npc_owen}} takes only his tools and joins your crew.
Get {{npc_owen}} out before the sweep
A patrol has found the hidden slipway where {{npc_owen}} repaired unregistered hulls. Boots close in while he pulls the last wedges keeping the ramp from collapsing.
The Hidden Slipway Exposed
You claim the final win. {{npc_childhood_rival}} snaps the notebook shut and joins the other crew.
Add one last point
You strike out the whole column instead of adding a point. {{npc_childhood_rival}} closes the notebook and joins your crew.
Erase the score and invite her
You write down a draw. {{npc_childhood_rival}} smiles, but still chooses her own road.
Settle on a draw
{{npc_childhood_rival}} puts down the notebook where she still counted your wins and debts. Another crew is already waiting at the end of the quay; only one line remains blank.
The Last Line on the Scorecard
The ledger becomes ash before the patrol arrives. {{npc_rohan}} leaves by another street to keep the network alive.
Burn the list and split
You turn the search into a public spectacle. The safehouse holds, but {{npc_rohan}} remains tied to the kitchen.
Keep serving under their eyes
You clear the kitchen before the search. {{npc_rohan}} abandons the ledger and continues the road with you.
Get {{npc_rohan}} out with the pots
A patrol works up the street while {{npc_rohan}} empties the safehouse’s last pot. The meal ledger carries enough marks to connect several couriers to the same network.
The Safehouse’s Last Pot
You leave before service ends. {{npc_rohan}} keeps the kitchen open without your help.
Leave him with the bill
You pay for the missing sacks. After the last bowl, {{npc_rohan}} closes the kitchen and accepts your berth.
Pay the shortfall
The argument turns physical and you take a hit. The supplier leaves with the rice and the debt grows.
You clear the debt by exposing the double ledger. {{npc_rohan}} hangs up his apron and joins your crew.
The supplier refuses the deal. {{npc_rohan}} finishes service with what remains.
You secure one last delivery and a delay. {{npc_rohan}} closes the kitchen and finally agrees to leave with you.
Turn the supplier around
{{npc_rohan}} is still serving when his supplier takes back the rice sacks and demands immediate payment. The dockworkers’ line grows, and the kitchen lacks enough stock to finish service.
The Pot Without a Supplier
You recover the tags and offer him a route instead of another shrine. {{npc_active_recruit_wake_keeper}} joins you.
Carry the tags with him
You search the quay until the tags are found. He thanks you, then returns to his watch.
Recover the tags, then part
You yield to the family. The bell carries far, but {{npc_active_recruit_wake_keeper}} refuses to abandon the other names.
Ring one name
A wave floods {{npc_active_recruit_wake_keeper}}’s quay shrine and sweeps away his brass tags. A family still demands the bell be rung before the next ship departs.
The Tags Taken by the Storm
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_entry.c: Read the water before it takes you
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_entry.o: You secure your footing while the deck rolls beneath you.
You reach the bow just as the current seizes the hull.
You mark the current's rhythm before the climb begins.
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_entry.t: The current catches the vessel carrying you before the Red Line fills the horizon. Water is climbing the mountain itself, and the deck tilts toward the first roaring channel.
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_i01_fir: Drop low and ride out the turn
Read the angle of the surge
You let the current spend its violence above you.
You misread the lift. The jolt throws you hard against the deck.
You read the surge before it breaks and move with it cleanly.
You correct too late and take the impact on your shoulder.
You catch the current's rhythm and keep your footing through the turn.
The climbing stream narrows between black stone walls. The vessel yaws sideways, and one bad angle could slam everyone into the rock.
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_i02_red: Hold the center of the deck
Lean into the spray for a clear look
The impacts settle into a pattern you can follow.
You keep your weight centered as the vessel claws upward.
The spray stings, but you catch a clear glimpse of the next rise.
The channel bends almost vertical. Red stone fills the sky ahead while spray hides the next ledge, and the deck shudders under the rising water.
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_i03_cli: You chase a false gap and the next surge knocks you flat.
You read the hidden flow through the spray before it changes.
The seam vanishes before you can use it, and the spray hammers you back.
You keep the seam in sight and anticipate the next violent lift.
You refuse the shifting water and hold to the only stable line.
Halfway up, the spray turns the world white. A darker seam in the water appears for only a heartbeat before the next surge reaches you.
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_i04_cre: Fix your eyes on the descending channel
Stay low and prepare for the drop
You pick out the descent before the vessel tips forward.
You make yourself small as the summit disappears behind you.
For one breath, fear gives way to the scale of the sea ahead.
The roar suddenly thins. For one impossible second, the vessel hangs near the summit and two seas seem to tilt beneath you before gravity takes over.
event.active_reverse_mountain_01_i05_des: Lock yourself down and endure it
You hold fast until the roar breaks and the water opens onto Twin Capes.
Your footing fails at the worst moment. You hit the deck hard before the channel releases you.
You flow with every drop and land the final impact as if you expected it.
You absorb one brutal impact and stay aboard through the rest of the descent.
You match the vessel's motion and reach the bottom on your feet.
The far side drops away beneath you. The vessel accelerates down the channel, bouncing from wall to wall as Twin Capes flashes into view below.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_clean_riv: You fill the margin without comment. You remain competitors, but each knows the other deserves to be measured seriously.
You put the ledger away without answering. The rivalry did its job: it forced you to become sharper without owning your life.
You praise only one figure. He knows exactly what it costs you to write it, and returns the gesture later.
A year later, your rival sends a copy of his new ledger. No challenge, no debt: only his best figures and a blank margin for you to answer with yours.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_cold_invo: Your file mixes insured losses with losses already reimbursed. Your rival rejects it all and adds the verification costs.
You find a duplicate in his invoice and an omission in yours. The books close even, with evidence on both sides.
You prove only part of your losses. He reduces his invoice, but keeps most of the claim.
Your receipts bring both claims to nearly the same total. You cancel the difference rather than prolong the debt.
You pay every justified line and reject the rest. He cashes it; the conflict remains, but the numbers stop being a weapon.
You return the invoice untouched. Two weeks later, all your contacts receive a copy stamped “unpaid.”
Fourteen months after the fire, an invoice arrives: handling, storage, losses, and a line for the hours his team cleared the aisle. Your rival signed the bottom without a greeting.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_empty_cha: One complaint came from your own former client. The assembly sees the maneuver and closes both files.
You prove a genuinely abusive practice and the assembly bars him from this berth. He cannot deny the evidence, only remember who brought it.
The complaints are too weak to remove him. He still understands that you tried to turn the vote into a public execution.
You connect enough complaints to sink his application. The berth is yours; the last bridge between you is not.
Turn his complaints against him
You cite an obsolete clause. Your rival corrects you before the assembly and wins the berth without rubbing it in.
You find the central error without attacking his reputation. He loses the berth and asks for your annotated copy.
His file is better that day. You admit it in front of everyone; the loss closes the vote, not the rivalry.
Your figures hold better. He signs the minutes after you and keeps a copy for the next contest.
Demand a file-against-file vote
Trying to save both files, you blur responsibility. The assembly freezes the berth and your rival blames you for making everything undecidable.
You turn the application into a transparent rule other merchants can use as well. The berth stops being a private trophy.
The assembly rejects the split but recognizes the proposal. Your rival loses with you rather than against you.
You show that your networks cover different risks. The assembly grants a shared berth under two signatures.
Defend both applications
The chart reminds everyone that you already made a shared network work. Your rival sits beside you instead of across from you.
Put the two-ink chart on the table
You demand a new vote with an arbiter present. After a long second, your rival agrees: neither of you will take this berth by default.
Refuse the vote without a chair
Eighteen months later, a merchants’ assembly must assign a strategic berth. The chairperson disappears before the vote, leaving an empty chair and two files: yours and your rival’s.
The Empty Chair
event.active_rival_civilian_01_fair_marg: You sign beneath his rules. For the first time, the rivalry has a line neither of you will cross.
You return the ledger unsigned. He keeps his three markets and merely notes that you prefer a boundary to a duel.
Decline the game, keep the markets
You add a crate’s worth of profit to the wager. He accepts immediately: respect has not made either of you less competitive.
Sixteen months later, your rival sends an annotated ledger. He marked three markets where your prices overlap and proposes a wager: both keep their books open, and better service keeps the clients.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_first_led: You promise too much to save the contract. The client withdraws the offer, and your rival sends you a copy of your own numbers.
You catch a clause he missed and save the client without crushing costs. Your rival writes “clean” in the margin.
Your price remains defensible, but too slow. Your rival takes the contract and circles the margin that cost you the job.
You keep an honest margin and win the shipment. Your rival sends the contract back with a single line under your price.
You give him half the stops for a clear margin. Nobody wins alone, but no client is left waiting.
Your calculation misses the dock fees. You win on paper and lose money as soon as loading begins.
You cut the right cost instead of wages. The contract lands with you; annoyed as he is, your rival respects the math.
The client sees two successive discounts and walks away. Your rival leaves you with the wasted handling costs.
You slip just under his price and take the contract. The win pays, but he knows exactly how you got it.
Slash his price at the last moment
A news bird drops two bids for the same shipment. One bears your old neighborhood merchant’s seal: he undercut you by a handful of Berrys and expects your answer before noon.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_joint_cha: You take one half, he takes the other. The route remains workable, and so does the boundary between you.
You keep separate books but share the stops. Clients start talking about you as a pair before they mention the rivalry.
You propose the same start and open books at the finish. He agrees before the ink dries.
Turn the route into another wager
Eighteen months later, your rival sends a chart in two colors: his contacts on one side, yours on the other. A new route crosses both networks; neither of you can hold it alone.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_line_in_i: You sign the separation. Your networks stop crossing by choice; hostility becomes a rule instead of a daily war.
You return the contract unsigned. You remain declared opponents, each ready to contest the next berth, client, or route.
You refuse friendship but propose a limit: no false figures, no threats, no pressure on workers. He signs.

A year later, a contract arrives with an unusual clause: your rival refuses to work with any intermediary representing you. He has drawn a commercial boundary and leaves you to decide whether it becomes permanent.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_name_arri: You refuse to win on an anonymous recommendation. He comes to defend his file in person; the hearing finally becomes a clean contest.
Call your rival before the council
You put his invoice on the table as evidence of the feud. The council sees that your rivalry can jam an entire market.
The copy carries your annotation on the back. The council traces the leak to you and closes your application.
You choose a real discrepancy rather than a lie. His file is suspended; yours passes, but he knows who supplied the document.
The rumor does not take, but your rival immediately recognizes the invoice you picked.
The council delays his file long enough to approve yours. You get access and a durable enemy in his books.
The shared signatures end the suspicion. The council sees two competitors able to share one ledger without falsifying it.
You mix up two figures under questioning. The council chooses your rival and charges for your wasted filing.
You show that both networks can share the docks without duplication. The council opens two windows and credits your plan.
Your case holds, but his is clearer. The council grants him access and leaves you the next window.
You demonstrate the reliability of your commitments without smearing his. The council chooses you; he accepts the verdict.
Win the hearing on the facts
Twenty months later, a new port already knows both your names. The local council received two conflicting recommendations and will grant only one of you access to the public warehouses.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_public_le: You publish an old figure as current. Your rival corrects it in public, and your own board becomes his best evidence.
You also correct an error that favored you. The board becomes less accusatory and harder to use as a weapon.
Your receipts explain some gaps, but not all. The board stays up and several clients wait before calling you again.
You answer line by line with verifiable evidence. The public mostly learns how closely the two of you have watched each other for years.
You let the board yellow without an answer. Some clients leave; others stay to see whether your work is enough.
You send three rules: no false figures, no pressure on workers, no sabotage. He signs two lines and strikes out the third before returning it.
Eighteen months later, your rival posts a table of delays, prices, and complaints with both your names at the top. There is no obvious lie—only the version of events most favorable to him.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_shared_sa: You let him make the calculation. He gives you exactly what the receipts justify, then keeps a copy signed by both sides.
You count every loss and sign the same total. The payout does not erase the fire, but nobody leaves shorted.
You take what you believe you are owed. He recalculates after you and remembers the difference.
Fourteen months after the fire, the insurer pays one sum for both lots. Your rival sets three stacks of receipts between you and refuses to touch a Berry until you choose the split.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_stolen_in: You pay only documented costs and send the receipts back. He cashes it without comment; at least the books are factual again.
You count two fees twice. Your rival spots the mistake, boxes the total in red, and sends your own invoice back to you.
You reconstruct both accounts and find an error in your favor that you do not claim. He sees it anyway.
Your total does not survive the receipts. He rejects the offset and keeps the original invoice.
Your losses almost exactly offset his. You cancel both invoices without settling the rest of the feud.
You send the pieces back in the same envelope. The message is clear: nothing will be settled out of courtesy.
Sixteen months later, your rival sends an invoice in your name: fees for a contact you both courted, plus a blank line marked “trust.” He expects you to fill in the amount yourself.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_two_route: The factor repeats your offer word for word to your rival. You pay the promised advance and get nothing.
You secure passage without lying about the numbers. Your rival is furious, but cannot dispute the signed contract.
The factor refuses and closes his books. Your rival still learns you tried to go around him.
The factor switches sides and your load goes first. Your rival loses the client, not the memory.
You force a bad current and damage part of the cargo. Your rival arrives first and has his corrected chart delivered to you.
You arrive early and warn the port about the reef that would have cut his route. He loses the contract, not his ship.
You arrive after him with no excuse to offer. He takes the contract and leaves his chalk mark on the dock post.
You find a safer passage and win narrowly. He checks your chart, then shakes your hand without smiling.
You turn in both loads together and split the margin. The client complains, but the shipment arrives complete.
Split the delivery at the dock
A year later, the same seal appears on a delivery chart. Your rival promised the northern route; you promised the southern one. The client will pay only for the first intact load.
event.active_rival_civilian_01_two_signa: You decline the renewal but offer a meal at the next port. He accepts faster than any contract.
Decline the joint contract, keep the friendship
You sign, then add a clause: best result of the year chooses the next berth. His reply comes back with one word: “deal.”
You add your name. The rivalry does not disappear; it becomes a friendship that knows exactly what it is worth.
A year later, a letter comes back from the shared berth. Your rival already signed the renewal and left the other line blank for you, with a note: “we keep our own books.”
event.active_rival_civilian_01_warehouse: You mistake a reflection for an opening and lose precious seconds. Your rival drags you out of the wrong aisle.
You find the exit and the point where the flames will meet. Everyone clears out before the aisle disappears.
You find the door after he does. You evacuate the handlers, but almost no crates follow.
You read the airflow beneath the smoke and guide both teams to the exit.
Read the exit through the smoke
You trap yourself behind your own cargo and have to abandon several crates to get out.
You recover your lot, then point the handlers to the shortest exit. Efficient, but not generous.
You save little cargo and leave his team to move the crates blocking the exit alone.
You recover your lot before the collapse. His team gets out too, but your choice leaves no ambiguity.
Force a path to your crates
A stack collapses and cuts you off from the crates. You get the handlers out, but both lose part of the stock.
You spot a sound beam and organize a chain around it. You save the people, the ledgers, and most of the crates.
You open a path too late to save the goods. Both handlers get out; the month’s profit stays in the smoke.
You alternate loads and clear the door. The handlers get out with enough crates that nobody is ruined.
Work together to clear the aisle
Eighteen months later, a shared warehouse catches fire before inventory. Your rival’s crates block the exit for yours; behind the smoke, two handlers are still looking for the door.
event.active_rival_marine_01_after_actio: You fixate on a minor phrase and lose the substance of the case. She has your disagreement recorded separately.
You turn your disagreement into a clear decision rule. Even she admits the report is better with both signatures.
The discussion bogs down and the board requires two separate reports.
You rewrite the disputed point without erasing the facts. She finally accepts a joint signature.
You refuse to share responsibility for the wording. She takes back her copy without comment, and the distance becomes official.
You keep the disagreements on record but sign the same conclusion. The board sees a team that can disagree without coming apart.
A year later, a review board compares your accounts of the pier incident. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} sets her report beside yours and refuses to erase the disagreements.
event.active_rival_marine_01_broken_conv: The order is misunderstood and your teams cross at the worst moment. She takes over long enough to get the convoy moving again.
You anticipate the convoy split and propose the swap before impact. She understands immediately, and both teams pivot together.
The switch comes too late and feeds an argument over who was supposed to decide.
You make the case for swapping sectors clearly. She agrees without wasting time, and each of you covers the objective best suited to them.
You centralize both sectors and impose your priorities. The convoy survives, but she records that you erased her responsibility at the critical moment.
You move the civilians through fire too early and go down hard. She holds the evidence, then comes back to cover your withdrawal.
You clear the civilians fast enough to reinforce her flank without taking over. The convoy leaves with both objectives intact.
The civilian passage is costly, but you do not take over her sector. She keeps the evidence intact and finally rejoins your group.
You secure the civilians while she saves the evidence. Neither of you tries to command the other’s sector.

An attack splits a Marine convoy in two: evacuated civilians on one side, seized evidence on the other. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} finally asks for one shared decision, not two reports.
event.active_rival_marine_01_contested_r: Your argument mixes times and orders. The board mainly comes away thinking the two of you cover each other poorly.
You show exactly where the orders contradicted each other and propose a concrete fix. She backs your conclusion before the board.
You prove the situation was confused without explaining your coordination.
You reconstruct the sequence and show the failure cannot be pinned on one decision. She completes your account instead of contradicting it.
You record your own mistakes before discussing hers. She does the same, and the case stops being a weapon between you.
You build the case around her decision. She answers with facts, then stops speaking to you except in writing.
Command reopens the convoy failure and wants one clear line of responsibility. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} files her report without shielding you or condemning you.
event.active_rival_marine_01_cut_off_tog: You take the hit that would have cut her off and barely stay upright. She comes back to pull you clear.
You lock down the passage and give her a clean exit. She returns with her team at the exact moment you need to break away.
You open her route at the cost of several hits. She refuses to leave until you are back inside the line.
You hold long enough for her to recover her team, then she covers your withdrawal without needing an order.
You build the plan on a bad estimate and take the first breach head-on.
You anticipate the second attack and turn it into a trap. For the first time, your methods fit together without friction.
The plan contains the attack without really giving you the initiative back.
You reduce the field to simple decisions and each hold the half you promised. Support arrives to find a coherent position.
You limit cooperation to positions, timing, and signals. It is cold, but enough to get out together.
An operation turns bad and your detachment is isolated before support arrives. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} has no superior left to invoke: the two of you have to decide.
event.active_rival_marine_01_formal_dist: You refuse any coordination beyond written orders. The mission gets through, but the distance becomes a habit.
You hold your sector without crossing into hers. The mission stays cold, but neither of you can blame the other for a mistake.
You push too far to beat her there and enter the wrong street. She pulls you out without hiding her irritation.
You neutralize the threat before your sectors even meet. She records the result instead of looking for an excuse.
You gain a few meters, then have to double back to cover a gap. The competition costs both of you time.
You take the right shortcut and secure your sector first. She concedes the point without smiling.
Separate reports do not stop command from assigning you to the same escort. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} demands separate sectors and unambiguous orders.
You move together on a bad assumption. The perimeter breaks and you have to force an exit under fire.
You launch two complementary moves on the same signal. The families get out and the target gets no opening.
The initiative saves civilians but disrupts the capture. You have to repair your own plan under pressure.
You split rescue and arrest without waiting for another order. Both objectives remain possible.
You hold the perimeter exactly as written. The operation stays controlled, but she sees clearly which priority you chose.
You follow her on an overly optimistic read of the ground and the civilian exit closes around you.
You understand her intent before she says it and move your team at the right instant. The order is obeyed in purpose, not merely in wording.
Her idea saves part of the group, but you have to fight for the rest of the route.
You let her control the opening while you hold the perimeter. The families get out without losing the target.

The investigation leads to an operation where written orders require holding the perimeter while families remain trapped behind the target. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} looks to you before acting.
event.active_rival_marine_01_old_report_: You cite the exact decisions that earned your trust. She gets the lead without turning your support into a debt.
You revive an old grievance the record no longer supports. She does not even need to answer.
You demonstrate a precise limitation and propose a split that works around it. Even she accepts the case is stronger that way.
You raise real tensions, but they look more like rivalry than professional misconduct.
You identify a real weakness in her method without distorting the history. She takes the criticism and corrects the point.
The board reads your old disagreements as proof that two leads would create one more risk.
You show that openly managed disagreement produced better decisions. The board assigns the investigation to both of you.
Your request looks mainly designed to stop the other from deciding alone. She does not help defend it.
You tie your failures and successes to a clear two-person decision rule. She adds to the argument instead of competing with it.
An old convoy report returns to the file just as a cross-unit investigation needs leadership. Your history with {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} suddenly becomes an official argument.
event.active_rival_marine_01_same_unifor: You stop looking for a safer word. She accepts it, then immediately resumes your argument about the last operation.
You agree not to work together unless duty requires it. Future contact will go through orders and reports.
You keep score, not grudges. Every future meeting will be a test the other deserves a fair chance to win.
You ask for your names to be paired on difficult cases. It is not friendship; it is professional trust.
After years of meeting on the same cases, {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} asks one thing: what the two of you have become to each other.
event.active_rival_marine_01_shared_cred: You present the operation as your plan and the board identifies several decisions that were not yours. Her expression hardens.
You secure recognition for your decision while putting her role on record. The rivalry stays sharp, but clean.
Your account stretches the truth too far, and she calmly corrects the record point by point.
You defend having made the call without denying her execution. She accepts the competition as long as the facts remain intact.
You refuse sole credit and detail what she held without you. She does not thank you in front of the board, but she does not forget it.
You answer that the convoy would not have survived a ranking contest between officers. She gives a brief nod.
The convoy report comes back with a single box for primary credit. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} lets you speak first before the review board.
event.active_rival_marine_01_shared_watc: You misread a diversion and take the ambush before you can warn the convoy.
You read the ambush before it starts and signal her the right lane. The convoy barely slows.
You spot the trap too late. The convoy holds, but she has to cover the delay under fire.
You catch the diversion before it cuts the route. She shields the witnesses while you clear the way.
You give her point and take the witnesses. The gesture matters more than the report: each of you finally accepts the other’s judgment on their sector.
Your joint report puts you on another escort together. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} lets you decide who takes point and who guards the witnesses.
event.active_rival_marine_01_two_signatu: You force entry too fast, get hurt, and scatter part of the evidence. She has to rebuild the perimeter behind you.
You free the dockworkers and close the gap in the perimeter yourself. She has nothing to correct.
The dockworkers get out, but the move costs you a hard hit and leaves a hole in her perimeter.
You open the hold without compromising the perimeter. She admits your judgment saved time.
You preserve the evidence while she covers the evacuation. Your first clash still looks like a workable division of duty.
Your orders cross and two teams duplicate the same sector. She cuts in sharply to restore the chain.
You divide the teams in a few words and leave her exactly the room she needs. The operation looks rehearsed.
The split works poorly and you lose time correcting each other.
You divide rescue and seizure cleanly. She follows the plan without argument and the pier clears safely.
A smuggling skiff burns beside a crowded pier. {npc_active_rival_marine_01_peer_officer} wants the evidence secured while trapped dockworkers call from below deck.
Her rope drops into the harbor. You take the wreck, and her smile disappears with it.
A rotten spar snaps under you. She catches the claim rope while you hit the deck hard.
You vault the last spar and ring before her boots touch the mast. The whole quay notices.
She reaches the bell first and hooks the claim rope before you can recover.
You ring the bell first. She laughs, memorizes your flag, and yields the claim.
Your split sounds like a trap. She rejects it loudly enough for both crews to hear.
You turn the argument into a public pact: equal shares, equal risk, no knives behind backs.
She refuses the terms and takes your caution for weakness.
She bites the coin marking the claim, then accepts an exact half. Neither crew looks pleased.

A cracked brass bell rings over a wreck auction. {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}}, captain of another pirate crew, has one hand on the same salvage line as you. The dockmaster will recognize only one claim.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s02_second_: You refuse ownership by memory. First captain to the next prize gets first pick.
You divide the chest by weight. She leaves her half of the bell mark scratched into the lid.
You claim the chest and the story around it. Her crew leaves with empty hands and a reason to remember.
A year later, {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} finds you beside a seized contraband chest. She sets the same cracked bell on the lid. “Last time set the rule. Does it still hold?”
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s03_blood_s: She sweeps your footing and opens your guard before the crate is even loose.
You disarm her cleanly and stop the blade at her throat. She laughs once and yields.
You lose the exchange and leave blood on the deck.
You take the crate after a hard exchange. She salutes with the flat of her blade instead of striking again.
You lower your weapon and name a future prize instead. She accepts, suspiciously relieved.
The chain snaps back across you while she secures the crate.
You rip hook and chain from the deck in one pull. Even her crew falls silent.
You wrench the hook loose, but the recoil drops you and costs the prize.
You tear the crate free before she can turn the duel into a boarding fight.

The next prize is a chained supply crate, and {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} boards beside you with steel already drawn. The old claim has become personal; neither crew is pretending otherwise.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s03_clean_s: You commit to the wrong channel and arrive last, with her wake washing over your bow.
You cross her wake perfectly and land on the skiff before either crew understands the move.
She steals the inside line and reaches the skiff first.
You read the opening and touch the strongbox a heartbeat before her.
You toss a coin against the cracked bell. She accepts the absurd verdict and remembers that you did too.
You chase the false turn exactly as she hoped and give her a clear route.
You call her feint before she makes it. She grins and abandons the trick.
You spot the trick late. She keeps the edge.
You ignore the false turn and force her to race honestly for the last stretch.

Fourteen months later, both crews spot a courier skiff carrying an unguarded strongbox. {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} rings the cracked bell once: no shots, no sabotage, first hand on the box wins.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s04_hunter_: The charge stalls against chained hulls and leaves both crews exposed.
Your two charges land on the same heartbeat. The hunter line folds in public view.
You break one fire-ship but take the worst of the counterattack.
You hit the center together and open a corridor for both crews.
You shout the old half-and-half rule over the gunfire. She answers with the cracked bell and commits beside you.
You turn on the wrong note and both crews collide under hunter fire.
You answer her signal before the third note. The two crews move like one formation for a minute.
You understand too late; the gap closes and the escape costs blood.
You follow her three-note turn and both crews slip through the same opening.
The hunters see the betrayal coming and pin you beside her anyway.
You turn every hunter toward her flag and vanish through the smoke with the whole quay watching.
Your feint fails; she notices exactly what you tried and the hunters still close in.
You sell her position to the hunters long enough to cut yourself free.

A private hunter flotilla closes both crews inside a chain of fire-ships. Through the smoke, {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} rings three sharp bell notes—the same signal she used during your earlier races.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s05_splinte: Your cheap opening fails and she answers without restraint.
You crush the setup before it begins and make the betrayal part of your legend.
She catches the early strike and turns it back on you.
You land first and end the duel before the bell can ring. She will not call it a victory.
You lower your weapon and offer sixty minutes with no score to settle. After a long silence, she lowers hers.
She puts you down hard and leaves before you can stand.
You take her weapon without breaking the rules she demanded. That matters to her more than the loss.
You lose the exchange and carry the cut away with you.
You win by a narrow margin and let her retrieve the bell.

Eighteen months later, {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} blocks a warehouse exit with her blade drawn. No crews, no audience. She taps the cracked bell against the wall. “We settle what the hunters started.”
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s05_truce_d: You name a price before opening the back room. She pays every Berry and remembers the invoice.
You refuse the room but mark a drain route the pursuers missed. She disappears before the boots reach your door.
You bar the door and treat the wound in silence. At dawn, she leaves without pretending the debt is small.

Eighteen months after the hunter net, {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} reaches your hideout wounded, with no crew in sight. Pursuers are searching the waterfront. She does not ask for friendship—only one closed door.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s06_same_po: You send her half the broadsheet with a meeting mark scratched beside the headline.
You tear away her flag and burn it in the gutter where her lookouts can see.
Burn her half of the page
You leave the paper on the wall. The argument follows both flags without your help.
You sign beneath both flags and send the print back into circulation as a joint story.

A broadsheet vendor nails up a fresh print: your flag and {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}}’s share the front page beneath one exaggerated headline. Dockhands are already arguing over which captain deserves the story.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s07_friend_: Your false signal exposes both flags and adds fresh attention to your own.
You make the hunters chase a ghost convoy for hours. Her cracked bell answers once from safe water.
The hunters distrust the message and keep pressure on her line.
You feed them a convincing false bearing. They peel away long enough for her to vanish.
You choose a dead channel and her pursuers gain ground while she fights clear.
Your route carries her straight through the reef and leaves the hunters trapped behind broken water.
Your route is too tight. She escapes, but only after abandoning part of her lead.
You mark a clean channel and her ship cuts through before the hunters can turn.
Open a route through the reef
You silence the signal. She survives without you, and the next bell message never comes.
Eighteen months later, a coded bell pattern reaches your lookout: {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} is boxed against a reef by bounty crews. Her message contains coordinates, not a plea.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s07_knife_w: You accuse the wrong hand in her crew, and she tears your evidence apart in front of you.
You reconstruct every handoff and leave her no lie worth using. She respects the work despite herself.
The proof is real but incomplete. She refuses to admit more than watching your wake.
You catch the exact order in her handwriting. She admits she tracked you and stops pretending otherwise.
You rush angry and she punishes every opening.
You dominate the exchange and turn the grudge into a story repeated across the docks.
The fight turns ugly before either captain proves anything.
You drive her back and make the confrontation public enough that neither crew can ignore it.
You slide the proof across the crate instead of drawing steel. She pockets it and agrees to stop tracing your landfalls.
A dock clerk slips you proof that {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}}’s people have been tracing your landfalls. She waits alone beneath a cargo crane, cracked bell on the crate between you.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s07_race_fo: She reaches the bell first by a clean margin. You honor the rule without inventing an excuse.
You trust a false eddy and reach the landing after her bell has already rung.
You spot a hidden countercurrent and arrive with enough time to ring, bow, and step aside.
You find the safe line, but too slowly to keep the lead.
You ride the return current and reach the beacon just ahead of her.
Loose stone gives way and you hit the ledge hard while she passes above.
You climb the impossible-looking line cleanly. She reaches the top laughing at the nerve of it.
The shortcut costs skin and still leaves you second.
You take the exposed face and pull over the rim one hand ahead.

{{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} hangs the cracked bell from a cliffside beacon above a newly exposed cache. No crews may cross the marker. The first captain to ring it earns first choice below.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s08_storm_s: You promise nothing beyond sunrise. She nods, and both crews finally sleep under the same roof.
You propose one final contest with rules neither captain can twist afterward. She accepts immediately.
Ask for one last clean race
You put steel on the floor before asking anything of her. After a beat, she does the same.
You refuse another year of unfinished business. She picks up the bell and names a place.

A violent squall drives both crews into the same abandoned customs shed. Rain hammers the roof; weapons stay within reach. {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} sets the cracked bell between you. “Before dawn, what are we?”
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s09_broken_: You commit too hard. She breaks your attack, leaves you bleeding, and takes the bell out of your life.
You break guard, chain, and bell in one brutal finish. The story spreads farther than either of you intended.
She wins the exchange and cuts the rivalry short on her terms.
You smash through her guard and ring the bell with the pommel. She leaves without looking back.
You leave the bell hanging and walk away. She calls it cowardice once, then never comes looking again.
She reads your first step and punishes the pattern until you can no longer chase.
You never give her a clean target. At the end, she salutes the better captain and disappears into the docks.
Your spacing fails under pressure. She takes the final clean opening.
You make her miss until the last strike has nowhere to land. She sheathes first and walks away.

At the agreed meeting place, {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} hangs the cracked bell from a chain and draws steel. “No crews. No hunters. No story afterward unless one of us walks away with it.”
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s09_clean_h: You ring first by half a step and refuse to exaggerate the margin. She accepts the loss cleanly.
You step aside and let her take the clean win. She looks almost offended before she smiles.
Both hands strike the bell at once. The argument about who won survives because neither of you wants it settled.

The final race ends at a weathered sea-marker. {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} arrives within seconds of you and hangs the cracked bell between both hands. No treasure remains—only who rings first.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s09_paralle: You take opposite channels and leave the truce exactly where it belongs: useful, temporary, finished.
You mark the safer channel for both crews. Two flags leave separately through the same opening.
You exchange one useful bearing each, then part before cooperation starts looking like loyalty.

Months after the storm truce, a patrol net closes the harbor exits. {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} points to two different escape channels. Neither captain trusts the other enough to share a deck.
event.active_rival_pirate_01_s09_two_fla: You say it plainly. She rings the repaired bell once and answers with your name, not your flag.
You call her friend only after demanding the next race. She accepts both terms at once.
You refuse the word but clasp forearms. Neither captain needs the dock to name it.

A year later, {{npc_active_rival_pirate_01_captain}} meets you on a quiet pier with no crew behind her. She has repaired the cracked bell but left the fracture visible. “Rival is still true. Is friend true too?”
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_bord: You misread the checkpoint movement and she takes over mid-run. The witnesses mostly see your mistake.
You turn two checkpoints against each other without losing a group. She immediately demands a rematch on less favorable ground.
She reads your detour first and wins control of the operation. She still leaves you the last group to extract.
You find the opening she missed. She yields the lead for the night and scratches a point onto your side of the seal.
You give her the signal reserved for impossible retreats. She answers with hers: for the first time, neither of you keeps a secret exit.
Both signals go out at once and one column gets trapped between checkpoints. You extract it, but the district loses faith in your coordination.
The district holds, the families get out, and the checkpoints empty in the wrong place. Your paired command becomes the story of the night.
Shared command slows the evacuation. You save the strike, but each of you leaves convinced the other talked too much.
Your signals complement each other and groups move in waves without breaking the picket. She salutes you as a partner, not a superior.
You keep your groups separate but share checkpoint changes. The distrust holds, and so does the circumstantial alliance.
Two years later, a strike locks down a district while Government forces close the exits. The agent arrives with her own groups: your signals must coexist or compete.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_brok: You put your own codes on the table before asking for hers. She accepts a truce limited to this hunt.
Your accusation points at the wrong relay and she has to burn a safe address to protect the innocent.
You turn the false courier and recover the watchers list. She gives back the half of the seal she had reclaimed.
You prove a leak exists without finding its source. She accepts the fact, not your judgment.
You trace the copy to a false courier. She destroys her compromised channel and acknowledges your diagnosis.
The watcher reads the trap and closes it on both of you. She drags you out of the alley, furious at being used as bait.
Your trap catches the watcher and his notebook. She admits it worked, then warns you never to do it to her again.
The bait fails and her cover is burned for nothing. She stops sharing her routes with you.
The watcher bites and you isolate him. The proof is clean, but she notes that you asked for no consent.
You follow two trails without sharing sources. The leak is contained, but your rivalry becomes a procedure.
Your separate channel appears word for word on a Government order. The agent with the cracked seal says the leak comes from your chain; you think it comes from hers.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_burn: You throw the compromised pages into the fire before leaving side by side. No pursuer gets the names, and neither of you keeps the advantage.
You hand her your half of the seal before choosing. She understands that, despite the years, you still trust her with the shared exit.
The beam gives way on both of you. You crawl out injured while the relay's last notebook burns behind you.
You get her out, recover the list, and draw the pursuers toward the already empty room. She is not joking when she says she owes you her life.
You free her too slowly to save the archives. She grips your arm for a second before looking back at the fire.
You drag her clear before the ceiling falls and still recover the list of families that need warning.
You grab the wrong bag and the collapse separates you. She emerges alone and injured while the real ledger burns.
You spot the right bag instantly and use it to brace the beam long enough to free her. Even she admits your calculation saved both.
You save a few pages but she has to free herself. Her look makes the calculation impossible to defend.
You recover the names, then come back for her before the second collapse. She accepts the result, not the order of your priorities.
A Government raid tears through a relay during your meeting. The ceiling comes down between the agent, a contact ledger, and the only exit still open.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_coun: You name the exact order that cost the most. She answers with her own mistake and puts the cracked seal back between you.
You turn the debrief into a trial. She leaves you the room, then cuts two relays that refused to pick a side.
You get an apology without demanding submission. She responds by proposing a shared rule for the next emergency.
She refuses the word you want to hear and points back to your own mistake. The discussion ends without agreement.
She admits she crossed your order without warning, provided you admit the impossible order you gave her.
You refuse to erase the incident. She carves a black tally into the cracked seal: not a debt, a warning.
Keep the fault on the score
Two years have passed, but the report from your fracture returns with new arrests tied to the same network. She is waiting with both contradictory orders covered in notes.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_cros: The crowd panics, a patrol spots your exit, and the agent blames you for promising a route you could not hold.
Dockers and families vanish through three exits without exposing the relay. She pockets her detonator and yields the field to you.
You get the nearest families out, but several crates are seized and your disagreement becomes public among the couriers.
You open a clean corridor before the patrol arrives. She still disputes your priority, but admits nobody was left behind.
You reach the records, but the retreat turns into a brawl. Her wax seal splits when she drags you through a locked door.
You empty the ledger, divert the escort, and leave the depot blaming an internal failure. For the first time, she smiles at your plan.
The depot only half burns and you abandon part of the files. She faults your timing, not your choice of target.
You destroy the seizure lists before the guards return. She gives you half of her cracked red seal as a marker of debt.
You block her detonator and force a withdrawal. The operation remains unfinished, but no civilian becomes cover for your dispute.
An agent your age sets a detonator beside seizure ledgers while a quay evacuates its families. The patrol returns in minutes: she intends to burn the records, with or without you.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_last: The escort changes formation and traps you between the wagons. Several detainees escape, but you pay for the exit in injuries.
You draw the escort into an empty street, free the route, and hand the lists to the agent without losing a single name.
You open a route for the civilians but miss the wagon carrying the lists. She protects your retreat without hiding her frustration.
The civilians get clear before you hit the command wagon. She admits your order of priorities cost nothing from the objective.
She sees the lie one second too late. Your double game breaks the attack and leaves both of you surrounded.
The feint works without exposing her group. She acknowledges the calculation, then snaps her half of the seal in front of you.
She realizes you moved her like a piece and pulls her group before your plan can work.
Your false window draws the escort exactly where you wanted it. The objective falls, but she now knows your alliance was a tool.
The wagon holds and its guard drives you back into the crowd. She has to abandon the lists to prevent a massacre.
You drop the axle without touching the crowd. The agent grabs the lists while the rest of the escort chases an immobile wagon.
You break the escort without taking the lists. She covers you, but you lose the only proof linking the arrests.
The wagon gives way, the lists spill out, and the escort scatters. She admits the direct strike was the right read.
You give her the final call and run her cover without correcting it. She chooses the lists and protects the civilian exit herself.
A convoy carries arrest lists behind an armored wagon while civilians cross the same avenue. After all these years, the agent asks one thing: which priority commands the strike?
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_no_m: You pocket the seal and give her your private signal as a permanent address. She says the next debt will no longer need counting.
You snap your half of the seal and refuse any future shared channel. She accepts the break without promising to stop opposing you.
You put the cracked seal back on the table and propose that you keep counting wins. She adds one tally, then returns your half.
You part without a promise. The cracked seal stays on the table: enough memory to know why you might meet again, or oppose each other.
You keep your networks separate but exchange one last emergency code. The trust has a limit, not an expiration date.
Eighteen months later, the agent places both halves of the seal on an empty table. No coordinator from your first operation still runs this file. She asks what your rivalry becomes.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_same: You vouch for her route in front of the other agents. She agrees to share the next cipher instead of working around you.
Your instructions contradict each other at the worst moment and a courier is arrested. She takes back the cracked seal without a word.
Your forged order makes the escort move itself. The target walks out the front gate and the agent trusts you with half the cipher.
The plan holds just enough to save the target, but each of you blames the other for leaving an exploitable trace.
You turn two incompatible plans into a quiet extraction. She marks both your initials on the new code.
The coordinator rejects your power play and she exposes the flaw in your own plan in front of everyone.
The briefing follows your plan without argument. She lets you win the room and promises to judge the result in the field.
Nobody rules in your favor. You leave with two versions of the same order and no shared channel.
You secure control of the operation, but she keeps her own sources and stops sharing her codes.
Cut her out of the briefing
A year later, the cracked seal reappears on a briefing table. The agent wants to extract a printer across the roofs; your network proposes the drains. Only one instruction can go out.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_shar: You remove one contact from the shared list. She finds out later and understands that your trust now has a precise limit.
You chase the wrong shadow and return injured while she secures the contact alone.
You find the source, the watcher, and the exit before her. She accepts the loss with a sharp, almost proud salute.
She reaches the contact first and scratches a small tally into the cracked seal: one point for her.
You arrive first, but leave her a seat in the questioning. She scratches a tally on your side of the seal.
You miss a copied mark: a forged message passes through your code and forces the rendezvous to be abandoned.
You identify three poisoned messages and their source. She hands you the full matrix, keeping no copy outside your agreement.
You catch the leak too late to save the rendezvous. She does not blame you, but takes back half the code.
You spot the false punctuation before the exchange. Together, you turn the trap on the Government watcher.
Eighteen months later, your shared cipher carries an unfamiliar mark. Someone is copying your messages; follow the wrong trail and several relays will be exposed before dawn.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_spli: Your story embellishes one checkable detail. She dismantles it in three questions in front of the couriers who admired you both.
Even she laughs when the couriers vote for your operation. She keeps the score and demands the next difficult field.
Nobody decides and your competition becomes a distraction for the people who need the lessons.
You defend your result without erasing hers. She scratches another tally into the cracked seal and promises a rematch.
You reduce the damage to numbers too quickly and she leaves after naming the people your tally forgot.
Your debrief becomes the one procedure two feuding relays both adopt. The rivalry finally produces something worth passing on.
Your debriefs do not agree on what counted as success. The respect remains, but the method stays unresolved.
You find three shared mistakes and two complementary strengths. She keeps the sheet instead of tearing it up.
You report the two operations as one victory with shared responsibility. She stops publicly correcting your version.
Two years after your split operations, both reports arrive in the same envelope. The results are good, the costs differ, and everyone wants to know which method deserves to be copied.
event.active_rival_revolutionary_01_two_: Your argument stalls both teams long enough to lose the barge and burn the ledger access point.
You win both teams over to one plan without humiliating her. She yields command this time, not forever.
She rejects your order in front of the teams. You save the contacts, but the fracture becomes impossible to hide.
She follows your single order and the operation works, but afterward asks you not to confuse efficiency with obedience.
You trust her with the names while you divert the barge. She takes responsibility without claiming authority over your half of the plan.
You grab a decoy ledger and trigger the alarm. She abandons the barge to keep the contacts from being arrested.
You recover the ledger and send her the barge route before the alarm. Two objectives, no superior order needed.
You recover only part of the names. She covers your exit, then demands that the next command be split.
You identify the real ledger and extract it without touching her barge. She accepts that each of you won your objective.
An arrest ledger leaves an office while a barge of seized rations casts off. The agent wants the barge; you know the names will be distributed before noon.
event.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.ou: The coating holds through the pressure and current. Fish-Man Island appears in the depths.
event.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.te: At Sabaody, the ship is coated for the descent beneath the Red Line. The deep current leads toward Fish-Man Island.
event.career_civilian_01_fresh_start.cho: You separate the urgent issue from the old resentment and put the concessions in writing in front of the tenants. The quarrel loses at least one reason to restart tomorrow.
You open the pump, replace what can be replaced, and improvise the rest. It runs long enough to deliver the service people need.
You resurvey from the bank and mark the two passages that were fooling boatmen. The channel remains temperamental, but it is no longer blind.
You trace the crate that changed hands without a signature and correct the ledger before departure. Your first margin comes from a problem nobody wanted to own.
event.career_civilian_01_fresh_start.tex: A year after choosing to remain Civilian, nobody has handed you a uniform or a fixed post. Four paid problems need someone today: disputed cargo, a poorly charted channel, a broken pump, and a rent quarrel.
event.career_civilian_01_inherited_stake: You cover the difference instead of pushing it onto the people counting on you. The expense hurts, but your word becomes more credible.
You state what you can still guarantee and remove the rest before signing. The promise is smaller, but nobody discovers the limit afterward.
As the job closes, one unexpected expense remains yours. You can advance 500 Berrys to keep the promise exactly, or state the limit now before anyone commits further.
What Your Name Means Now — The Limit
You make the neighbors name what they actually refuse to give up. The compromise satisfies nobody completely, but the street stops being held hostage.
You strip the pump, salvage the sound parts, and put it back into service. The returning mechanism finally drowns out the spectators' advice.
You walk the route, compare the conflicting markers, and return a usable survey. The next crossing leaves with fewer unknowns than the last.
You rebuild the accounts, get every transfer signed, and keep a small margin. The loaders now know whose name to look for when a deal is about to break.
A year into your active life, your name already circulates among people looking for someone reliable. On the same day, four problems reach you: cargo, a route, a pump, and a neighborhood dispute.
event.career_civilian_02_community_the_a: The attempt turns against you; the problem worsens and your judgment is challenged in public.
You turn the situation around cleanly. The result becomes an example others start citing.
You do not get the result you wanted. The immediate cost remains visible and trust slips.
Your approach holds. The problem recedes, and the people there remember that you took responsibility.
Form a chain to the homes
You attack the concrete mechanism. The fix is imperfect but solid enough to change the situation.
You favor movement and information. A path opens, at the cost of more uncertainty afterward.
Open a route across the roofs
You route the problem through accounts and commitments. The deal holds, but it creates a new expectation around you.
Pay hands to move the stalls
A fire catches behind the market and blocks the only alley to several homes. Merchants want their stalls saved; families shout that the passage must be cleared first.
event.career_civilian_02_craft_the_split: You put the people affected inside the decision. The result is slower, but harder to ignore.

The pump feeding a district with fresh water splits during a heat wave. Its owner wants a quick patch; residents demand a repair that will last.

event.career_civilian_02_fallback.text: A storm closes the port for six days. Casual work vanishes, prices rise, and your landlord wants their share before nightfall.
event.career_civilian_02_fallback.title: The Week Without Wages
event.career_civilian_02_horizon_the_pas: You carry the commitment through. The people depending on you do not pay for the change of plan.
You state clearly what remains possible and what no longer is. Trust suffers less than if you had bluffed.
Your first move is not enough: one detail still blocks the course. Everyone waits to see whether you absorb the cost now or narrow the promise.
