You push the basin away from the customer. It slides to your mother, who understands exactly what you are reacting to.
You pull your hands out and splash the rim. The customer steps back again; your mother puts down her coins to look at you.
Pull your hands from the water
You cling to your mother's leg. She steps between you and the customer before answering his demand.
A customer pushes the washbasin away after seeing your Fish-Man hands in it. Your mother is still holding his change; he demands another basin before accepting his order.
event.family_civilian_01_giant_narrow_co: You pin the board with one foot while your father serves the customer. It holds just long enough to finish the order.
Hold the board with your foot
You pull your knee away and refuse to stay wedged under the counter. Your father moves the order instead of forcing you into the space.
You shove the stool away from the counter. Your father understands the patch is not enough and serves the customer standing with you beside him.
The counter tilts as soon as your father adds the board. The customer pulls back his basket: either the order is served now or the furniture is taken apart in front of him.
You pat the board your father just wedged in. It shakes enough to make the customer's basket move back.
Your knee nudges the stool into the counter. Your father immediately sees the added board still leaves too little room.
Nudge the stool with your knee
You reach over the too-low counter. Your father stops before you can knock over the waiting order.
In the small family shop, your Giant knee already knocks beneath a counter built for humans. Your father wedges a board under the table while a customer waits for an order.
event.family_civilian_01_household_fallb: You hold the small wedge the neighbor gives you while he lifts the hinge. He takes it back before the next strike.
You drag the parcel away from where the hammer is falling. The adults finally clear a safe space around you.
Drag the parcel from the hammer
You drop the wedge and back away into the room. The neighbor stops involving you and finishes the repair with the courier.
Drop the wedge and back away
The neighbor slips the hammer under the hinge while the courier sets the parcel down. Every strike risks breaking the wood even further.
You slap the shutter with your palm. It barely moves, enough to make the waiting courier laugh.
You grab the hammer handle left too close to you. The neighbor gently takes it back and moves it from the edge.
You push the parcel on the floor toward the light. The courier catches it and shows the neighbor the entrance is still blocked.
Push the parcel toward the window
In the morning, the household shutter refuses to rise and blocks the only window to the street. A neighbor brings a hammer; the first delivery of the day is already waiting at the door.
event.family_civilian_01_orphan_supper_k: You place the key in the baker's hand. He sighs, then says he will keep you tonight and look for another door tomorrow.
Give the key to the baker
You pull the blanket toward the neighbor. She takes it with you still wrapped in it and makes the adults deal with tonight before tomorrow.
Offer the blanket to the neighbor
You tuck the key under your blanket and refuse to give it back. The adults realize their back-and-forth already costs you something.
Hide the key under the blanket
The baker counts the occupied beds while the neighbor folds your blanket. They discuss your next roof like a delivery that still needs an address.
You offer the key to the neighbor. She does not take it right away and looks to the baker to see who will open the next door.
Offer the key to the neighbor
You close your fingers around the key. The neighbor stops talking long enough to make sure you do not put it in your mouth.
You leave the table and crawl toward the baker. He holds you against his leg while the neighbor folds your blanket.
After supper, a neighbor sets a key on the table and reminds the baker he is only housing you until tomorrow. No adult wants you outside; none can keep you without a cost.
event.family_civilian_01_poor_patched_ro: You hold the small dry sack against you while your father moves the rest. The landlord has to wait until the flour is safe.
You bang the rim when the water rises. Your father leaves the landlord's notebook alone and empties the bucket first.
You reach until your father picks you up. The landlord keeps his notebook open, but the negotiation waits behind your immediate need.
The landlord points to the date in his notebook. Inside, the bucket is nearly overflowing and the flour must stay dry until the morning market.
You grab a flour sack and tug it away from the water. Your father comes to help you, leaving the landlord waiting in the doorway.
You push the bucket toward the drip with your foot. Your father rights it without taking his eyes off the landlord.
Push the bucket under the leak
You cry when the landlord raises his voice. Your father picks you up with one arm and the argument changes tone immediately.
A short rain comes through the patched roof and fills a bucket beside your bed. Your father moves the flour sacks while the landlord is already asking for rent at the door.
event.family_civilian_01_two_parents_ren: You place the coin in your father's hand. He keeps it by the receipt while your mother points out the pot still has to last.
Give the coin to your father
You drop the coin into the pot. Your mother smiles despite herself; your father retrieves it without hiding that he disagrees.
Drop the coin into the pot
You refuse to open your hand. Your parents have to stop treating you like a tie-breaker and make the decision themselves.
Keep the coin in your fist
Your father lines up the coins beside the receipt. Your mother sets the cracked pot next to it: paying one now means making the other wait.
You pat the cracked pot with your palm. Your mother steadies it; your father immediately looks at the receipt under the bowl.
You grab the large coin in the middle of the table. Your parents stop arguing to keep it from falling.
You slide the receipt out from under the bowl. Your father takes it back while your mother brings the pot beside the coins.
Your mother slips a rent receipt under a bowl to keep it from blowing away. Your father wants to pay today; she wants to keep enough Berrys to replace a cracked cooking pot.
event.family_civilian_01_wealthy_shop_ke: You choose the largest key and offer it to your father. He takes it as a game, not as your opinion on the business.
Offer the large key to your father
You offer a key to the employee still waiting on his feet. Your mother laughs and finally asks which storeroom actually makes his work harder.
Offer a key to the employee
You press the keyring to your belly. The adults have to come to you and the business argument loses its urgency for a few seconds.
The employee keeps the keyring extended while the adults compare sales, wages, and repairs. Everyone is waiting to know which storeroom opens first.
You nearly pull off a small key and offer it to your mother. Your father notices before the employee takes the ring back.
Give a key to your mother
You shake the keyring until every key jingles. The adults stop comparing papers and look at which one you grabbed.
You drop the keyring on the floor. The employee crouches to pick it up, interrupting the expansion argument.

Before opening, an employee brings the keyring to the adults running the family business. Three doors lead to three full storerooms; they are already arguing about which one should be expanded this year.
event.family_civilian_02_enterprise_fall: You keep the measuring cord taut to the wall while the courier turns the crate. He finds the missing angle without emptying the whole shop.
You carry only the light boxes to the pavement. The adults move the heavy load and keep the task at your scale.
You sit against the wall and leave the adults to solve their delivery. They stop asking you where to move goods too heavy for you.
The courier measures the doorway again and taps the crate. It is only a hand’s width too wide to pass without taking everything apart.
You point to a gap behind a smaller stack. An employee checks whether moving a few boxes would clear the angle.
Point to the space by the wall
You duck under the corner of the crate sticking through the doorway. The courier immediately sees where it actually catches.
You point to the door you remember from the old keyring. An employee immediately checks whether that storeroom can take the smaller boxes.
Point out the small storeroom behind the crate
You push a small box out of the way. The adults stop you before the big stack, but realize a corner of floor has opened up.
An oversized delivery blocks the entrance to the family workplace. The courier refuses to unpack in the street; inside, no one wants to move the goods already stored.
The Parcel That Will Not Fit
event.family_civilian_02_family_room_fal: You put the visible screws in the little jar and stop there. The adult finishes the rest as the plates arrive.
Put the screws in their jar
You put your plate in the only clear space. The adults have to move their invoices if they want to keep talking shop through dinner.
Put your plate in the middle
You sit down without tidying anything else. The adult sighs, packs the tools away, and owns the mess as theirs.
Leave the tools where they are
A bill remains stuck under a plate and a screw rolls toward the edge. Dinner can begin only if someone restores a little order.
Make a Table Inside the Work
You gently pull the invoice from under the plate. The adult takes it and puts it off the table before serving.
Slide the invoice from under the plate
You push the tools to the edge first, like during earlier interrupted meals. The adult recognizes the gesture and clears a real place to eat.
Push the tools back like your father did
You catch the screw before it falls. The adult shows you the small jar for it while clearing space for a plate.
You push the twine into a pile to make room. The adult realizes dinner will never start if work keeps the whole table.
Pile the twine in one corner
Work has swallowed the family table: screws, bills, and twine occupy the plates’ place. An adult sweeps everything aside with one arm to serve dinner before the next order arrives.
event.family_civilian_02_father_customer: You trace the lines with your finger and find a mark your father forgot. He checks it himself before returning the item to the customer.
Look for a mark on the page
You push the book toward your father and refuse to decide. He checks every page again while the customer waits for his answer.
You put the repair back out of the customer's reach. Your father handles the dispute himself and asks you to leave the book alone.
Put the item back on the counter
Your father turns two pages and stops: no payment is recorded. The customer points to an ink stain she says she saw on the day she left the item.
You repeat that the customer 'already paid.' Your father closes the book for a second and asks when she remembers coming.
You point at the stain before your father turns the page. The customer seizes on it and insists that is exactly where he wrote down her payment.
You pull the repaired item toward you instead of handing it over. Your father and the customer have to finish their argument before it leaves the counter.
At four, you recognize the regulars before your father does. He searches his order book while a customer insists she already paid for the repair sitting on the counter.
event.family_civilian_02_fishman_slipper: You fill exactly the cone your mother shows you. She takes the payment herself and reminds the customer you are helping her, not working for him.
At every new request, you look to your mother before moving. The customer quickly learns he cannot order you around directly.
Route every request through your mother
You close the lid and keep your hands on it. Your mother takes over the whole order, slower but on her terms.
Your mother pushes the crate toward you and keeps the Berrys. This time the customer lists his order without going through her.
You repeat every word to your mother instead of serving the customer directly. She keeps the coins and takes over the conversation.
Repeat the order to your mother
You separate the slippery greens into small handfuls. The customer sees you are faster than the tongs and starts dictating his order to you.
You keep both hands on the crate without making his parcel. The customer has to wait for your mother to say what to take.
Keep your hands on the crate
Your mother gives you a crate of sea vegetables too slippery for the counter tongs. Your Fish-Man hands sort them quickly; an impatient customer asks you directly to prepare his order.
event.family_civilian_02_giant_rebuilt_b: You hold one end of the rope while your father shifts the bench. He finds an aisle where your stool and a customer can finally pass each other.
You back away from the corner where your father wants the stool. He gives up that measurement instead of making your body the part that has to adapt.
Refuse the corner that traps you
You push your stool all the way outside. Your father sees the new bench is pointless if you have to stay out for customers to pass.
Push the stool out of the shop
Your father pushes the wheel against the wall and measures the aisle with a rope. Two customers wait outside because they can no longer pass your stool.
A Workshop for More Than One Size
You move the wheel with your foot. Your father sees it blocks the passage much more than your stool does.
Roll the wheel with your foot
You try to squeeze between the raised bench and the wheel. Your shoulder nudges the furniture before you reach the stool.
Squeeze between the bench and wheel
You point to the two customers waiting in the doorway. Your father stops measuring and finally looks at the aisle the way they do.
Your father has raised the workbench with beams, but a cart wheel now blocks the customers’ path. The choice is between a workshop where you can help and a shop where others can move.
event.family_civilian_02_local_fallback_: You carry the marked parcel to the neighbor in front of the courier. The favor is simple and no one can claim another parcel was delivered.
Carry the parcel to the neighbor
You shut the door on the two remaining parcels. The neighbor gets his without turning your entryway into a depot for the whole street.
Keep the other two behind the door
You call after the courier instead of handing parcels out yourself. He comes back to manage the delivery he left with your family too quickly.
The courier stacks the parcels just under cover. One bears a neighbor’s mark, and that neighbor is already asking for the order from across the street.
You recognize the painted mark on one parcel and point it out. The neighbor across the street immediately starts asking for his.
You move the marked parcel away from the water without being asked. The courier realizes shelter has to be organized before distribution.
Keep the parcel away from the puddle
You take the smallest parcel and put it under cover. The courier thanks you before stacking the other two himself.
You hold the door with your foot while the courier slides the parcels inside. The neighbor can clearly see where his order has been stored.
The delivery cart loses a wheel in front of your home. The courier knows your family and asks you to keep three parcels dry while he looks for a repairer.
event.family_civilian_02_orphan_borrowed: You carry the folded blanket to the door. The caretaker promises another layer for tonight instead of pretending the cold is not a problem.
Carry the blanket to the door
You refuse to let go of one corner. The caretaker cuts an old lining for your bag before returning the rest to the other family.
Keep one corner of the blanket
You sit on it and refuse to move. The adults have to find a concrete replacement before they can take it back.
The guardian folds the blanket over her arms. Your small bag still has room, but nothing warm enough for the night ahead.
You point to the black letters on the corner. The caretaker explains they belong to another family returning tonight.
You wrap yourself in the marked blanket before it is folded. The caretaker has to look at you while explaining why she wants it back.
You put your small bag on the blanket as if to claim it. The caretaker stops before pulling it out from under the bag.
Put your little bag on it
The blanket you have used for months suddenly bears another family’s name in charcoal. The evening guardian says it must be returned before night, even though your next bed has nothing ready.
event.family_civilian_02_parents_expense: You run to the door and wave the apothecary inside. He agrees to prepare only what is needed while your parents keep enough for some coal.
You pull the blanket toward the sick person and look at the dead fire. Your parents see both needs are real and cut each purchase down.
Pull the blanket toward the sick person
You put the coin back in your mother's hand and leave the table. Your parents have to decide without making a four-year-old carry the choice.
Give the coin back to your mother
The apothecary waits at the door and the coal seller holds his cart in the street. Your parents refuse to pretend both costs can be covered.
You move the coin toward the empty coal sack. Your mother pins it with a finger and your father reminds her the medicine cannot wait long.
Put the coin on the coal sack
You put the large coin on the doctor's note. Your father nods; your mother immediately points to the nearly cold hearth.
Put the coin on the prescription
You hide the coin under your bowl. Your parents stop looking at you as a tie-breaker and resume the disagreement themselves.
Hide the coin under your bowl
Your parents place the last large coin of the week between a prescription and a coal bill. Your father wants the medicine; your mother argues that without heat no one will work tomorrow.
event.family_civilian_02_poor_credit_cha: You rub at an old mark your father says was already paid. The merchant checks, erases it himself, and frees a little space on the board.
You take the smaller rice sack the merchant agrees to release today. The household leaves with less rice, but without adding a full new line of debt.
You put the chalk back in his hand and step away from the counter. Your father has to negotiate without treating your gesture as consent.
The merchant holds the chalk between two fingers and shows you the slate. The rice sack stays behind his foot until someone accepts the new debt.
You point to the sack behind his foot. The merchant pulls it closer but keeps a hand on it until an adult answers.
You count the large visible chalk marks with your finger. The merchant corrects you, then shows your father the board is nearly full.
You close your hand around the chalk. The merchant asks for it back and your father steps in before the game turns into a new promise.
Hide the chalk in your palm
The merchant adds another chalk mark to your household account before handing over the rice sack. The old slate is almost full; he warns he will add nothing more after today.
event.family_civilian_02_scarcity_fallba: You hold the cloth taut while the adult ties the knot again. The last thread is enough for the button, not to reinforce the rest.
You stop the adult from using the last few inches on a hidden seam. They save it for the next urgent tear.
You take off the coat and refuse to stand by the needle. The adult finishes the stitching alone before giving it back.
The thread breaks on the first knot. There is just enough left to try once more, not enough to reinforce the whole seam.
You point to the button under the chair. The adult picks it up and decides to reuse it instead of looking for new cloth.
You hold the spool while the adult threads the needle again. They tell you not to move so the last length is not lost.
You move the spool away from the edge and any damp, like the sacks saved under the leak. The adult notices you protect what cannot easily be replaced first.
Keep the spool safe like the flour
You press your hand over the hole in the coat. The adult laughs, then sees one button will not be enough if the seam gives again.
Cover the hole with your hand
A button comes off your coat again. The person housing you takes out an almost empty spool and explains that a new garment must wait; this one has to last at least until the next market.
event.family_civilian_02_wealthy_wage_en: You carry the sealed envelopes one by one without opening them. The adults have to discuss the machine while the wages actually go to the employees.
You push away the large quote covering the names. The foreman rolls it up and the envelopes become the first thing visible on the desk again.
Give the quote back to the foreman
You take your toy and leave the office. The adults stop presenting the argument as something you are expected to decide now.
Leave the office with your toy
The envelopes remain sealed on the desk. The foreman unrolls the machine quote beside them, close enough to cover one employee’s name.
You carry the envelope you are shown to its owner. He thanks the child before asking the adults why his pay is late.
Carry an envelope to the employee
You sort the envelopes like cards without understanding the amounts. An employee notices one is missing and calls the foreman.
You repeat the word the foreman has been saying for five minutes. The adults laugh for a second, then the employee reminds them wages come before projects.
An employee brings the wage envelopes while a foreman asks for a new machine. The people running the family business can fund both, but not without delaying the expansion announced for months.
event.family_civilian_03_care_fallback_i: You bring a cushion, water, and the blanket. The traveler sleeps sitting up for one night without turning your bed into the family's default spare resource.
Make the chair ready for the night
You return with a bed next door for tonight. The traveler stays nearby without squeezing the household until someone else is displaced.
You refuse to give up your place or carry the problem. The adults figure out where the traveler will sleep themselves.
Leave the hosting to the adults
The traveler is already sitting by the entrance. A dry blanket hangs over the back of the only chair wide enough to sleep in.
A Bed That Does Not Exist
event.family_civilian_03_care_fallback.c: You go next door to ask whether they have a bed. The answer turns the welcome into a concrete problem instead of an endless debate.
Ask the neighbor if they have a bed
You put the dry blanket on the chair before the adults finish arguing. The traveler understands they can at least rest tonight.
Bring the blanket to the chair
You put your things on your bed before anyone volunteers it. The adults have to find a solution that does not automatically displace the child.
event.family_civilian_03_care_fallback.t: A distant relative arrives with an injured leg and asks for only one night. There is no free bed; someone will have to sleep in a chair or find another door for him.
event.family_civilian_03_child_runs_coun: You gather only the items you can identify safely and leave the complicated price to the adult. The customer leaves a little later, but with the right order.
You slide the coins behind the counter and wait. The customer can no longer pressure you by waving money under your nose.
Move the Berrys out of reach
You close the small counter gate until the adult returns. The customer complains, but no one can turn your help into full responsibility.
The customer sets down his Berrys and begins listing what he wants. The adult is still downstairs; answering now means making a real decision for the household.
You call the adult's name down toward the storeroom. The customer sighs but stops talking to you as if you already ran the shop.
You keep the Berrys separate until a clear line is written, like your father did after the payment dispute. The customer stops pressing you.
You keep your hand in front of the coins instead of taking them. The customer realizes he will have to wait for the adult to finish his order.
Keep the Berrys on the counter
You copy the three requested items onto a scrap of paper without touching the money. The adult can decide the rest when they return.
At seven, an adult lets you mind the counter while they fetch a crate downstairs. A customer pushes a complicated order toward you and says he is already late.
event.family_civilian_03_employees_know_: You count the overtime marks with the employee and find a missed line. The adult corrects the envelope in front of both of you.
You call in the person concerned before anyone decides for them. The difference is explained aloud instead of vanishing into the books.
You return the envelopes without agreeing to hand them out. The adults have to own the wage differences they created.
Return the whole stack to the manager
The employee makes you rebuild the stack in the right order. One envelope is lighter than last week and its owner is already waiting in the corridor.
You bring the lighter envelope to its owner instead of hiding it in the stack. They immediately ask why Berrys are missing.
Bring the light envelope to its owner
You read the names aloud one by one while rebuilding the stack. The employees correct two mistakes and the argument stops being only about abstract numbers.
You set the light envelope aside instead of burying it in the stack. The adults have to fix that one before you resume handing them out.
Hand out only the complete envelopes
You put it on top of the pile so it cannot disappear. The adult signing wages has to deal with it before moving on.
Keep the light envelope on top
An employee stops you before you put the wage envelopes on the wrong desk. He shows you the names and overtime notes on the back: every envelope belongs to someone you see each day.
event.family_civilian_03_fishman_backroo: You accept the tasks but keep the curtain open. The merchant protests, then lets the first customer see you doing the same work as everyone else.
You agree to help only if counter duties remain open to you. The merchant has to choose between your work and his discriminatory rule.
Demand the counter for the same tasks
You hand the apron back without stepping behind the curtain. The pay disappears with the offer, but your place in the street does not.
Give the apron back to the merchant
The merchant hangs the apron on a nail behind the curtain. The wage is fair; only the place he assigns you is the problem.
You point to the other shop helper and ask why your jobs would be different. The merchant can no longer hide behind 'difficult customers.'
Ask for the same job as the other child
You take the apron and wage offer to your mother before answering. The merchant realizes he cannot isolate you to impose his rule.
Route the offer through your mother
You take the apron and hang it in front of the curtain where customers can see it. The merchant has to explain why he wanted it behind.
Hang the apron on the counter side
You leave it there. The pay remains tempting, but the merchant has to decide whether he actually wants your help or only wants you hidden.
Leave the apron on the counter
At seven, a neighboring merchant offers you occasional work, then hands you an apron meant for the back room. He claims some customers are “not ready” to see a Fish-Man at the counter.
event.family_civilian_03_giant_delivery_: You reposition the rollers as the crate turns and call out when it nears the wall. The delivery gets through without closing the whole alley.
Guide the rollers through the turn
You refuse to start while younger children are still playing near the rollers. The neighbors clear the alley before the crate moves.
Clear the children from the alley
You ask to leave the crate at the start until the stalls close. The workers complain, but the neighborhood is not treated as an obstacle to bulldoze through.
Make the crate wait for a quieter hour
The workers set the crate on two rollers and neighbors already start moving their stalls. One bad maneuver will close the alley for everyone.
You ask the two neighbors whose stalls stick out most. They agree to move back a little if the crate goes through in one pass.
Ask the stalls to move back one step
You reuse the rope once used to adapt the workshop and mark the crate's width through the corner. The workers stop guessing by eye.
Measure with the old bench rope
You try turning the crate on the ground. It touches the wall before the corner, showing exactly where the alley is too narrow.
Turn the crate without lifting it
You mark the crate's width and turn in chalk on the ground. The workers see they can move two stalls instead of the whole street.
A heavy crate must cross an alley too narrow for you to carry it normally. The workers want to roll it; the workshop manager thinks the route can be changed without blocking the whole neighborhood.
event.family_civilian_03_neighbor_debt_c: You mark the return time in the book and give him the good screwdriver. If he is late, everyone will know tomorrow's repair is at risk.
Lend the good one until sunset
You give him the old screwdriver and keep the good one in the shop. The favor is real without sacrificing tomorrow's job.
You put both screwdrivers back in the drawer and close it. The neighbor leaves to find another solution instead of adding a debt to the old one.
The neighbor keeps his hand out. Behind him, his own shutter hangs crooked; at home, tomorrow’s repair is already written in the order book.
You point to the broken piece already waiting on the bench. The neighbor finally sees what the tool he wants is needed for.
You mark the promised return time on the doorframe like a debt that can be checked. The neighbor laughs less once the deadline is visible.
Mark the return time in chalk
You hide the screwdriver behind your back while the neighbor promises 'tonight' again. He has to speak to your family instead of only to you.
Hold the screwdriver behind your back
You offer the bent old screwdriver instead of the good one. He can patch his shutter without taking the tool needed for the paid repair.
The neighbor who still owes a sack of flour comes to borrow the household’s only good screwdriver. He promises to return it tonight; tomorrow morning, a paid repair depends on that exact tool.
The Screwdriver That Never Came Back
event.family_civilian_03_orphan_receipt_: You carry the box to all three adults and each adds what they remember paying. Your host finally gets a clear enough account to keep you for the month.
Carry the box to all three adults
You ask for one paper per week kept in the box. The adults agree to a rule simple enough for you to check yourself.
Ask for one receipt per week
You push the papers back toward the adults who created them. They have to settle their accounts without making you the accountant of your own housing.
Push the receipts back to the adults
She empties the receipts onto the table and adds an empty box. If the adults cannot agree, your next lodging will be decided before dinner.
You write your name on the empty box. The adult realizes the papers deciding where you live cannot keep being scattered.
Write your name on the box
You sort the receipts by paper color and recognize which adults wrote them. The woman hosting you can finally call each person by name.
You tie each receipt to a night someone actually housed you. Your host stops counting indistinct favors.
Ask for one paper per night
You put all three receipts together without deciding who is right. The box becomes at least one place the adults will all have to look.
Put all three receipts in the box
The woman housing you finds three receipts for your meals in different pockets. She wants to know who pays what before keeping you another month; no one has kept the account properly.
event.family_civilian_03_school_or_shift: You help until the next bell, then reopen your workbook in front of everyone. The household gets your help without swallowing the whole evening.
Work one hour, then reopen the book
You finish your homework while an adult takes the first order. Only then do you put on the apron.
Finish the homework before the till
You hand the apron back and keep the workbook open. The adults have to find another pair of hands for this order.
Give back the apron without closing the book
The notebook stays open by the till while work piles up. Finishing one before night means leaving the other to someone else.
You ask whether the help means ten minutes or until closing. No one can answer with just 'a little' anymore.
Ask how late you are needed
You finish the line you started before closing the workbook. The adult can clearly see what they are asking you to interrupt for the order.
Finish the line in the workbook
You push the tools just far enough to make a real place for the workbook, repeating the boundary set at the table years earlier. The adult understands before you answer.
Clear space for the workbook like a plate
You place the apron over the workbook without putting it on. The gesture leaves both obligations visible before you choose one.
Lay the apron over the workbook
An exercise book sticks out beneath your apron when a new order arrives. The teacher expects the work tomorrow; the household needs another pair of hands until closing.
event.family_civilian_03_trade_fallback_: You take his coins on condition he helps fix the handle now. The basket will be ready tomorrow and the old favor stops dragging on.
Take the coins and repair it together
You keep the basket at home and ask him to return with enough to cover the rest. Tomorrow's delivery is delayed, but the debt does not grow.
Keep the basket until it is fully repaired
You give his money back and ask for a repaired basket, not another promise. He leaves carrying the problem he caused.
The merchant sets two small coins on the broken basket. They will not cover a new handle, but refusing means reopening an old favor.
You point to where the basket should be ready for tomorrow morning. The merchant sees his delay is already affecting another job.
Point to the empty delivery spot
You lift the basket by the handle and it gives way immediately. The merchant stops claiming it will 'hold tomorrow.'
You put his two small coins on the broken wood. Even at seven, the gap between the repair and his offer becomes obvious.
Put his two coins on the handle
A merchant finally returns the household’s large borrowed basket, but one handle is broken. The morning delivery depends on it, and he offers to pay later rather than repair it now.
event.family_civilian_03_work_fallback_i: You take apart the two simple pieces while the adult handles the delicate part. The repair moves forward without swallowing the whole evening.
You tie a note to the repair and sit back down. The neighbor gets a guaranteed place tomorrow, not a family that cancels dinner.
You give the item back and tell the neighbor to return at opening. Dinner stays dinner even if the customer is unhappy.
The neighbor sets the item on the counter without pressing. Behind you, the plates are already served and someone calls that dinner is getting cold.
event.family_civilian_03_work_fallback.c: You carry the broken item to the adult closing the shop. They can see the problem without fully reopening the counter.
Carry the item to the adult
You inspect the break under the lamp and say it is not as simple as it looks. The neighbor stops insisting it will 'only take ten minutes.'
Inspect the break under the lamp
You place the repair beside the meal so it will not be forgotten tomorrow. The neighbor leaves without turning the evening into another hour of work.
Set the item beside the plate
event.family_civilian_03_work_fallback.t: The shutter is already half lowered when a neighbor arrives with a broken item he needs tomorrow. The household promised an evening without work; the repair would still take less than an hour.
event.family_civilian_04_apprenticeship_: You offer two trial days before accepting the full schedule. The artisan holds the place and the household can see what your absence actually changes.
You accept the apprenticeship while keeping one fixed day for home. No one gets everything they wanted, but the schedule can work.
Keep one fixed day for the household
You return the letter without insulting the offer. The artisan gives the place to someone else and the household knows the choice has a real cost.
Turn down the place this year
The letter stays open between your notebook and the order book. The craftsperson wants an answer before offering the place to another child.
You ask to see the workshop before promising three days a week. The artisan agrees to a short visit instead of demanding a blind answer.
You read the three days listed in the letter and compare them with the days the household relies on you most. The conflict becomes concrete.
You place on the letter the workbook you refused to abandon at seven. The artisan understands the apprenticeship will also have to leave room for school.
You tuck the letter into your workbook instead of answering in front of everyone. The household has to give you at least until tonight.
Fold the letter into your workbook

At ten, a craftsperson from another district brings an apprenticeship letter. They want you three days a week; the household would lose your help on those days, but you would learn a trade outside the family.
event.family_civilian_04_business_expans: You suggest keeping the room flexible until a real need appears. The expansion moves forward without writing your job ten years in advance.
You ask that the first shop keep enough staff before the second opens. The employees get a transition plan instead of a vague promise.
You refuse to have any room reserved for you before you have chosen a trade. The adults can expand the business, not decide your place inside it.
Refuse any room in your name
On the second-shop plan, a small room has your name penciled in. An employee points to the current shop counter: nobody has yet been named to stay there during construction.
The Office Already Has Your Name
You point to the main counter with no name beside it. An employee answers before the managers and reveals where the plan actually lacks someone.
Ask who will run the first counter
You erase your name from the small room and ask why it was already reserved for you. The adults have to separate the expansion from your future.
Erase your name from the future office
You place an old corrected wage envelope over the room drawn in your name. The managers remember expansion means little if the first shop loses its people.
Put the corrected envelope on the plan
You redraw 'your office' as shared storage. The adults realize the plan can change before assigning you a role.
Change the office into shared storage

In the family business office, the managers unroll plans for a second shop. Your name is already written on a future floor, while employees wait to learn who will run the first counter during the expansion.
The Plan Drawn for the Second Shop
event.family_civilian_04_enterprise_race: You propose keeping the price if the customer accepts a deadline the shop can actually meet. He chooses the date over an impossible discount.
You make the adults count what the deadline would cost in late hours. The customer sees his discount would be paid by workers, not an abstract margin.
Calculate the cost of late hours
You return the paper unsigned and without banking on future orders. The good customer remains a customer, but this bad contract does not become your standard.
The customer places his pen on the price line and promises more orders later. Today, nothing guarantees that promise.
A Good Customer, a Bad Contract
You ask where the 'future orders' he promises are written. The client admits none are guaranteed on paper.
Ask which promise is written down
You put the lower price beside the shorter deadline. Even without running the business, you can see the customer is asking for two concessions at once.
You move the pen away from the price line and let the adults talk without a rushed signature.
Move the pen off the price
A regular customer brings a larger contract than usual, then hesitates over the terms. He wants the work, but only if the household accepts an unrealistic deadline and a lower price.
The Contract Refused at the Counter
event.family_civilian_04_fishman_counter: You cross out the sentence and return the contract. The merchant accepts the same price without the restriction because he genuinely wants the goods.
You ask for the contract to state that roles do not depend on Race. The merchant signs under a rule opposite to the one he tried to impose.
You tear the page before the household can sign. The large contract disappears, but the humiliating condition does not enter your working rules.
The trader taps the added clause and promises the same price. The contract stays open in front of you so you can answer before it is signed.
You ask which specific customer demanded not to see you. The merchant cannot name one, and his excuse weakens.
You lay the old apron once meant to hide you over the sentence trying to do the same thing again. The merchant sees exactly what history he is repeating.
Lay the old apron over the clause
You circle the handwritten sentence in charcoal until it becomes the most visible part of the contract. The merchant can no longer pass it off as a detail.
You push the pen away from the signature line. The household gets time to answer before one merchant's habit becomes a written rule.
Push the pen away from the contract

A trader offers the household a regular contract, then adds by hand that you will work out of customers’ sight. He says it will “avoid trouble”; the person signing for the household asks why your face appears in his terms.
event.family_civilian_04_giant_public_de: You move only when each merchant confirms their stall is clear. The load crosses above the crowd without turning the market into a spectacle forced on everyone.
You refuse to carry above a packed crowd. The delivery is late, but it crosses after most customers have left.
Wait for the square to clear
You refuse to let your size automatically replace safe transport. The adults reorganize the delivery with the cart and several porters.
The merchants clear a narrow line between their awnings. The load is strapped; the remaining question is whether you carry it through or wait until closing.
You ask the three most exposed merchants to raise their awnings. They agree if the crossing happens in one attempt.
Ask to clear the low awnings
You reuse the rollers-and-markings method instead of relying only on your strength. The merchants take part in the passage instead of merely enduring it.
You lift the load just enough to feel its balance without moving. The straps pull to one side and the merchants see the risk before the start.
You mark in chalk where your feet will go. The vendors move only what actually intrudes into that lane.
Mark a path on the ground
An important delivery must cross the market at its busiest hour. Your size lets you carry the load above the stalls, but a fall would cause more damage than an ordinary cart.
event.family_civilian_04_landlord_deadli: You identify the crates no longer in use and the household sells them first. It does not cover everything, but it protects the tool that earns money.
You show the landlord that removing the tool would make payment even harder. He agrees to a shorter extension rather than destroying the income source.
Keep the tool and negotiate the room
You stop the household from promising a date it knows it cannot meet. The landlord leaves without an easy guarantee, but no one adds a lie to the debt.
The ledger remains open on the table. Behind the landlord, the threatened room holds a bed, crates, and the household’s most profitable tool.
Keep One Room of the Home
You ask the landlord exactly how much is overdue, not how much he would like. He has to give a number before talking about taking the room back.
You measure the bed, crates, and the most profitable tool against the walls. Selling things or losing the room stops being abstract.
Measure what fits in the room
You recall the old chain of favors and repairs that never quite settled. The household drops the idea of adding another vague favor to the rent.
Refuse to pay with another favor
You copy the red date onto the wall by the door. The whole household can now see how many days remain before the room is taken.
Mark the date on the wall
The landlord circles a date in red in his ledger: after that day, he takes back the rear room. The household can pay part of it, sell equipment, or ask for more time.
event.family_civilian_04_neighborhood_di: You recount only the moment you actually saw and refuse to fill in the rest. The neighbors have to settle the unknown part without using your name as a verdict.
You propose each pays part of the repair now and argues about blame later. The tool stops being unusable while they fight.
Get the tool repaired before the argument
You say your family will not witness what it did not see. The neighbors leave carrying their dispute instead of dropping it at the shop.
Take your family’s name out of it
One neighbor sets the broken tool on the sill; the other demands that you confirm who had it last. The whole street is listening now.
You ask each neighbor to describe the loan without the other interrupting. The customers hear two stories that do not match.
You find on the tool the mark added after the screwdriver that did not come back. The neighbors have to compare their memories with a real trace.
You inspect where the tool broke before listening to either story. An old visible crack makes at least one accusation less convincing.
You take the tool out of the street. The argument continues, but no one can wave it at customers as evidence.
Take the tool inside the shop
Two neighbors argue outside the shop over a broken tool and name your family as witness. Customers slow down to listen; answering could settle it or tie your household name to their quarrel.
event.family_civilian_04_orphan_signatur: The adult hosting you signs for the school year after the secretary limits the obligation. You get the place without pretending they become your parent.
You get one main signature and two notes confirming who can be called as backup. The school has a responsible adult without erasing your real network.
Attach notes from the other two
You refuse to let an adult sign while pretending to be something they are not. The secretary keeps your file open while looking for an honest administrative solution.
The clerk pushes the form to the edge of the desk. Without a signature today, the place goes back to the waiting list tomorrow.
You ask the secretary what the signer would actually be responsible for. He explains calls, absences, and obligations instead of merely pointing at the blank line.
Ask what the signature commits to
You take the form to the adult hosting you this week. They can no longer leave the signature as an abstract problem for the other two.
Take the form to your latest host
You put down the box that has tracked your housing for years. The secretary sees real responsibilities even if they do not fit under one name.
You write the names of all three adults who hosted you this year. The secretary finally sees the problem is not a total lack of help, but the lack of one sole guardian.
Write all three names in the margin

A school accepts your late enrollment, but the form requires the signature of a stable guardian. Three adults have housed you this year; at first none agrees to be the one the administration will call afterward.
event.family_civilian_04_scarcity_care_f: You set aside the medicine money first and the household negotiates the rest separately. Treatment begins without pretending the whole bill disappeared.
The doctor accepts one delivery to the clinic for part of his visit. The debt becomes limited, dated, and verifiable.
You reject a schedule that would consume the next weeks of income. The doctor keeps the bill open, but the household does not sign up for its next crisis.
The bill is folded beneath the medicine box. The doctor is only waiting to know what form the payment will take.
Treat the Illness Without Emptying the House
You ask what concrete service could replace part of the payment. The doctor names a specific delivery instead of a vague debt.
Ask what service he would accept
You ask the doctor to separate the cost of medicine from the visit. The household can finally see which part cannot be postponed today.
You write the proposed due dates directly on the bill. The household can see whether the plan is realistic before agreeing.
Write the due dates on the bill
The doctor leaves a bill after a short visit and refuses to remove the basic medicine. The household can pay in installments, offer work in exchange, or delay another expense.
event.family_civilian_04_work_family_fal: You help with the simple part so the shop can close sooner, then you return together with the plate still warm.
You turn the sign and the adult eats with the family before reopening. The customer waits, but the evening does not vanish entirely into work.
Close for ten minutes to eat
You leave the plate by the tool and go home without working. The adult can choose to finish, but that choice does not automatically become yours.
Leave the plate and go home
The plate is already wrapped in a cloth. Outside, the workplace light is the only one still burning in the street.
You ask the customer directly whether they can wait ten minutes for a hot meal. Their answer stops the adult pretending there is no choice.
Ask the customer to wait ten minutes
You take the wrapped plate across the street. The adult sees dinner arrive in the middle of the urgent order.
Carry the plate to the shop
You refuse to clear the absent person's place. The empty chair stays visible until they return or accept missing dinner.
Keep the chair empty at the table
Dinner starts without the adult who is still closing the workplace. An urgent order pushed closing back; someone suggests carrying a plate there instead of waiting any longer.
event.family_civilian_05_adapted_place_i: You keep a place already adapted to you and the habit of demanding practical solutions.
The household announces that the adjusted setup and rules will remain available to any worker who needs them.
You leave without claiming the place. What stays with you is the concrete precedent that an organization can change when it harms or excludes.
The changes remain even if you leave. The question is whether they become your personal access, a rule for everyone, or simply proof that the household learned to change.
event.family_civilian_05_adapted_place.c: You ask whether the changes will remain after you leave. The household has to decide whether they were only for you or because the old setup was wrong.
Ask whether the adaptation stays without you
You ask for the useful adaptation to become a general posted rule. What began with your body can remain an improvement without belonging to you.
Ask to post the rule for everyone
You walk the adapted route once more as you have for years. What used to be a problem has become an ordinary rule of the place.
Walk the adapted route once more
You remove your name from one posted instruction. If the rule is good, it should survive without being framed as a favor to you.
Remove your name from the instructions
event.family_civilian_05_adapted_place.t: Before you leave, the household walks you through the adjusted passages, posted service instructions, and redistributed tasks. Nothing forces you to stay, but the house has learned to change around your body instead of deciding for you.
event.family_civilian_05_business_stewar: The business turns its name into a recommendation rather than a reserved job.
The managers liquidate a clearly defined share of your stake in the business to fund your own departure.
The commercial neighborhood now knows you as someone authorized to speak for the family business.
The page waits between employee accounts and supplier accounts. Writing something here does not bind your whole future, but it defines what the business owes you.
You ask what the business actually owes you if you take no position. The adults have to separate trust, recommendation, and capital.
Ask what your share is worth
You ask for the ledger of the shop that already exists before discussing inheritance. The managers have to show what actually works, not just what they plan.
Ask for the first shop’s ledger
You write 'no position' under your name. The managers have to start from that blank instead of turning the page into automatic succession.
You pass the ledger to the employees before signing it. Their reaction is a reminder that your inheritance affects the people who work here too.
Pass the ledger to the employees

The business ledger now contains a page with your name but no job written beside it. The managers offer you the choice to preserve the business, learn elsewhere, or take limited capital to begin differently.
event.family_civilian_05_community_fallb: The neighborhood speaks about you because it knew you through concrete situations, not because an institution celebrates you.
You keep a quiet network of doors and correspondents without turning it into public reputation.
You turn received help into a specific future obligation, concrete enough to bring the neighborhood back later.
The round ends at your old door. You can turn those ties into visible reputation, a quiet network, or a specific obligation toward the people who helped you.
What the Neighborhood Keeps of You
You ask each person what they would actually do for you later. The answers are modest, but specific enough to be kept.
You keep only the letters that name a concrete form of help. Two neighbors rewrite their promises so they become doors you can actually use.
Refuse letters with no specific commitment
You sort the letters by the doors they actually open. The ties become a readable small network instead of a pile of good wishes.
You return the letter promising 'anything you need' without naming anything. The neighbor rewrites it with a real address and a specific kind of help.
At thirteen, several neighbors use a delivery round to hand you a letter, a recommendation, or a simple “come see us again.” Nothing is grand; every gesture comes from a relationship actually lived.
The Last Round Through the Neighborhood
event.family_civilian_05_father_boundary: Your father grips the travel bag before handing it back. His support remains in your relationship even when the shop door closes behind you.
You refuse both bags and the disagreement remains real. You part without false forgiveness, but without pretending the bond is gone.
Your bond with your father grows stronger because you finally name the difference between helping him and working under his authority.
Stay his partner, not his employee
Your father keeps his hands away from both bags. He asks only what the two of you should promise each other before your childhood ends.
You give him back the work key before touching either bag. Your father understands the conversation has to be about your relationship, not your next shift.
Give him back the work key
You remind your father of the nights work left his chair empty. He understands the travel bag is also about the time you still want to share.
Recall the empty chair at dinner
You open the travel bag and ask your father what actually belongs in it. For once, he helps you leave instead of teaching you how to stay.
Pack the travel bag with him
You set the two bags side by side until they touch. Your father sees leaving does not automatically erase the possibility of returning.
Set both bags side by side
Your father closes the shop early and sets two bags by the door: one for working tomorrow, the other for leaving when you decide. He refuses to choose yours.
event.family_civilian_05_household_savin: The merchant strikes out the oldest line in front of you. The debt leaves the books and the neighborhood sees the household kept its word.
You leave the money with the household and keep the certainty that a future emergency already has an answer.
The household gives you a liquid share large enough to begin without erasing years of caution.
The coins and small notes are counted three times. Everyone knows exactly which expenses were postponed to fill this box.
You ask which debt waited the longest so this box could exist. A specific name finally replaces years of 'later.'
You set aside the next rent payment before discussing your share. The household knows exactly what it can pass on without recreating the old emergency.
Set aside the next rent first
You count only what the household could give you without emptying the box. The rest stays visible as shared security.
Count the share that could be yours
You lower the lid without taking a coin. The household has to decide whether this reserve opens for you or for itself.
The household finally opens the small savings box hidden beneath a floorboard. It holds enough to solve one real problem, not enough to change everything: debt, departure, or emergency reserve.
event.family_civilian_05_livelihood_fall: You claim nothing now and let the household keep its share. You leave the door open to a future conversation instead of forcing a settlement today.
Your share becomes a small real stake, useful enough to matter without buying an entire future.
You take no money, but the household explicitly recognizes your right to return for work.
The accounts are clear enough to avoid an argument. The household lets you decide whether your share becomes money, future access, or simply a promise to return.
You ask what the household would guarantee a year from now if you leave with nothing today. The answer has to become more specific than 'we'll see.'
Ask what would still be here if you returned
You write down the tools, debts, and obligations that must stay with the household. Your share becomes clearer precisely because not everything can leave with you.
Write down what cannot be passed on
You make two piles: what can actually leave with you and what must stay to keep the household running. The share stops being symbolic.
Separate the cash from the tools
You count again so you know what exists, then push your share back. The household has to distinguish declining now from giving it up forever.
Count it again without claiming anything

The household empties a small cashbox reserved for work expenses and separates what truly belongs to you. There is no ceremony or title: only a few resources and the question of what you still owe the place.
event.family_civilian_05_neighborhood_na: You refuse new debt; what remains is only a local reputation for reliability.
You gain concrete access to credit because the neighborhood has watched your actions, not because of your social class.
You leave one clearly defined reciprocal favor with the merchants who watched you grow up.
The book is not official, but several merchants recognize the page. What you accept today will decide how your name travels when you are no longer here every morning.
You ask which shops actually honor this page. Three names are given; the neighborhood trust stops being a vague promise.
Ask who actually honors the credit
You ask the ledger to record the time you refused to lend your name as a verdict. Local trust now includes the boundaries you set.
Record the dispute you refused to judge
You read the few lines under your name: favors returned, delays owned, disputes settled. The credit rests on specific acts.
You close the ledger without accepting new debt. The merchant has to explain what remains if you refuse the credit itself.
After years of favors and arguments, a merchant opens his credit book to a page bearing your name. He makes clear that this trust belongs to you, not automatically to your whole family.
Your Name in the Neighbors’ Book
event.family_civilian_05_orphan_network_: You keep an imperfect but real network of people who accepted concrete obligations.
You reduce the network to one reliable person future employers or landlords can contact.
You leave without keeping a fallback address. The decision feeds your pride without erasing the people who actually housed you.
The paper passes from hand to hand. One address offers a bed, another occasional work, the third only someone who will answer a letter.
You ask which of the three adults would actually answer a call for you six months from now. Each has to answer for themselves.
You add the adult who once agreed to sign for school. Their address becomes a responsibility already proven, not just another promise.
You read the three addresses and recognize what each actually offers: a bed, work, or simply someone who will answer.
You fold the paper without thanking anyone too quickly. The adults understand addresses only matter if they remain true after you leave.
Fold the paper into your pocket
Three adults who housed you each write an address on the same sheet of paper. None claims to be your parent; they are only offering specific doors you can knock on later.
event.family_civilian_05_two_parent_futu: You keep recognized access to family work without turning the choice into an imposed career.
You write a third plan that belongs to neither parent's camp. Your parents now have to learn to discuss a future they did not prepare.
You leave with a concrete address and an imperfect but real family agreement.
Your father corrects the cost of the first plan; your mother adds an address to the second. They ask you to choose your future without turning their disagreement into one parent’s victory.
You ask each what they would give up to make the other plan work. The argument leaves principles behind and returns to real costs.
You reuse the idea of a limited trial instead of a permanent choice. Your parents have to judge the plan by what it produces, not by their separate fears.
Propose a one-month trial away from home
You swap the two plans in front of your parents to break their camps. Each has to argue for the option they were criticizing a minute ago.
You place a blank sheet between the two plans. Your parents realize they may not have written every option.
Your parents place two plans side by side: take on more family work or continue training elsewhere. Neither claims one is more honorable; they simply disagree about the risk.
event.family_civilian_05_workshop_inheri: You return the key. The workshop's grey cat follows you to the door and refuses to go back to its crate.
The family hands you the savings set aside for your first departure.
You keep access to the workshop. Along with the key, your family gives you a small toolkit so the craft can travel with you.
The key stays between you as the last customer leaves. No one asks you to choose a profession today; only what this door will mean after you leave.
You ask whether the key stays yours when you leave or only while you help here. The family has to define access before talking about a trade.
Ask who could take the key back
You place the apprenticeship letter from three years ago beside the key. The family has to discuss the workshop as one access among others, not the only serious future.
Set the apprenticeship letter beside the key
You try the key in the workshop door. It still turns: the access is real before anyone decides what it should mean.
Try the key in the lock
You set the key beside the till instead of taking it. The gesture forces the family to state what it is actually passing on.
Set the key beside the till
At thirteen, the family places the workplace key in front of you. It is not a career promise: it only means you can return, help, learn, or lock the door behind you.
event.family_civilian_adult_01_father_le: You answer without polite cover. The conversation gets harsher, but finally precise.
You propose a rhythm you can actually keep. The bond becomes more reliable without turning back into work.
Set a regular time to write
You ask him to stop using orders as an excuse to write. He takes it badly, then accepts that your relationship deserves its own language.
Keep work out of your letters
You refuse to manufacture closeness your life cannot support. Your father keeps the letter, but at least the distance is no longer disguised.
Your father crossed out the old “hours owed” column. In its place he left a blank space where you can write what you still owe each other as adult parent and child.
You leave the receipt folded and read what he finally dares to ask without hiding behind the counter.
Read his lines without checking the price
You write the first words before you have finished reading. The tone of your answer becomes a decision of its own.
The price and date pull you straight back to the shop. His letter feels less abstract with the work laid out in front of you.

A letter from your father contains a receipt from the old shop, folded around a few hurried lines. He is not asking you to return: he wants to know whether that work still belongs between you or only to childhood.
The Receipt Folded by Your Father
event.family_civilian_adult_01_home_post: You answer once without giving a new address. The distance becomes deliberate rather than accidental.
You leave one precise way to reach you without promising where you will be next.
You send a limited amount for one named expense. The gesture helps without rebuilding an unlimited family debt.
The package contains no order to come home. It only forces you to decide whether the old address remains somewhere people can still reach you through.
An Address That Is No Longer a Leash
You answer the person who actually found you, without pretending the whole neighborhood speaks with one voice.
You separate memories from actual requests. Only one thing truly needs an answer now.
You count the ports and offices the package crossed. Distance becomes a concrete history instead of vague silence.

A small package finally catches up with you after several redirects. It comes from your old neighborhood: a paid bill, a clipping, and three lines show that family life kept moving without waiting for your return.
The Postmark From the Old Address
event.family_civilian_adult_01_two_paren: You show them what your adult life actually costs. The conversation leaves assumptions behind and returns to concrete limits.
You cover one named expense, not an endless obligation. Your parents know what the gesture means and what it does not promise.
You write down what you will not carry from afar. The disagreement stings, but no one can later pretend the promise was different.
Write a limit in the margin
Because the trust still holds, you return to limits you had already learned to set together.
The ledger does not ask you to resume your old life. It only shows what your parents still carry, what they stopped carrying, and what they actually expect from you.
What You Still Pay for One Another
You wait for a moment when you can answer without treating home like one more task between others.
Keep it closed until things are quiet
You read their letter first. The accounts then become concrete proof of what changed at home.
Read the letter before the accounts
You look at the numbers first. The margins show what your parents stopped paying for you after you left.
Open the ledger before the letter

A parcel catches up with your route, both parents’ handwriting on the label. Inside, the old household ledger carries new expenses and one question: what still counts as “home” now that your life is elsewhere?
Two Handwritings on the Same Parcel
event.family_civilian_adult_02_career_na: You make clear that your service grants your family no status and imposes no institutional loyalty on them.
Separate the uniform from the family name
You refuse to let the neighborhood turn your family into an imaginary crew. That flag is your choice, not their inheritance.
You tell them what concerns them and nothing more. Your family gets facts instead of a role to perform.
You give them enough truth to understand the risk, not enough to turn them into unwilling keepers of operational details.
You cannot make your career private again, but you can decide what explanations, protections, or silence you ask from people who knew you before it.
You prepare an answer that does not ask your family to defend a story they do not know.
You cut your name out of the notice and leave the rest. The gap is enough to show how far your career entered a life that was not its own.
Neighborhood comments crowd around your name. Some are proud, others worried, none neutral.
Read what others wrote in the margin

A public notice bearing your name and career reaches the old neighborhood before your own news does. Neighbors already showed it around; the question is no longer hiding what you became, but deciding what your family should have to carry.
Your Career Arrives Before Your Letter
event.family_civilian_adult_02_civilian_: You decline the contract and keep the conversation open. Saying no erases neither your childhood nor your skill.
You help solve the need without making yourself indispensable. The offer stops being a loyalty test.
You take the limited job, correct the bundle, and send the accounts back before the deadline. The family gets help without reclaiming your daily life.
The message finally states the price, deadline, and pages to send back. You can help from your current life without letting temporary work become a reserved place back home.
An Offer With an End Date
You draft a clean no without inventing a storm or illness. Their offer deserves an answer, not endless justification.
Prepare a refusal without an excuse
You ask for the terms before answering. The invitation becomes a short contract instead of a sentimental call to duty.
You ask what they actually need from you. The job fits in a few lines and stops carrying the whole weight of the word “family.”

An old work contact forwards a bundle of orders and offers to pay you for a week of checking the accounts remotely. The work reaches you where you are, without turning family help into an order to return.
A Week of Work, Not a Return
event.family_civilian_adult_02_distance_: You state the limit clearly. It sounds cold, but it prevents promises your life cannot keep.
You accept that not every childhood relationship survives distance. The loss remains real without becoming a debt.
You choose one relationship you can actually maintain instead of an imaginary intact household.
The pile becomes short enough to read. You can maintain one precise bond, answer only emergencies, or accept that some relationships have come apart.
You remove contacts that no longer answer. The family network becomes smaller and more honest.
You refuse to answer everyone out of guilt. One specific relationship comes before an impossible catch-up.
You reconstruct what actually happened instead of filling the silences with assumptions.

Four years after the first adult message, a bundle of replies shows the gaps: months without news, changed addresses, promises kept too late. No one asks you to catch up on everything; you only have to decide what you still want to maintain.
event.family_civilian_adult_03_father_sh: You fund a few weeks of help instead of promising to return. Your father keeps time, and you keep your trajectory.
You tell him clearly he has to decide without counting on you as a future replacement. The honesty hurts, but gives the decision back to him.
Refuse to promise you will return
You refuse to treat every removed hour as a loss. He grumbles, then crosses out two more shifts.
Your father agrees to discuss cutting hours, paid help, or partial closure. For the first time, aging is not treated as a failure to work.
Help Without Taking Over His Life
You ask which tasks he still hates and which ones genuinely matter to him.
Ask what he wants to give up
You measure what he already cut without telling you. The problem is no longer future; it has begun.
Compare it with the old schedule
You price outside help before offering your own return. A concrete option appears between “do everything” and “close.”

Your father sends the shop’s new hours: he now closes early several days because his hands and back no longer carry the same weeks. He is not asking you to take his place; he is asking what to do with what has become too heavy.
event.family_civilian_adult_03_household: You let the place become something else without treating it as a personal erasure.
You ask for one thing they deliberately kept. The answer gives that choice more weight than an entire room frozen for you.
You do not disguise the loss as perfect maturity. The place changed, and part of you resents it.
The photograph closes no doors; it only removes the idea that returning would mean stepping back into exactly the place you left.
A Home That Knows How to Live Without You
The few lines explain the changes without asking your approval. You are no longer an automatic co-owner of every memory.
Read the back all the way through
You study the details before deciding what the image means to you. Some landmarks remain; others do not.
You keep a record of the new place instead of protecting a version that no longer exists.
File it with the old papers

A recent photograph shows the place where you grew up: a changed sign, rented room, moved counter, or sealed doorway. The note on the back asks no permission. It simply warns that the scenery of your childhood is not waiting intact.
event.family_civilian_adult_03_neighborh: You prefer to give limited help rather than lend a reputation you cannot control.
You explain what you do not know and refuse to turn real solidarity into a dishonest guarantee.
Refuse to put your name on it
You guarantee only what you know to be true. Your name opens one door without becoming a lifetime bond.
The request becomes precise: an address, a duration, and a responsible person. You can now help, limit your guarantee, or refuse without leaving them in the dark.
A Favor That Uses Your Name
You refuse to be only a name on a page. You want to know what the teenager is asking for personally.
You ask what the teenager can do, what they need, and who answers if it goes wrong.
You reject the idea that shared childhood is enough to guarantee someone. If you say no, you will say why.

A teenager from the old neighborhood is looking for a room or first job away from home. A letter asks for your reference because your name has already opened doors—and because you know what a vague promise can cost.
Your Name Requested for Someone Else
event.family_civilian_adult_04_career_co: You give them a line that promises nothing and tells no lie. The boundary becomes easy to hold.
You explicitly ask that your service buy neither favors nor obligations for your family.
Refuse any institutional favor for them
You refuse to let your flag turn home into an annex of your risks. The boundary costs convenience, not their safety.
Forbid using the address as a safe harbor
You keep home out of messages and meetings. They did not choose your struggle and will not become a dead drop.
The answer has to protect their autonomy as much as your information. What you choose now tells the neighborhood whether your relatives are contacts, witnesses, or simply people who knew you.
A Public Name, a Private Family
You turn dangerous subjects into simple limits instead of opaque instructions.
List what they should never confirm
You look for one sentence any relative can repeat without learning your secrets or lying for you.
You remind them they owe the world no answers on behalf of your career.

Strangers have started asking about you in the old neighborhood: admiration, suspicion, or plain curiosity depending on your career. A letter asks one thing: what can your family say without becoming your office, alibi, or showcase?
event.family_civilian_adult_04_no_reserv: You accept that coming back means visiting rather than returning to childhood.
Accept being a guest in your old home
You ask for practical access, not ownership of a room. The difference clarifies what home still owes you.
Ask only for a spare key
You ask them to stop arranging the place around your possible returns. The freedom leaves a gap too.
Home offers you somewhere to sleep when you visit, not a room frozen all year. The compromise looks smaller, but it fits your actual life better.
A Place That No Longer Depends on a Room
You confirm that an empty room was never proof of love. The space can serve the living without erasing you.
Tell them they were right to use it
You ask the practical question instead of claiming the old room. A temporary solution already exists.
Ask where you would sleep on a visit
You refuse to play the perfectly detached adult. Home can change and the loss can still hurt.

A letter says the space once kept for you now serves someone else: a tenant, apprentice, aging relative, or plain storage. Nobody is throwing you out; the household is simply done arranging an entire home around a hypothetical return.
The Room No Longer Kept for You
event.family_civilian_adult_04_old_work_: You honor this one case and clearly date the end of the old agreement. The favor does not become a transferable right.
You help the client find the right person without using your name as inherited currency.
Redirect them to the right contact
You have the document struck through. Home loses a commercial shortcut but gains a boundary nobody can misread.
The customer accepts that the old recommendation cannot last forever. You still have to decide whether to honor this case, redirect it, or close the old access.
You want to know whether the paper slept in a drawer or was used repeatedly without your knowledge.
Ask why the client kept it
You read exactly what your name promised back then. The document is narrower than the customer claims.
You consider ending the ambiguity without accusing the customer of inventing the document.

A customer presented an old recommendation bearing your name to obtain a service from home. Nobody accepted it yet: the family wants to know whether that old access still means anything or whether the paper should finally stop circulating.
The Order Signed With Your Old Name
event.family_civilian_adult_05_community: You put a small amount into the fund that will help the next young person leave without turning your gesture into personal debt.
Your name stays in the new ledger with a limited meaning: people may say they knew you, not speak for you.
Keep your name as a reference
You help close the old accounts before copying anything over. The neighborhood mainly remembers that promises had an end.
The new ledger is waiting. Your choice can keep your name as a reference, settle old favors, or turn the network into help for someone just starting out.
You consider letting the new ledger begin without you. The gesture would close a system, not necessarily the people.
Cross out your name before copying
You choose one living obligation instead of copying your whole childhood forward by habit.
You read what was settled too. A real network is measured as much by finished debts as by doors still open.

The neighborhood favor ledger is nearly full. Before replacing it, someone sends you a copy of your page: addresses, returned favors, crossed-out promises. Nobody asks you to come back; they ask what should survive into the next ledger.
The Last Page of the Ledger
