event.family_civilian_adult_05_father_cl: You keep the key as a memory, not a deed. Your father finally accepts that it may never need to work again.
You leave him the last object from the place. What remains between you no longer depends on a work tool.
You refuse to let the closure erase what hurt. The relationship loses some softness but gains an ending that does not lie.
Your father gives you a small, clearly counted share. The settlement closes an account instead of opening a new one.
Take your share of the final sales
The business stops; your relationship has to find another subject. Your father asks what you want to keep when there is no till, schedule, or useful key left.
You refuse to let the closure become a chain of postponed messages. You set a precise time to finish the conversation.
Choose a date for one last call
A few tools, two chairs, and an empty till are enough to tell the story without turning the place into compulsory inheritance.
Read the list of what remains
You ask what a useless key still means to him. His answer is less about the business than about the two of you.
Ask why he kept the key

Your father writes that he is finally closing the shop while he is still alive. The lease is ended, the last orders finished, and the old key no longer opens a future—only a decision about what the two of you keep from that work.
The Key Your Father Will No Longer Use
event.family_civilian_adult_05_last_enve: The neighborhood keeps one simple way to reach you. Your name still travels there, but only as someone who actually lived there.
You pay the last small amount that is genuinely yours. The account closes without transferring the rest of family life onto you.
Settle one remainder you still owe
An old deposit finally comes back to you. The amount is modest, but it cleanly closes a right that stayed open since you left.
Accept the balance still in your name
There is no guaranteed family chapter after this one. You can keep an address, settle one concrete remainder, or accept a small balance still owed to you without turning it into professional destiny.
A Tie That No Longer Needs a Debt
You check the numbers and old promises. Nothing requires a forced return to be settled.
Check that no account remains open
You keep the address as a conscious choice, not a family respawn point.
You refuse to manufacture a grand closing speech. A few words are enough when no account is waiting behind them.
Send back an almost blank sheet

An envelope finds you with one last statement, an updated address, and no urgent request. After years of family returning through debts, work, arguments, or news, the letter finally asks something simple: what do you still want to receive from here?
The Last Envelope Without an Emergency
event.family_pirate_01_bread_wrapping_i0: The adult gathers the pieces instead of throwing them away.
The bounty vanishes inside your fists. The adult flips the sheet too quickly, then hesitates. On the back, someone once wrote a port and a date beside a salt stain.
The adult carefully folds the paper and puts it beyond your reach.
You keep the loaf. The adult flips the sheet too quickly, then hesitates. On the back, someone once wrote a port and a date beside a salt stain.
The forbidden face stays beneath your fingers for a few seconds.
The adult does not move your hand. The adult flips the sheet too quickly, then hesitates. On the back, someone once wrote a port and a date beside a salt stain.
event.family_pirate_01_bread_wrapping.ch: The paper crackles in your fists, tearing the portrait around the loaf.
You take the loaf and leave the wanted notice open on the table between you.
Your fingers press a crumb into the portrait; the adult stops and lets you look at the face.
event.family_pirate_01_bread_wrapping.te: The person feeding you unwraps a loaf from an old yellowed sheet. When the paper opens, a wanted portrait bearing your family name appears beneath the crumbs.
event.family_pirate_01_crew_at_cradle_i0: Your father yields on the bedroom, but not on abandoning his man.
Your mother lifts you close. The wounded man groans as footsteps race outside. Your father asks for one minute; your mother refuses to let blood, weapons, or pursuers cross this threshold.
They both use it, each in their own way, without settling their disagreement.
The cloth ends up under the wound. The wounded man groans as footsteps race outside. Your father asks for one minute; your mother refuses to let blood, weapons, or pursuers cross this threshold.
The wounded pirate stays out of the bedroom, but your father does not abandon him.

Your gesture stops their argument long enough for them to move the wounded man into the kitchen, away from you. The wounded man groans as footsteps race outside. Your father asks for one minute; your mother refuses to let blood, weapons, or pursuers cross this threshold.
event.family_pirate_01_crew_at_cradle.ch: You cling to your mother; she lifts you at once and forces your father back from the threshold.
The cloth slides to the wounded pirate, and both parents stop arguing long enough to grab it.
The wounded pirate reaches toward your hand; your father steps forward while your mother still blocks the bedroom.
event.family_pirate_01_crew_at_cradle.te: A wounded pirate collapses against the table beside your cradle. Your father, {{npc_player_parent_1}}, wants to hide him here; your mother, {{npc_player_parent_2}}, blocks the way to the bedroom with her forearm.
event.family_pirate_01_silver_in_flour_i: When the adult finds it, nobody laughs at your game.
The buckle disappears behind you. An adult rushes in and gathers everything too quickly. The buckle still bears the arms of a raided merchant ship, half-scratched away but perfectly legible.
The adults hide the objects again without explaining where their comfort comes from.
You back away from the flour. An adult rushes in and gathers everything too quickly. The buckle still bears the arms of a raided merchant ship, half-scratched away but perfectly legible.
The box closes, but you now know that some of the household's meals are paid for with that money.

The coin rests in your palm before returning to the box that also pays for the household's meals. An adult rushes in and gathers everything too quickly. The buckle still bears the arms of a raided merchant ship, half-scratched away but perfectly legible.
event.family_pirate_01_silver_in_flour.c: You slip the buckle behind your back, and the arriving adult stops short when one piece is missing.
You step back through the flour while the adults scoop up the coins as fast as they can.
The foreign coin rings in your palm; the servant rushes to close the box.
event.family_pirate_01_silver_in_flour.t: A box falls from a kitchen shelf, spilling flour, foreign coins, and an engraved silver buckle. The servant freezes: none of these things were bought here.
event.family_pirate_01_tarred_ribbon_i01: The adult hides the sleeve rather than washing it by the window.
The ribbon stains your sleeve before it is taken back. Tar sticks to your fingers and leaves a black mark on the table. Outside, someone pauses just long enough to look at the window.
The ribbon stays hidden under the ash instead of disappearing into the flames.

The adult takes the ribbon and buries it beneath cold ashes instead of burning it at once. Tar sticks to your fingers and leaves a black mark on the table. Outside, someone pauses just long enough to look at the window.
The person outside moves on, but the window stays shut until evening.
You watch the ribbon blacken. Tar sticks to your fingers and leaves a black mark on the table. Outside, someone pauses just long enough to look at the window.
event.family_pirate_01_tarred_ribbon.cho: You close your hand around the ribbon before it reaches the flames; tar blackens your fingers.
You hold out the ribbon; the adult takes it but hesitates in front of the lit hearth.
You stay still as the ribbon nears the fire; the adult looks first at the door, then at the flames.
event.family_pirate_01_tarred_ribbon.tex: A gust pushes a tar-stained black ribbon under the door, torn from a pirate flag. The nearest adult wants it in the fire before a neighbor sees it.
event.family_pirate_01_trapdoor_knock_i0: They finally leave. Your mother holds your small hand for a long time.
The rug stays flat. Your mother opens the door a crack. Two soaked strangers remain on the threshold and inspect the room; one stares at the rug you just pulled, but nothing shows beneath it.
You press close to her. She rocks you without taking her eyes off them; they eventually leave.
Your crying covers the small sounds in the room. Your mother opens the door a crack. Two soaked strangers remain on the threshold; one stares at the rug still folded back near his boots.
The first man returns from the window having found nothing. After one last look, both men leave in the rain.
While one man goes around the house toward the window, your mother smooths the rug flat, then opens the door only enough to speak to the one still at the threshold. Neither man has entered.
event.family_pirate_01_trapdoor_knock.ch: The rug slides over the trapdoor just before the handle moves from outside.
You burst into tears; your mother leaves the trapdoor shut and puts herself between you and the door.
Your mother follows your gesture and knocks against the shutter. Outside, one man leaves the threshold to check beneath the window, leaving the other alone at the door.
event.family_pirate_01_trapdoor_knock.te: Three knocks strike the door through the rain. Inside, your mother, {{npc_player_parent_2}}, slips a satchel into the hiding space beneath the floor and shuts the trapdoor; the rug is still folded back. Outside, a man demands that you open up.
event.family_pirate_04_chain_below_quay_: You get an answer only because you stop the job.
Demand to know what is inside
The crew admits the box holds stolen documents. Under the pilings, the box is heavier than promised and bears a merchant seal. Above, the crew whistles: the patrol has just turned into the street.
At the End of the Chain
The box reaches the quay with you; the crew can no longer pretend your dive was a harmless favor.

You bring the chain back to the edge, but now you know exactly what they expect from your body. Under the pilings, the box is heavier than promised and bears a merchant seal. Above, the crew whistles: the patrol has just turned into the street.
At the End of the Chain
The crew must choose between losing the box and exposing themselves to the patrol.
You let the chain sink. Under the pilings, the box is heavier than promised and bears a merchant seal. Above, the crew whistles: the patrol has just turned into the street.
At the End of the Chain
You keep your feet on the planks; the pirate stops smiling and puts a hand on the chain.
Demand to know what is inside
You dive beneath the quay and the chain pulls taut in your hands, heavy with an unseen box.
You drop the chain; it strikes the quay and vanishes into the water.
A crewmate shows you a chain vanishing beneath the pier. Because you are a Fish-Man, he wants you to retrieve a submerged box before the patrol returns.
event.family_pirate_04_empty_berth_i01_a: You are taught the return signal: two low lanterns. A lookout confirms no familiar flag passed the headland. A rumor mentions a pursuit; nobody yet knows whether to wait or run.
event.family_pirate_04_empty_berth_i01_p: Nobody dares take it down a second time in front of you.
The mug goes back on its hook. A lookout confirms no familiar flag passed the headland. A rumor mentions a pursuit; nobody yet knows whether to wait or run.
event.family_pirate_04_empty_berth_i01_t: It weighs little, but nobody asks for it back.
You carry the mug upstairs. A lookout confirms no familiar flag passed the headland. A rumor mentions a pursuit; nobody yet knows whether to wait or run.
event.family_pirate_04_empty_berth.choic: Your question silences the innkeeper, who looks toward the harbor entrance instead of taking down the mug.
You put the mug back on its hook; the innkeeper slowly withdraws his hand.
You take down the mug yourself and hold it close; no one dares take it back.
event.family_pirate_04_empty_berth.text: The small boat due at dusk does not return. At the dockside inn, someone is already taking your mother's mug off its hook as if the absence will last.
event.family_pirate_04_empty_berth.title: The Empty Berth
event.family_pirate_04_fallback_househol: His place at the table becomes an exchange, not an entitlement.
Ask what he is bringing
He finally offers to repair the roof in the morning. The visitor stops joking when he sees the bottom of the pot. For once, crew loyalty is measured in spoonfuls instead of grand speeches.
What a Place Costs
He protests, then sees there is no hidden reserve.
Push his bowl away
His bowl goes back to the other side of the table. The visitor stops joking when he sees the bottom of the pot. For once, crew loyalty is measured in spoonfuls instead of grand speeches.
What a Place Costs
The visitor eats more slowly and leaves the last piece in front of you.
Split your portion
You split your portion in half. The visitor stops joking when he sees the bottom of the pot. For once, crew loyalty is measured in spoonfuls instead of grand speeches.
What a Place Costs
Your question stops his spoon; he empties his pockets onto the table to show what he is actually bringing.
Ask what he is bringing
You push his bowl off the cloth; the pirate catches it before it falls.
Push his bowl away
You pour half your bowl into the pirate's; the household adult silently counts the portions again.
Split your portion
A visiting pirate sets his bowl beside yours without asking. The adult running the household counts the portions: there is not enough to feed both crew and home tonight.
One Bowl Too Many
event.family_pirate_04_fallback_hunted_i: The answer never says who may come, only that the exit must stay clear.

The only answer is, “So we can leave fast.” It is enough to change the shape of the room. Nobody comes that night. The bag is still beside the door in the morning, proof that a pirate household may need to stop being a home within minutes.
The escape bag now carries something that is truly yours.
Put a toy in the bag

Your toy stays on top of the clothes, the first thing you could save if the door opened. Nobody comes that night. The bag is still beside the door in the morning, proof that a pirate household may need to stop being a home within minutes.
By morning, nobody has unpacked the bag.
You sleep with your laces tied. Nobody comes that night. The bag is still beside the door in the morning, proof that a pirate household may need to stop being a home within minutes.
event.family_pirate_04_fallback_hunted.c: Your question stops the adult at the door; they check the lock one more time.
You put your toy on top of the bag; the adult removes a shirt to make room for it.
Put a toy in the bag
You lie down with your shoes on; the bag stays upright beside the door within reach.
event.family_pirate_04_fallback_hunted.t: Before putting out the lamp, the adult in the household makes you keep your shoes on and puts a bag by the exit. Someone asked too many questions about the family today.
event.family_pirate_04_fallback_legacy_i: The silence becomes information about the family in its own right.
Nobody gives you a name. Inside are ordinary tools, cloth, and a cracked shell. Nothing is valuable; the uncertainty about where they came from remains.
When it finally disappears from the room, you still do not know who once owned it.

The crate stays by the wall for days before an adult opens it without you. Inside are ordinary tools, cloth, and a cracked shell. Nothing is valuable; the uncertainty about where they came from remains.
The adults now have to answer in front of an already opened crate.

You touch every object without finding an answer hidden at the bottom of the crate. Inside are ordinary tools, cloth, and a cracked shell. Nothing is valuable; the uncertainty about where they came from remains.
event.family_pirate_04_fallback_legacy.c: No one answers; an adult simply puts a hand on the lid to stop you opening it.
You take your hands off the crate; it remains in the middle of the room like a guest nobody introduces.
The lid creaks open, revealing objects wrapped in newspapers from different ports.
event.family_pirate_04_fallback_legacy.t: A small crate marked with a distant port arrives with the family's belongings. Nobody knows, or wants to say, whether it was bought, won, or taken.
event.family_pirate_04_household_line_i0: Both adults have to restate their argument without an easy boundary.

The chalk disappears under your hand. The pirate crewmate smiles awkwardly. Your father talks about loyalty to those who risked their lives; your mother says the household is not an extension of the ship.
Your father yields on the room, not on giving shelter.

The boots go back to the kitchen. The pirate crewmate smiles awkwardly. Your father talks about loyalty to those who risked their lives; your mother says the household is not an extension of the ship.
The crewmate picks up his own boots and moves.

You make the line impossible to ignore. The pirate crewmate smiles awkwardly. Your father talks about loyalty to those who risked their lives; your mother says the household is not an extension of the ship.
event.family_pirate_04_household_line.ch: Your palm smears the chalk into a gray blur; your parents look at each other over the erased line.
The boots scrape back across the floor to the crew's side; your father watches them go.
You thicken the chalk into a white band; your mother moves your belongings behind it.
event.family_pirate_04_household_line.te: Your father, {{npc_player_parent_1}}, sets a crewmate's boots near your bed; your mother, {{npc_player_parent_2}}, immediately draws a chalk line across the floor. “The crew sleeps on that side. The child stays on this one.”
event.family_pirate_04_price_on_name_i01: The poster stays behind, but the other people's stares follow.
You leave the stall empty-handed. The neighbor arrives, then another. Nobody accuses you of a crime, but the face on the wall is enough to turn an ordinary errand into a spectacle.
A few eyes drop, but not the merchant's.
The basket contains only bread and soap. The neighbor arrives, then another. Nobody accuses you of a crime, but the face on the wall is enough to turn an ordinary errand into a spectacle.
The merchant shouts louder than if you had robbed his till.
The paper tears with a sharp sound. The neighbor arrives, then another. Nobody accuses you of a crime, but the face on the wall is enough to turn an ordinary errand into a spectacle.
event.family_pirate_04_price_on_name.cho: You take your basket and leave without buying anything; the merchant's whisper follows you into the street.
You set the basket on the counter; the merchant reads your name, then looks at the door as if already expecting someone.
The poster corner tears under your fingers; the merchant immediately shouts that someone is tampering with it.
event.family_pirate_04_price_on_name.tex: A merchant suddenly refuses to serve you. He has recognized the same name on a wanted notice and on your basket, and quietly calls to his neighbor.
event.family_pirate_04_search_room_i01_d: Your mother retrieves the chart while they curse the wet floor.
Water reaches their boots and their attention. One hunter moves toward the bed; the other asks your mother how much her freedom is worth. She says nothing and keeps her eyes on you.
event.family_pirate_04_search_room_i01_l: Your mother memorizes his face instead of lunging at him in front of you.
The hunter tears out the chart. One hunter moves toward the bed; the other asks your mother how much her freedom is worth. She says nothing and keeps her eyes on you.
event.family_pirate_04_search_room_i01_s: The seam stays intact beneath your weight.
The hunter grunts and moves to the next piece of furniture. One hunter moves toward the bed; the other asks your mother how much her freedom is worth. She says nothing and keeps her eyes on you.
event.family_pirate_04_search_room.choic: The washbasin tips over at the hunters' feet; they curse and step back from the dirty water.
You move off the bed; a hunter pulls away the pillow and finds the opened seam.
You sit on the pillow; the corner of the map vanishes beneath you as a hunter approaches.
event.family_pirate_04_search_room.text: Two bounty hunters turn over your blankets while your mother stands against the wall with both hands visible. A small chart sewn into your pillow sticks out by a finger's width.
event.family_pirate_04_search_room.title: They Search Your Room
event.family_pirate_04_stolen_purchase_i: The adult stops calling it ownerless loot.
The mark matches her story. The clerk shows a small filed mark inside the ring. The adult beside you whispers that this ring has helped feed the household for months.
The purchase goes unpaid, but the clerk asks nothing else of you.
The ring stays on the counter. The clerk shows a small filed mark inside the ring. The adult beside you whispers that this ring has helped feed the household for months.
The clerk wraps the goods without looking at you.
The purchase is completed with the ring. The clerk shows a small filed mark inside the ring. The adult beside you whispers that this ring has helped feed the household for months.
event.family_pirate_04_stolen_purchase.c: The shopkeeper takes the ring and points out an inner scratch the adult had never noticed.

A Network Is Not a Password
You pull the adult to the curtain; he finally looks for himself before opening anything.
Pull the adult to the window
You pull the curtain; the stranger looks up at the window that just vanished.
You tap the known signal; the stranger does not answer and shifts on the bench.
A stranger has waited on the bench beneath the window for too long. The refuge adult says he knows 'someone in the network,' but nobody in the room recognizes his face.
event.family_revolutionary_04_orphan_gua: The guardian box stays blank and the medic keeps only the information needed for care.
The form names one precise responsibility without artificially giving you a parent.
The name is paired with a written limit: responsible only for this medical visit.
The medic can record an emergency contact without pretending he is your parent. The revolutionary admits that a network sheltering you is not automatically a family.
A Box Does Not Make a Parent
You draw across the name; the revolutionary sets down his pencil and lets you finish.
You point to yourself; the medic writes a separate note instead of inventing a family on the form.
You tap the box; the medic takes the form back before he can invent an address.
At the back of a clinic, a revolutionary fills out your medical form and writes his own name under 'guardian.' The medic asks whether he actually lives with you; he hesitates before answering.
event.family_revolutionary_04_parents_sa: The contact will need another refuge; your walls stop being treated as an automatic passage.
Close the house to the network
Your mother agrees to one opening at a fixed time, then the key returns inside immediately.
Your father places a discreet marker farther away; the family door stays locked until confirmation.
The contact may be in danger if the door stays shut, but opening the home exposes the whole family. Your parents look for a solution that treats neither side as disposable.
A Home Is Not a Passage
Your father takes the key, but your mother blocks the door before he can open it.
Your mother closes her hand around the key; your father goes to check the back window.
You hide the key; both parents have to stop deciding as though it were just a detail.
Hide the key in your pocket
Your father wants the back door left unlocked for a late contact. Your mother refuses: a neighbor has already noticed nighttime visitors. They find you holding the key while arguing in the hall.
The Door That Must Stay Family
event.family_revolutionary_04_ration_deb: The column disappears; families keep the sacks already given with no added obligation.
The ledger keeps both columns; your family now knows this aid may later be invoked as a debt.
A second sheet appears at the other end of the table; nobody is listed unless they come forward themselves.
The coordinator says he is only noting 'reliable' people. The neighbor demands a choice: distribute aid, or recruit openly, but do not mix the two afterward.
You rub at the charcoal column; the coordinator grabs the ledger before the names disappear too.
You share a handful; the neighbor keeps it without looking at the debt column.
You put the sack on the open book; the neighbor laughs and the coordinator has to move it to continue.
Put the sack on the ledger

At the distribution, a coordinator records how many sacks your family received, then adds a 'future help' column. A poor neighbor objects: nobody mentioned service in exchange before the baskets were filled.
event.family_revolutionary_07_aid_regist: Notes already linking relief and recruitment are burned in front of both teams.
The two ledgers share no address without explicit consent from the person concerned.
An address enters the political ledger only if the person explicitly requests the transfer.
The shelter must make its separation real in the records. Otherwise relief remains a back door into a political file recipients never chose.
Separate the Data Like the Tables
You put a blank ledger before the organizer; if he wants to recruit, he must build his own list.
You keep the relief ledger against you; the organizer cannot copy any address without taking it from you.
You swap the covers to show how similar the books look; the cook demands a distinct code.
The shelter separated relief from recruitment, but an organizer now proposes copying the same addresses into both ledgers 'to save time.' The cook refuses to hand over the recipients' book.
event.family_revolutionary_07_code_in_sc: You accept this specific trip after getting the destination and fallback plan; it is not blanket permission.
The paper goes back with an adult; your school route stops being an operational route chosen without you.
Remove the message from the bag
Your mother hides the paper in a fixed dead drop an adult will retrieve later. It is her final relay from the household before leaving, without using your schoolbag.
Your mother admits the network is using your age to lower suspicion. She must decide whether urgency truly justifies turning you into discreet transport.
Less Visible Does Not Mean Available
You ask for the recipient's name; your mother realizes she was about to send you without telling you to whom.
You put the bag down and refuse to take it; your mother is left holding the message she wanted moved.
You pull the paper out in front of her; your mother has to answer before she can close the lining.
Your mother slips a coded strip into the lining of your schoolbag before school. When you ask why, she says a child draws less attention than an adult courier.
event.family_revolutionary_07_false_name: The names remain circled; the network chooses caution at the cost of suspicion that may become its own evidence.
The report is isolated until reviewed by someone outside the original accusation.
Names without concrete evidence are removed from the alert list.
The cell must decide whether to keep suspicions with no evidence. A false accusation can protect a network for hours and ruin a person for years.
You point to the name and ask why; the organizer finds only a note saying 'refuses to commit.'
You pull the papers apart; the organizer has to explain what truly connects each name to the police report.
You erase the circle; the woman stops being marked by a simple pencil stroke.
An organizer compares the shelter list with a police report and circles three names as 'possible informants.' One belongs to a woman who simply refused to join the cell after receiving aid.
The List That Accuses Too Quickly
event.family_revolutionary_07_guardian_p: You receive a simple copy of the names and handoff points so you know who is supposed to be responsible for you.
Keep a copy of your route
The forms state who travels with each child without pretending that person becomes their parent.
Each leg has a distinct responsible adult; nobody is made universal guardian for convenience.
The evacuation needs clear responsibilities, not a fictional family printed on every form. Adults must list escorts, contacts, and handoff points separately.
A Refuge Must Know Who Is Responsible
Your question forces the organizer to bring out the actual escort list rather than the administrative list of fake guardians.
You scan the names; several children are assigned to the same adult who is not even in the room.
You cross out the column; the organizer stops writing and asks how escorts should be identified instead.

An organizer prepares an evacuation and wants to list the same revolutionary as guardian for every parentless child in the refuge. You recognize the name from the clinic and ask whether he will actually travel with you.
event.family_revolutionary_07_household_: The documents leave the house for a safe box outside the home.
The cell must find another place; this piece of furniture stops becoming organizational property by accumulation.
Return the drawer to the family
One area is reserved for clandestine papers; the rest clearly returns to the household.
Limit the cell to one drawer
The cell needs hiding places, but the household needs places that do not slowly become clandestine offices. Adults must set a material boundary.
A Home Keeps Its Own Things Too
You put the clandestine papers on the table; their volume can no longer be treated as a domestic detail.
You rescue the family letters before an adult pushes them into an unlabeled basket.
You put a box in the middle of the drawer; the adults understand the idea immediately.
The family drawer will no longer close: false papers, keys, and messages have displaced household letters and small belongings. An adult suggests emptying the rest to make room.
The Drawer That Will Not Close
event.family_revolutionary_07_network_fa: One clearly named person opens the note and records why the exception was made.
The message goes back to the last known handoff rather than being absorbed by any network member.
An adult goes to verify the handoff chain; the note stays sealed until then.
The network must choose between speed and chain of responsibility. Opening the note may help, but it destroys the rule that tells anyone who was supposed to read it.
You ask for the last handoff; the courier can at least name the house where he received it.
You hand the note back; the courier realizes a correct code phrase does not create a recipient.
You keep the note sealed; the courier stops offering it to adults volunteering to open it.
A courier arrives at the refuge with the correct coded phrase but no recipient name. Two adults want to open it 'so the information is not lost,' though nobody knows who it was meant for.
event.family_revolutionary_07_relief_nam: The leaflet gives place, quantity, and remaining needs; no family becomes political proof without consent.
Only people who volunteer appear; receiving a sack does not authorize anyone to speak for them.
The distribution remains useful even without a public story to showcase it.
The leaflet can mention the distribution without identifying recipients. The movement must decide whether to lose a more emotional story to protect the people involved.
Aid Does Not Grant Story Rights
You place a blank sheet over the column; the organizer can see only the quantities distributed.
You show only the sack totals; the organizer realizes the aid can be reported without exposing recipients.
You tear the copy carrying the names; the woman collects the pieces where hers appeared.

After a distribution, an organizer asks for the list of aided families for a leaflet praising revolutionary action. A woman from your neighborhood refuses to be used as an example while she still hides her rent debt from the landlord.
event.family_revolutionary_07_respectabl: The couriers leave by another route; the reception stays respectable without turning staff into human cover.
The employee agrees to one passage and sets the time herself; employment is not permanent consent.
The false receipts now bear the name of the household that chose the risk, not an employee drafted by default.
The operation can still continue, but the employee refuses to be officially responsible for access she never accepted. The network must decide who signs and who controls the cover.
You call the employee over; the organizer can no longer use her signature as silent cover.
You point toward the front entrance; a parent realizes the family's respectability will have to carry its own risk.
You take the receipt; the courier stops at the service door and the employee finally sees her name.
Take the receipt from the courier

During a respectable reception, an organizer sends three couriers through the servants' entrance disguised as deliveries. An employee discovers her name on the false receipts without ever being asked.
event.family_revolutionary_07_search_at_: The adult opens the hall but refuses bedroom access without clear authority, taking the confrontation personally.
The most dangerous papers disappear into the stove before the patrol gets farther.
The visitor leaves through a prepared back exit; residents do not become human shields for his escape.
The patrol says it is looking for a clandestine printer. The household can mislead it, limit the search, or sacrifice material so residents do not become the price of the cache.
You shove the shoes under a cabinet; the visitor retreats in socks toward the back room.
You open an empty room near the hall; an adult moves the conversation there before answering the door.
You wipe the first print; behind the door, the patrol knocks a second time.
A Marine patrol knocks while a clandestine visitor removes muddy shoes in the hall. The soles leave a trail toward the room where papers were just hidden.
event.family_revolutionary_07_split_inst: Your father takes responsibility for explanations; you are no longer tasked with making the lie convincing.
Your mother tells the visitor that adults will carry the risks of the cover themselves.
You agree false names may be used in the house without requiring you to invent extra stories.
The visitor explains the false name protects him, but he does not want children forced to lie for him. Your parents must distinguish safety from family obedience.
You ask the visitor what he wants to be called; the decision stops belonging only to your parents.
You use the false name; your father nods while your mother stays silent in front of the visitor.
You introduce the visitor without naming him; both parents realize you made your own rule.

At dinner, your father asks you to introduce a visitor under a false name. Your mother interrupts him: protecting the cell, she says, should not force you to lie in your own kitchen. The visitor waits.
The False Name Asked at Dinner
event.family_revolutionary_10_civilian_t: The team disperses; no threat turns a weak suspicion into real punishment.
The team leaves despite the empty file; the tactic may protect the network, but knowingly creates risk for a civilian.
Two people outside the original file must confirm a fact before any confrontation.
Some want to frighten him 'just in case.' Others point out a threat can create the enemy they only claimed to suspect. The cell must decide before the team leaves.
Nobody in the room can name a direct witness; silence replaces certainty.
You put the old file beside the plan; the lack of evidence becomes visible before anyone leaves.
You cross out the address; the team leader can no longer pretend the visit is already settled.
A cell prepares to intimidate a foreman accused of informing the Marines. You recognize his name: the accusation comes from the same file where recruitment refusals had been treated as suspicious.
event.family_revolutionary_10_donor_dema: The donor must choose: support the safehouses without dictating a target, or leave with his money.
The organizer refuses the warehouse but offers the donor a way to fund needs chosen collectively.
Refuse the target, keep dialogue open
The envelope leaves with the donor; the network accepts a material loss rather than selling tactical authority.
The donor threatens to withdraw support if the cell refuses. Without his money, several safehouses lose supplies; with it, the cell risks becoming an instrument of private interest.
Money Funds, It Does Not Command
Your question forces the donor to explain why this specific rival matters so much to him.
You circle the food stores on the plan; the organizer turns the sheet so the donor has to see them.
You push the envelope back toward the donor; he stops speaking as if the money already bought the decision.

In the family parlor, a major donor puts a new envelope on the table and demands the next action target a rival's warehouse. The organizer replies that the building also stores food for the neighborhood.
event.family_revolutionary_10_household_: The household opens one extra space for this emergency, with a clear boundary before the next one.
One room remains outside the shelter operation even under network pressure.
Another safehouse takes over on a written date; the shelter is real without becoming permanent by inertia.
The injured person must stay safe, but the household cannot expand forever. The adults finally set a duration, a replacement bed, and a plan if someone else arrives.
You ask for a precise duration; the adults stop using 'a few' as a sufficient answer.
You look for blankets and a bench next door; the refuge gains an option without taking the entire common room.
You move a chair to mark the area that must remain available to residents.

An injured person reaches the family refuge and two adults already unroll the spare mattress in the common room. They promise 'only a few nights,' but nobody knows where residents will sleep if a second emergency comes.
event.family_revolutionary_10_medicine_b: The political list takes priority over the medical register; aid clearly becomes a benefit tied to commitment.
Doses go to the most urgent cases, whether or not they ever helped the cell.
A small reserve remains for people exposed by an ongoing operation; the rest follows medical triage.
There will not be enough medicine for everyone. The medic wants triage by medical need; the political organizer wants priority for people who helped the network.
A Limited Crate, Not a Reward
Your question pulls the discussion back toward symptoms rather than affiliation.
You help count the people waiting; the number already exceeds the available doses.
You move the political list aside; the medic puts her medical register in its place.

A crate of medicine reaches the neighborhood, but an organizer wants the first doses reserved for families already listed as sympathizers. The medic opens it anyway before a line containing several unknown families.
event.family_revolutionary_10_minor_cour: An adult takes the longer route and carries the operational risk the cell wanted to shift onto you.
Give the satchel to an adult
The satchel moves in stages without turning any child into a discreet courier.
You accept this one route after setting fallback point, contents, and right to abort; nobody presents it as your new role.
Volunteer once with an exit plan
The leader must choose between exploiting your low-suspicion profile and finding another route. You can support the objective without accepting selection precisely because you are a minor.
Less Suspicious Is Not Less Endangered
Your question exposes the real calculation: the danger is exactly why the route is being offered to you.
You do not touch the satchel; the leader has to keep explaining the plan without implied consent.
You open the satchel with him; it holds wanted printing plates, not harmless letters.
After an adult courier is searched, a cell leader puts a small satchel before you and says Marines search children less often. He promises a short route to a nearby print shop.
event.family_revolutionary_10_mother_abs: The note stays sealed in a neutral place until an identified adult retrieves it; you do not become its handler.
The courier leaves to find the adult formally replacing your mother.
The sealed note goes back to the previous handoff instead of turning your home into an inherited station.
The network must recognize that a clandestine role does not automatically pass to a child when a parent disappears. The message can wait, change hands, or be returned.
Her Absence Is Not Your Assignment
You ask who replaced your mother; the courier realizes he was given no replacement contact.
You keep your hands behind your back; the courier remains holding the note and his unresolved problem.
You point to the box where your mother kept messages; nobody now has the key.
A courier arrives with a note for your mother, but she is no longer present in the household. He wants to leave it with you 'because you know how the house works' and refuses to take it back.
The Message After Your Mother Leaves
event.family_revolutionary_10_network_fa: The crates are moved and the second exit becomes usable again.
An adult inspects the route before deciding whether it should remain forbidden.
The refuge replaces inherited notes with a plan verified that day.
The evacuation plan posted in the refuge decides who leaves by which door if Marines arrive. The cell must check the exits now instead of letting an old fear become an automatic instruction.
The Evacuation Plan Must Be Checked
You count the residents; one door will not move everyone out quickly.
You ask why it is crossed out; nobody knows whether the danger still exists or the note was simply copied.
You follow the route to the yard; a stack of crates is in fact blocking the second door.
An evacuation plan in the refuge shows three exits, but one was crossed out after a contact's arrest. Nobody has checked whether the second exit is still usable.
The Exit Crossed Out in Pencil
event.family_revolutionary_10_orphan_cal: You may call certain people close without turning the whole organization into a collective parent.
The organizer withdraws the phrase; nobody imposes an emotional bond to justify shelter.
Each task gets a named person and backup; help becomes accountable rather than sentimental.
The shelter must define who handles what: nights, care, school, evacuation. The movement can support you durably without claiming the word 'family' in return.
An Organization Can Help Without Declaring Itself Parent
You ask who will actually be there tonight; several adults stop nodding along with the slogan.
You name specific people; the organizer can no longer replace their actions with the organization's name.
You reject the word; the volunteer asks everyone to speak in terms of concrete responsibilities.

After an argument about your housing, an organizer declares before the shelter: 'The Revolution is your family now.' A volunteer replies that a slogan decides neither who cares for you nor who comes for you at night.
event.family_revolutionary_10_parent_or_: Your parent agrees to one hour; the exception is explicit, limited, and does not become the new norm.
The meeting continues in the kitchen; your parent learns the household boundary can vanish whenever the organization declares urgency.
The cell changes rooms; the household rule survives precisely because it also applies during urgency.
The network needs a place immediately, but the home already has a discussed boundary. The cell must negotiate with the household instead of treating domestic refusal as disloyalty.
Backing Your Parent Is Not Leaving the Cause
You stand beside your parent; the objection can no longer be framed as one person's inconvenience.
You stack the papers and clear the table; the organizer must physically take them back to continue the meeting.
Clear the papers from the table
You point to a room already meant for visitors; urgency loses its excuse for annexing the kitchen.
A cell meeting begins in the kitchen, the room your family had reserved for meals and rest. Your present parent objects; the organizer says urgency allows the exception without asking the household.
The Cell Takes the Family Kitchen
event.family_revolutionary_10_recruiter_: The table stays visible, away from the exit, with a sign stating relief depends on no answer.
The shelter separates time as well: no political ask during relief distribution.
People must choose to enter the recruitment room; nobody passes through it by necessity.
The recruiter says he forces nobody. The cook replies that a request placed between the ration and the exit is not neutral when people depend on the next meal.
You repeat his phrase aloud; the cook immediately asks for the same explanation.
You drag the chair toward the back; the food line exit becomes clear again.
You open a side door; several families use it without passing the recruiter.
The shelter separated its records, but a recruiter puts his chair directly behind the food line exit. People must pass him carrying their rations; he starts asking who 'wants to give something back.'
event.family_revolutionary_10_sabotage_a: Your parents keep the plan; they now explicitly accept that the military objective may cut a civilian service.
The bridge stays intact; the operation becomes riskier for the cell but safer for civilians.
The operation is delayed and may lose its target, but nobody confuses urgency with a right to collateral harm.
The operation still matters to the cell, but the bridge is not abstract. Your parents must decide whether they can slow the convoy without cutting the village's medical access.
Rejecting a Tactic Without Leaving the Cause
You mark the medical cart's route; your father has to look at it beside the convoy's path.
You point to a stretch of road beyond the bridge; both parents recalculate the risk instead of arguing in principle.
Move the ambush past the bridge
You remove the explosive marker; your mother keeps it in her palm while your father searches for another option.
Your father lays out a sabotage plan: cutting a bridge would stop a military convoy, but also the village's only medical cart. Your mother wants to delay; he fears losing the chance.
event.family_revolutionary_13_household_: You keep the boundary without any promise to join; the family is no longer an implicit organizational reserve.
Keep the rule for civilian life
The network recognizes the household boundary as a condition of any future involvement from you.
Carry the rule into the cause
Your name remains invited at fifteen, but no parental role, room, or family resource is automatically included.
Keep an invitation without inherited role
The door may stay behind, but the rule can survive into your future choices. You must decide whether it travels with a revolutionary invitation or a civilian life.
You add the phrase; the adults reread the whole rule from the start.
You write that an emergency needs an owner and an end point; the organizer signs below.
You add the final line; no clandestine family role can now be presented as your natural inheritance.
Before you turn fifteen, the household writes on the back of the door what the cell must ask before using a room, a piece of furniture, or a family member. You are left to add the final line.
The Rule Written on the Door
event.family_revolutionary_13_invitation: Your future access to safehouses is recognized without any obligation to become a revolutionary.
You decline both lodging and recruitment; the shelter closes your file without treating refusal as betrayal.
The network keeps an open invitation in your name for age fifteen, based on your choice rather than your lack of parents.
The organizer confirms the card is neither a contract nor a family bond. It represents only two distinct doors you may open later—or never.
Shelter Does Not Create a Life Debt
You keep the whole card; joining remains an option, not a substitute parent.
You fold the recruitment part under the card; lodging access remains valid on its own.
You read the two separate lines; nobody can present lodging as political preregistration.
The shelter gives you a card bearing your name: at fifteen, you may ask to join a cell or simply use the lodging network while traveling. No box identifies you as a child of the organization.
The Invitation in Your Own Name
event.family_revolutionary_13_minor_cour: You choose a future civilian path and keep proof that refusing one mission never meant refusing your own worth.
Keep the boundary outside the cell
The cell records a durable limit: no minor is selected as courier merely to evade searches.
Your name stays on a future invitation, with a written condition that you may still refuse each mission.
The cell finally formalizes what this history established. You may still want to join later while refusing to let children be selected because they look less suspicious.
Your Age Must Not Be a Tactical Resource
You hang the empty satchel on the wall; every new courier entering can see it.
Hang the satchel on the wall
You keep the empty satchel at home; nobody puts a message inside or calls it your gear.
You give the satchel back; the leader must decide what rule to keep without a commemorative object.
The cell leader returns the small satchel he once wanted you to carry. It is empty. He asks whether it should remain a future invitation symbol or proof that minors must never be default cover.
event.family_revolutionary_13_money_with: You keep respectable introductions useful to the network, but access never becomes a vote on tactics.
Keep access without a bought voice
Ten thousand Berrys are transferred clearly into your name, with no tactical claim and no political repayment.
You leave the money with the family and keep one explicit boundary: no donor can claim your future choice.
You are asked what you actually want to inherit: personal money, social access, or the freedom to leave without funding. Nothing should turn your future professional choice into debt to a donor.
You agree to keep useful introductions and addresses, but leave the tactical promise unsigned.
You push both envelopes away; the donor loses his leverage and your family must decide what to do with its share.
You take the family envelope from the pile; the donor's conditioned money remains alone on the table.

After years of support, the adults managing the family's resources set aside money in your name before you turn fifteen. The same donor offers to increase it if you promise to defend 'his line' later.
event.family_revolutionary_13_mothers_un: The network records that the family bond remains private; none of your mother's duties are transferred to you.
Choose civilian life without rejecting her
You accept the idea of future commitment for your own reasons, without claiming her notebook or post.
Your name goes onto a future-invitation list, separate from your mother's post and without immediate commitment.
Agree to talk again at fifteen
The organizer accepts that the network must recruit you like anyone else. You may keep a bond with your mother, support the cause, or choose civilian life without those three answers being confused.
The organizer writes an invitation in your name instead of speaking of an inherited post.
You gently push the notebook away; the discussion stays on your future, not the role she left.
You refuse the specific post; nobody in the room can turn that refusal into a judgment on your mother.

The network finally shows you the clandestine post your mother held before her absence and offers training at fifteen. Her old handoff notebook stays closed on the table; nobody claims it belongs to you.
The Post Your Mother Did Not Pass Down
event.family_revolutionary_13_network_fa: You keep emergency access to the network without an active political invitation.
Keep the code as a civilian
You leave with neither code nor invitation; the network does not turn your refusal into family or political debt.
Beside the relief code, your name receives a separate invitation to discuss joining at fifteen.
The code can offer shelter in the future. By itself, it says nothing about the career you will choose at fifteen; that decision remains separate.
A Network Can Be a Resource, Not a Destiny
You ask before accepting; the organizer clearly separates relief access from recruitment.
Ask if the code requires joining
You decline future access; the organizer removes your name from the distribution list without political comment.
You memorize the code and the map is closed; you take no list of addresses.
The network shows you a safehouse map with names crossed out and replaced over the years. You are offered a simple recognition code for future help, without being given any cell role.
The Name on the Safehouse Map
event.family_revolutionary_13_open_door_: You remain recognized as a future relief volunteer without enrollment in a political cell.
You may support relief and ask to join later without either becoming a condition for the other.
Your name receives an open invitation for age fifteen, separate from any aid received or given.
At thirteen, you are not joining any profession yet. The shelter can only leave you accesses and invitations you may choose to use from age fifteen onward.
You take both papers without stapling them together; the separation stays visible even in your hands.
You take the invitation from the second room; the organizer leaves the relief card separate on the table.
You take a relief shift card; it carries no rank or oath.
The shelter finally puts up a simple sign: food and beds on one side, political volunteering in a separate room. You are asked whether you want to help maintain that separation when you are older.
The Open Door Without an Oath
event.family_revolutionary_13_parent_not: The family relationship strengthens without becoming an argument for or against a revolutionary career.
Stay civilian and close to your parent
You keep a future invitation to join elsewhere while the home remains explicitly outside the operational network.
Keep the cause outside the home
You consider joining at fifteen for your own reasons, with a written rule always separating parent, home, and cell.
Join later without conflating the bond
Your relationship can survive your future career choice. The household boundary becomes concrete inheritance: no cell may invoke your parent to automatically claim family space.
Your Parent Is Not the Organization
You ask whether future involvement could begin elsewhere; the kitchen stays outside the operation.
Ask to act outside the home
You state a future civilian preference; your parent treats it as neither family abandonment nor political betrayal.
You leave the rule posted; your parent knows you protect the home without necessarily rejecting the network.
Keep the rule on the door

The cell formally returns the kitchen to the household as non-operational space. Your present parent asks whether this family victory changes what you want at fifteen; nobody from the network is invited to answer for you.
The Kitchen Returned to the Household
event.family_revolutionary_13_protected_: You choose a future civilian path and the cell destroys its copies after receiving the testimony it needed.
The witness chooses a relay for possible verification; that permission remains limited to this case.
The network keeps only an intermediary chosen by the witness and bans political reuse of his address.
The testimony helps the cell repair a wrong, but grants no permanent right over the witness. They must decide what remains after the meeting.
Protecting Someone After Using Their Evidence
You ask him directly; he chooses an intermediary rather than his home.
Ask how to contact him later
You separate his words from his contact details; the file can prove the error without storing his private life.
You return the address card to the witness; the cell loses the copy it might have kept by habit.
A civilian agrees to publicly correct a false accusation by the cell, but only if his address enters no political file. Some want to keep his details 'just in case' after he testifies.
The Witness Who Keeps His Name
event.family_revolutionary_13_relief_wit: Five thousand Berrys in family savings are explicitly transferred for your first travels, with no political condition.
You choose a future civilian life with one durable boundary: receiving aid creates no political obligation.
You carry a network-recognized rule: future relief may never be claimed as recruitment debt.
Carry the rule into the cause
Scarcity never made your family virtuous. What remains is more concrete: knowing how to receive help without political debt, and give it without buying someone.
You keep the booklet; the medic says it proves relief work, not membership.
You leave the booklet with the next relief coordinator; your participation does not become personal property.
Leave the booklet with the neighborhood
You ask what remains of the small savings kept separate from distributions; the medic produces an envelope in your family's name.
The medic gives you the small booklet used to track distributions in your neighborhood. It shows what your family received and helped redistribute, with no loyalty column or political debt.
event.family_revolutionary_13_tactic_wit: You choose a future civilian path while keeping ties with people willing to repair their mistakes.
The foreman receives a public apology and your future invitation remains open without requiring you to forgive everything.
The network adopts independent verification before intimidation; you keep the option to join at fifteen.
Stay close with an evidence rule
The cell can apologize, revise its rules, or minimize the affair. Your inheritance need not be a choice between blind loyalty and total rupture.
You ask who will acknowledge the error; the organizer stops calling it mere 'caution.'
You close the empty file; the foreman stays in the room to hear what comes next.
You separate the failed tactic from the political goal; several members agree without asking you to forget the harm.
Say the tactic is not the cause

The once-suspected foreman comes to testify: nobody had recruited, threatened, or seen him inform. The cell removes his name from the file and asks what this mistake changes in your relationship to the cause.
The File Closed, Not the Cause
event.family_revolutionary_13_two_keys_t: The network takes back its access; you keep a family space that requires no future career choice.
You keep specific safehouse access, with a written rule that the family room is never included.
Two keys, two rules, and two responsibilities remain separate for your future.
Your parents ask for neither automatic loyalty nor rupture. They want a durable rule for what the network may open, what stays familial, and what you will decide yourself at fifteen.
Cause and Home Are Not the Same Lock
You bring the two keys together without mixing them; your parents understand you want both boundaries visible.
You choose the family key; your father returns the safehouse key to the network without argument.
You take the safehouse key; your mother leaves the family key on the table instead of taking it away.
Your parents put two keys before you: one opens a safehouse, the other the small family room they always kept outside the network. They ask what you want preserved before you turn fifteen.
event.family_revolutionary_a01_long_dist: Routine messages will wait; only family emergencies use the chain.
You keep the initiative to reconnect; the network stops trying to build a stable route to you.
One relay becomes the contact point; nobody receives your full itinerary.
The network must accept that distance and mobility are not a disappearance to fix. You can remain reachable without being permanently traceable.
A Family That Knows How to Let Go
You answer this specific request without giving a permanent address.
You send the packet back with a note that your adult route is not a family mailbox.
You write when and through whom the network may contact you without following every move.

A packet waits at your next safe relay: news from the old network, requests for help, and a note admitting they no longer know how to reach you reliably. Your clandestine childhood has caught up with your mobile life.
event.family_revolutionary_a01_mothers_c: You keep a version of the code for private family messages; the network no longer receives those replies.
You authorize one relay, with the right to revoke it if the channel becomes operational again.
You agree on a new channel; the old code stops being a shortcut into your relationship.
Your mother confirms she wants to keep a bond with you, not automatically reopen her old role. You must decide what the old code still means between you.
You use the family code; the relay immediately recognizes a reply the network can route.
You dictate a plain reply; the relay hesitates to put it into the clandestine chain.
You ask for a way to speak with your mother without turning every exchange into an operational message.
Years after you left home, a relay delivers a cipher using the old family code. Your mother can be reached, but she refuses to let the network decide what the two of you should say.
event.family_revolutionary_a01_mothers_u: You keep the information as part of your history without turning it into a new assignment.
You ask the network to stop contacting you about the lead unless something genuinely new appears.
The chain is verified handoff by handoff before any personal message is sent.
The relay agrees to separate a family search from operational succession. The lead can be followed, archived, or abandoned without transferring your mother's role to you.
A Lead Is Not a Succession
You ask whether anyone knows what became of her, without treating her old post as the starting point.
You refuse to open more of the message until its current recipient is verified.
You ask for the last handoffs instead of writing directly to the address.
An old relay finds a message your mother prepared before she vanished from the circuit. It contains a reply address, but nothing proves it is still safe or still leads to her.
The Trace Left by Her Absence
event.family_revolutionary_a01_two_keys_: You temporarily freeze both accesses until the leak is understood, at the cost of real family distance.
The repair keeps two distinct procedures instead of simplifying security into one lock.
The safehouse gets a new protocol; family access is not included in the rotation.
The incident recalls why the two accesses were separated: a safehouse can change protocol without turning the family home into an extension of the network.
You ask that no new relay receive a copy of the private key.
You propose changing the safehouse lock first rather than the family door.
You ask for an inspection before declaring either key compromised.
A courier tells you an old lock at the family refuge was forced. The network key and private family key had always been separate; nobody knows which one was copied.
event.family_revolutionary_a02_black_fla: You make it known that your flag guarantees no family debt; the declaration also draws more attention to you.
You stop answering requests routed through old Revolutionary relays, even when it costs useful information.
Old names and addresses stop appearing in your crew's business.
As your pirate name grows, more people will look for leverage. Protecting family mostly means reducing handles, not promising endless violence.
A Reputation Is Not a Free Shield
You send word that any pressure should target your career, not your family history.
Pull the risk back to you
You refuse to turn family safety into debt to a pirate intermediary.
You ask your crew to stop using old family contacts as references or guarantees.

An intermediary recognizes your Revolutionary family history and offers to protect your relatives from pirate rivals—in exchange for a service. The threat exists largely because your own name now travels the seas.
Your Flag Reaches the Old Family
event.family_revolutionary_a02_family_ad: Your team records that kinship and operational availability are different things.
Family access is used once, with a named owner and explicit closing point.
Name the exception and its end
The team builds a chain tied to the operation, not your family history.
You are no longer the child subjected to a protocol: you can now expose other people's relatives. The choice is an adult operational responsibility.
Your Methods Carry Your Name Now
You allow one use, but the operator wants to know who decides when the exception ends.
You ask for another dead drop before the family address enters the final plan.
You remove the contact from the plan; the operation will have to absorb the risk elsewhere.
A Revolutionary operator proposes using an old family contact as a relay for an operation now under your responsibility. The plan works precisely because nobody suspects that link yet.
The Family Address in Your Orders
event.family_revolutionary_a02_keep_one_: The relay rejects any political request you have not explicitly accepted.
Contact remains possible without creating a fixed address that can follow your whole career.
No permanent channel remains; you reopen the conversation when you decide.
The network accepts that access to you is not inherited. The chosen channel grants no right over your time, ship, uniform, or relatives.
You prefer to reconnect yourself rather than maintain a permanent door.
You accept the channel only for family news and emergencies.
You ask for an intermediary tied to neither your career nor the old cell.
The old network proposes keeping one channel to you for family emergencies. Nobody asks for a mission, but everyone knows an open channel can become politically useful as soon as pressure rises.
event.family_revolutionary_a02_uniform_o: The family-dependent portion of the file passes to another officer.
Your mother refuses. The file may gain a lead, but your trust absorbs the price of the uniform.
You help with what is already verifiable without asking your mother to become an informant.
Your mother accepts that your career is yours. She only refuses to let your family bond turn her memory into an automatic institutional source.
Serving the Marines Without Requisitioning Your Mother
You refuse to translate her history for her and hand the question directly back to her.
You confirm the known code without supplying names your mother might still recognize.
You state that your family history makes you a poor judge for this part of the case.
A Marine file on an old Revolutionary network contains a code your mother once used. A superior asks you, in front of her, whether that detail can identify other contacts.
The Uniform Between Your Mother and the File
event.family_revolutionary_a03_inherited: Whether you still have the object or not, it stops serving as proof, pass, or recognition sign.
The old keys leave your active possession; the access they symbolized will need to be renegotiated another way.
You stop carrying the recognizable notebook; its contents no longer travel with you.
What you received remains yours, but adult use can expose old relays. You must balance memory, utility, and safety.
An Inheritance Can Become a Beacon
You ask which detail ties the object to the old network.
You put the object away before the sympathizer explains its origin in front of others.
You ask what would actually be protected by no longer carrying or using it.

An old sympathizer warns that the object you received at the end of childhood remains identifiable by certain details. If you still possess it, showing it can expose the people who made or passed it on.
event.family_revolutionary_a03_parent_ch: You plainly ask her to abandon the relay; she hears the fear without mistaking it for an order.
You turn her personal choice into family duty. She rejects that interpretation immediately.
You help prepare her exit without turning support into command.
Support her choice with a clear limit
Any disagreement is about the risk, not her right to decide. The family boundary has to work both ways.
Protecting Someone Without Taking Their Choice
You want to know how she can leave if the mission changes midstream.
You ask the exact limits of what she chose instead of judging the principle.
You confirm her choice remains hers, even if the operation goes badly.
Your mother tells you she agreed to act as a relay one more time for someone from the old network. She is not asking permission, but refuses to let her decision become a debt you will inherit.
Your Mother Still Chooses for Herself
event.family_revolutionary_a03_shelter_h: You find a less comfortable solution and refuse a debt whose terms changed after shelter was given.
You reimburse a specific expense and get a receipt; no future favor is added.
You and the safehouse split the real cost; nobody turns the remainder into loyalty debt.
The safehouse can be reimbursed without buying your future service. The issue is not that a cost exists, but that it stays named and bounded.
You ask which costs actually belong to the shelter before accepting a vague debt.
You refuse to let urgency make any price acceptable.
You offer to cover a precise share rather than let the debt become political.

An old safehouse agrees to shelter someone tied to your family history, then presents an unexpected expense. Nobody speaks of loyalty, but the old confusion between aid and debt returns in another form.
The Shelter That Wants Something Back
event.family_revolutionary_a04_different: Only immediate danger to a relative can bypass the normal channel; everything else waits for your consent.
No institutional rule is created; you keep the right to help or refuse case by case.
The old contact leaves with a simple boundary: asking never means receiving in advance.
Write the rule in one sentence
The principle becomes independent of flag, uniform, or profession: inheritance explains a relationship, it does not buy a resource.
A Rule That Survives Career Change
You agree to hear each request without turning old trust into a general obligation.
You accept that immediate family danger may open one door, but nothing more.
You state that family history grants neither a pass nor automatic service.
An old family contact asks you to settle a dispute: can your family name be invoked to obtain protection, passage, or silence in your adult life? Your current career did not exist in the old rules.
The Same Old Principle in Another Life
event.family_revolutionary_a04_marine_ev: Her memories become usable only when an independent source confirms them.
You step out of the decision chain; she chooses what she is willing to say.
You continue questioning. She is answering less to the Marines than to the child who became an institution.
Your mother can testify, refuse, or request another interviewer. The case must remain valid even if your family relationship yields no information.
Testimony Does Not Come With Blood Ties
You choose to ask as an officer; she asks whether you will accept her refusal.
You ask another officer to conduct the interview so she can answer without answering you.
You remove questions that depend only on unverifiable family memories.

A Marine investigation reopens an old file and calls your mother as a possible witness. The name may belong to someone she once knew, but she refuses to let your rank turn your relationship into an interrogation.
The Name the Marines Want Her to Say
event.family_revolutionary_a04_revolutio: Your unit stops using relatives as a default solution and builds professional relays.
You accept the system's efficiency despite its pressure. Your mother stops pretending your methods still resemble hers.
Every relative gets an independent way to refuse or leave without going through their family agent.
Keep it with a real exit
The disagreement is no longer theoretical: your own methods can reproduce what you learned to challenge. Your mother wants a decision more than an excuse.
What You Do With the Inheritance
You admit formal consent is not enough if refusal harms a relative's standing with the unit.
You argue clandestine work sometimes requires these compromises; she asks who actually carries the risk.
You show her the safeguards, including the right to refuse each mission.

Your mother learns your Revolutionary unit uses agents' relatives as discreet relays, with consent but under heavy pressure. She repeats the same arguments your household once used against the network.
Your Mother Recognizes a Method She Hated
event.family_revolutionary_a05_fathers_l: He records his story in his own name and leaves yours for you to decide separately.
Let your father tell his part
Your entries reference each other without merging commitments or disagreements.
Your father accepts losing a neat lineage story rather than speaking for absent people. He also returns the remaining 2,500 Berrys from the old family emergency fund.
Your father can tell his part and your bond, but speaks neither for your absent mother nor for your adult career. That limit becomes your last shared decision.
One Remaining Parent Is Not Everyone's Voice
You first ask what he wants preserved rather than answering the network.
You propose the network keep only necessary operational facts without constructing a lineage.
You refuse to let your mother's absence turn your father into the voice of the whole family.
Your mother is no longer available, but your father kept the old rules separating home, network, and personal choice. The old network now asks whether it may attach your name to his in its archives.
What Your Father Kept When She Was Gone
event.family_revolutionary_a05_mothers_l: The entry presents you as perfect continuity. Your mother signs only to note she does not approve that reading.
The family bond remains visible, but no role, conviction, or debt is presented as inherited.
The archive separates your paths and explicitly records where your methods diverged.
There is no longer a room or key to protect, but the meaning of two lives. Your final family boundary is the right not to be reduced to each other.
You allow the family bond to be mentioned, but not as proof of political continuity.
You let the archivists write their version; your mother asks whether she can still correct hers.
You ask for two separate entries, with each person's choices and disagreements intact.

As you approach thirty-five, the old network wants to archive your mother's name with yours as one 'line of service.' She sends you the form before answering: she refuses to let two lives be summarized as automatic succession.
Your Mother's Name in the Last Register
event.family_revolutionary_a05_what_the_: The disagreements remain in the entry; your name gains visibility without being framed as automatic continuation.
The network publishes a restrained entry separating aid, choices, disagreements, and current career.
Your refusal itself becomes public and draws attention to the boundary you defend.
Refuse the tribute in your name
Whatever your career, Revolutionary origins remain part of your history rather than a second rank or parallel affiliation. How you correct that history becomes public in its own right.
You ask for actions to be dated and separated from political interpretation.
You reject a smooth legend and ask that methodological breaks remain visible.
You state that family history is not available as propaganda material without contradiction.

The old network prepares a short public history of your family: safehouses, disagreements, aid, and refusals mixed together. No available parent can correct it today; they ask which version may carry your name.
What the Network Will Say About Your Family
event.family_royal_01_empty_nursery_i01_: The miniature stays. The council will see it, even if it dislikes what it implies.
The box closes. You remember where the steward puts things people do not want you to see.
Your finger returns to the pale rectangle on the wall. The steward realizes absence is visible too.
The steward hesitates: leaving the portrait recognizes a family history the council wants to control; hiding it means deciding what your own room is allowed to say.
event.family_royal_01_empty_nursery.choi: You catch the corner of the box before it leaves the table.
You push his hand away. The steward stops, surprised that such a small child already refuses.
You let the box go, but not the key that locks the cabinet.
event.family_royal_01_empty_nursery.text: Before the wardship council visits, a steward takes a small family miniature from your nursery and boxes it away. “The register is not settled yet,” he mutters.
event.family_royal_01_fishman_balcony_ba: You get relief without the crowd seeing how. Comfort and image have already been split apart.
The basin remains visible beside you. The court will have to present your body as openly as your title.
The appearance begins without you. The adviser will have to explain why his perfect image lost its subject.
The adviser proposes wetting a cloth discreetly out of sight. A servant waits with the basin while the balcony doors are already opening.
You turn away from the light and refuse the position prepared for you.
You hit the railing hard enough to interrupt the preparations.
You reach toward the curtain until the adviser understands what you want.
Before a balcony appearance, an adviser slides your water basin behind a curtain: he wants the crowd to see “a royal child first.” Your skin is already starting to dry.
event.family_royal_01_giant_archway_i01_: The procession goes around the back. You will grow up knowing who pays when the décor refuses to move.
They carry you another way and the canopy goes on empty. The ceremony survives, but not exactly as planned.
The garlands come down. For once, the palace changes instead of making the people carrying you bend.
The bearers can force the service route, or the officer can finally remove two garlands from the main arch. The cost of convenience is not yours alone.
event.family_royal_01_giant_archway.choi: Your cry drowns out the orders. The whole procession stops on the stairs.
You push the cloth above you; a ribbon drops at the officer's feet.
You reach toward one of the bearers who is already struggling for breath.
event.family_royal_01_giant_archway.text: Your ceremonial canopy will not fit under the arch with your giant cradle. A household officer orders the bearers up the service stairs rather than move the decorations.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood_i01_reac: You endure the hood until the signal. The dresser avoids punishment, but you remember the price of silence.
Two openings are enough. The silence starts late, but no one can pretend your body was the mistake.
Hand over the hood to cut
You remain bareheaded. The master of ceremonies keeps his rule; you refuse to wear its flaw.
The dresser offers to cut two openings on the spot. The master of ceremonies refuses: uniformity matters more than a garment that can actually be worn, and the servant may keep the blame.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.choice.h: You hold the hood down yourself until your ears protest.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.choice.p: You yank the velvet off and drop it on the carpet.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.choice.t: You catch the dresser's hand as he is being blamed.
