event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.text: For an official minute of silence, a dresser presses a heavy velvet hood over your Mink ears. It slips at once; the master of ceremonies blames the dresser for cutting it badly.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.title: The Velvet Hood
event.family_royal_01_mothers_glove_i01_: She stays one second longer, enough for protocol to yield to your bond.
The glove falls. Your mother picks it up herself, and the usher understands you are not part of the ceremony's furniture.
You let her go. Before you have words for it, you understand that her role can interrupt yours.
Before the audience doors, your mother still holds your glove. The usher waits for the ceremony cue; she can leave, delay the opening for you, or ask him to change the planned order.
Your Mother Hesitates Before the Audience
event.family_royal_01_mothers_glove.choi: You refuse to release her sleeve; the usher stops looking at the clock.
You push the glove toward her. Your mother smiles before standing.
You stare at the man hurrying your mother. He finally looks down at you.
event.family_royal_01_mothers_glove.text: The usher calls your mother before the petitioners. She is still crouched to fix your shoe; he holds out her glove and reminds her the whole court is waiting.
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon_i01_re: You put the seal in her hand. For one second, the family symbol belongs to the person carrying the risk.
Give the ribbon to the nurse
You stop pulling. The nurse finally breathes, though no one asked you to understand why.
The ribbon tears. The clerk sighs, but this time the nurse says plainly that it was not her fault.
The register opens to your name. The nurse watches the ribbon more than you, because a royal child's smallest mistake can become an ordinary adult's fault.
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon.choice: You hold your wrist out to the clerk as if the gesture already belonged to you.
You immediately tug at the knot. The nurse catches your wrist without daring to grip hard.
You rub the seal between your fingers until wax marks your skin.
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon.text: A clerk ties a ribbon bearing the family seal around your wrist before entering you in the public register. He warns the nurse: if you tear it, she will answer for the delay.
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon.title: The Registry Ribbon
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver_i01_re: The silver returns to you. You learn that a title can demand hiding scarcity instead of solving it.
The steward has to retrieve the plate from the cook in full view of the visitor.
Hand the plate to the cook
The bowls remain in sight. The household looks less wealthy and much more real.
The steward wants the scene restored before the visitor enters. Behind him, a cook waits with the bowls she was told to make disappear.
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver.choice: You turn the fine plate into a drum. The visitor looks over.
You push the silver toward the edge of the table, toward the bowls being hidden.
Push the plate to the edge
Your hand leaves the silver to trace the crack in a mended bowl.
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver.text: An important visitor arrives. The steward puts the household's last silver plate before you and hides the servants' mended bowls. Your title is expected to look richer than the house.
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver.title: One Silver Plate
event.family_royal_01_two_seats_i01_reac: You stay still. The portrait will be perfect, and you already learn that perfection assigns everyone a precise place.
Your parents step closer despite the floor marks. The painter will have to work with your actual family.
You refuse to turn; they come to you instead. The master of ceremonies swallows his correction.
The painter waits. Your father finds the order absurd; your mother points out the servants will be blamed if the sitting collapses. Both look to you before taking their places.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.choice.g: You grab the cloth behind you. Two servants catch it before it falls.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.choice.r: You reach for him and immediately ruin the planned pose.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.choice.t: You turn toward your mother. The painter asks everyone to start again.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.text: For your first official portrait, servants line your parents up behind your chair. Your father makes you laugh; a master of ceremonies orders him one step back to preserve the order of titles.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.title: Two Places Behind You
event.family_royal_04_bread_beyond_rope_: You force the master of ceremonies to answer in front of the crowd. He permits the sharing rather than explain the refusal.
You leave the loaf where it is to protect the guard. Waste becomes the visible price of the rule.
You cross the rope yourself. The guard did not disobey; the crowd still saw who was allowed to cross.
The guard explains that breaking the line in public could cost him his post. The loaf will be thrown away after the ceremony if nobody changes the rule.
You push the loaf toward the guard and ask him to pass it across.
Ask the guard to give it
You call the child over. The guard blocks the very first step.
You lift the loaf with both hands. The guard immediately understands where you mean to go.
During a public festival, a guard stretches a rope to keep the crowd away from the royal table. A child on the other side stares at the decorative loaf before you; nobody is meant to eat it.
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback_i01: The clerk explains the full order. You learn that a court can turn almost any room into a ranking.
You refuse to choose between the floor and an empty rule. The corridor becomes your temporary seat.
You push the chair to the wall. The clerk may restore it later; for a few minutes, absence stops commanding the room.

In the waiting room, the clerk recites the rule: the empty chair belongs to someone of higher rank, even while absent. Nobody is offended, but everyone must arrange their body around that forbidden seat.
The Chair Reserved for Someone Absent
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback.cho: You ask the name of the absent person who still owns the seat.
You sit in the empty chair. The clerk opens his mouth, then looks at the door.
You sit on the carpet directly in front of the reserved chair.
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback.tex: In a small waiting room, a clerk forbids you from sitting in an empty chair: it belongs to someone higher in precedence, even though that person did not come.
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback.tit: The Chair You Must Not Touch
event.family_royal_04_creditor_bows_i01_: The pots leave under a perfect bow. You do not forget that respect can coexist perfectly with injustice.
The steward pales, but the creditor agrees to revisit the account. The title loses some of its display before the staff lose their tools.
You refuse to let the debt fall straight onto the kitchen. The steward will have to find another payment.
The creditor refuses the plate: it is worth less than the debt, but far more to appearances. The cook waits to learn whether she must make dinner without pots.
event.family_royal_04_creditor_bows.choi: You ask why he bows if he can still empty the kitchen.
You bring out the silver plate the steward saves for visitors.
You plant yourself in the doorway as the men reach for the pots.
event.family_royal_04_creditor_bows.text: A creditor bows deeply to you, then orders his men to take two cooking pots from the kitchen. The steward mutters that the royal branch will pay “when appearances improve.”
event.family_royal_04_fishman_proof_i01_: The minister has no concrete answer. For the first time, his staging produces a question he cannot control.
You leave before the visitors arrive. The minister keeps his speech and loses the living proof he wanted at its center.
You stay, but answer in your own words. The image slips out of his control without disappearing.
The minister simplifies: “It is a good image.” A palace worker looks away. Even at four, you understand that a good image can require someone to stay quiet.
event.family_royal_04_fishman_proof.choi: Your question cuts off the minister before the visitors arrive.
You drag your chair out of the planned position, inch by inch.
You leave the chair and sit beside the servant holding the damp towels.
event.family_royal_04_fishman_proof.text: A minister places your small chair beside the fountain for visiting dignitaries. You hear him say your presence “proves the kingdom welcomes every people.” Nobody asked you to be that proof.
event.family_royal_04_giant_servant_step: You receive the visitors standing. The palace discovers that a rule can survive without its official furniture.
The reception moves to an empty gallery. It is less impressive, but nobody has to carry the décor on your behalf.
You help move it. The servants save time; you learn that sharing a burden does not automatically make the burden fair.
The household officer proposes continuing: “Only one reception left.” The injured servant holds his hand while everyone decides whether palace convenience is worth the strain.
You shout for them to stop. The bearers freeze the platform in the doorway.
You lift one corner of the platform long enough to free his hand.
You stay on the floor when they ask you to climb onto the platform.
Every reception morning, four servants drag a heavy platform into the hall because the royal furniture is too small for you. Today one of them traps his hand under a step.
event.family_royal_04_household_fallback: The staff choose what actually needs tidying. For once, preparation stops being a cascade of orders.
Ask the staff what they prefer
You cross a room that suddenly feels less like yours. You learn what image requires without anyone explaining it.
The visitor finds a real room instead of a set. The staff hold their breath, then discover the world does not end.
The visitor is not coming to see you live; he is coming to see how a royal child lives. The difference is enough to transform your room and everyone's work.
You pick things up with the staff, not fully understanding why the urgency exists.
You slip your toy behind a cushion before a servant can take it.
You keep playing as if the bell has nothing to do with your room.
A bell rings in the corridor and the whole staff changes pace: your toys vanish, curtains are straightened, voices drop. An official visitor is approaching your rooms.
event.family_royal_04_mink_tailor_blame_: The tailor agrees to follow procedure. You gain an official route, but it is still controlled by people who do not bear the garment.
A few seconds make the problem visible. The rule can no longer hide behind ignorance.
The blame moves to you, where it suddenly loses much of its force. The tailor keeps his post.
The tailor says he altered the garment because you could not wear it otherwise. The wardrobe master says he should have asked permission from people who never had to wear it.
You repeat the word they keep using until the wardrobe master turns to you.
You stand against the tailor's leg before he can apologize.
You bring back the old hood and put it between the adults.
The ceremonial hood has been replaced with an open collar, but the wardrobe master summons the tailor: the alteration was never authorized. He wants someone held responsible.
event.family_royal_04_mother_keeps_door_: Your mother closes the file for exactly five minutes. The minister waits, and you learn that time can be negotiated.
You keep the book. She keeps the hearing. Neither of you pretends the two duties cost the same.
You sit at the back of the antechamber. Duty stops being only the thing that takes your mother away.
Your mother can delay the hearing, take you with her, or go alone. The minister points out that the petitioners travelled for two days; your story can wait.
Five Minutes That Belong to Someone
You hold out the open book. The minister remains in the doorway, file in hand.
You push the door against the minister. Your mother suppresses a laugh before reopening it.
You slip after her before anyone can send you back.
Your mother has just come to read to you when a minister opens the door without waiting: three petitioners are already in the antechamber. “Your presence is required now.”
event.family_royal_04_parents_two_lesson: They finally have to explain their disagreement instead of using you as a practice field.
You repeat it until you no longer hesitate. Your father stops joking when he sees what the effort costs you.
Your father helps you remember faces. Your mother agrees, provided you also learn what each title requires.
Your parents are not arguing about manners, but what manners should protect: the useful distance of office, or real relationships with the people who live around you.
What a Greeting Says About You
You repeat the guard's name loudly under the master of ceremonies' stare.
You repeat your mother's formula word for word. Your father raises his hands in surrender.
You combine the ambassador's title with the guard's familiar tone. Your parents look at each other.
Your father teaches you to greet the old guard by name. Your mother arrives with the master of ceremonies: in ten minutes you must receive an ambassador using the exact formal greeting.
event.family_royal_04_wardship_keys_i01_: He hands you one after recording the incident. You gain one page and discover the administrative cost of a simple request.
You recover the miniature without touching the letters. You choose which boundary to cross.
You return the key, but now you know the cabinet, the ledger, and the exact rule separating you from your mail.
The clerk wakes. He says the council reads all mail to a royal child first “for your protection.” He does not say who protects you from the council.
event.family_royal_04_wardship_keys.choi: You leave the key where it is and compare the seals on the envelopes.
You lift the small key without waking the clerk.
You tug his sleeve and point to your name on the letters.
event.family_royal_04_wardship_keys.text: You find the family miniature box in a wardship-office cabinet. The key hangs from a sleeping clerk's ring; on the next shelf, several letters bear your name.
event.family_royal_07_apology_written_i0: You refuse to make paper do all the work. The harmed person can at least answer someone who carries the palace name.
Your apology becomes more dangerous because it becomes verifiable. It can now be accepted, challenged, or used to demand repair.
The wording protects the house from any clear obligation. You learn how a polite sentence can close a door.
The clerk explains that naming a specific fault could bind the house. A vague apology protects the image; a precise one could force someone important to repair something.
event.family_royal_07_apology_written.ch: You refuse to begin until you know who the apology is actually for.
You copy the formula unchanged. The text becomes neat, official, and almost empty of people.
You strike the word from the polished draft. The clerk presses his lips together.
event.family_royal_07_apology_written.te: After a public incident, the palace gives you an apology to copy. It admits to “an unfortunate misunderstanding” without naming the guard, servant, or resident who actually paid for the scene.
event.family_royal_07_bell_for_crowd_i01: You refuse to be the only spectacle. The workers come onto the platform and explain what they had to reinforce.
You pull off the show. The workers do too, but nobody applauds them for keeping the danger out of frame.
The crowd waits while the brace is reinforced. When the bell finally rises, nobody is underneath holding it together.
The organizer wants to use the crowd's excitement. The workers warn that the brace is shifting. Everyone knows you can lift the bell; the real question is what others must risk to prove it.
event.family_royal_07_bell_for_crowd.cho: You ignore the bell and crouch to see what the workers are holding.
You take the bell; the crowd roars before it fully leaves its cradle.
You fold your arms in front of the bell. The presenter holds his smile one second too long.
event.family_royal_07_bell_for_crowd.tex: For the palace festival, you are asked to lift a great bell before the crowd “because everyone will be impressed.” Two workers are still holding a badly fixed brace under your platform.
event.family_royal_07_council_signs_for_: The decree stands. You now know that not deciding does not stop your name from producing consequences.
The next notice will also name the responsible councillor. Your seal at least stops fully erasing the actual author.
The council accepts a limited review. You do not erase the rule, but you refuse to let your name make debate impossible.
The council explains that a royal minor cannot decide, but the royal name guarantees continuity. The merchant answers that continuity does not pay for her market stall.
You ask which council member chose the increase. The clerk first answers with the institution's name.
You ask the merchant what the increase costs her rather than what the decree claims to raise.
You take the notice and read your own name in the closing formula.
An angry merchant produces a notice bearing the family seal: the wardship council raised her stall fees “in the name of the royal house.” You had never seen the decree.
event.family_royal_07_court_fallback_i01: The rule is clear, and so is the consequence. You learn that a decision can be perfectly proper and still humanly incomplete.
The file gets an extra note: check rehousing. It is not a solution, but it is no longer an administrative ending.
You memorize the name before the file closes. Administration has a number; you keep a person.
The officials can explain the unpaid rent, the rule, and the signature. They are much less certain about what happens after the housing door is taken back.
event.family_royal_07_court_fallback.cho: You repeat the word. The two officials immediately stop speaking as though the bench were empty.
You ask where the family will sleep now. Neither file contains that answer.
You keep your eyes elsewhere and let them finish the sentence.
event.family_royal_07_court_fallback.tex: You wait for a ceremony on a side bench. Two officials discuss a family removed from royal housing in front of you; they speak as if you are too young to understand the word “eviction.”
event.family_royal_07_fishman_harbor_que: You walk the detour with the workers. The rule stops being a sentence and becomes extra time, distance, and inspections.
You promise only to raise the question, not to solve what you do not yet control. The escort writes down every word.
You give the prepared answer. The visit continues neatly, but nobody on the dock mistakes your presence for change.

On the dock, the escort talks about cargo control. The workers show the separate gate they must use, while the same crates pass elsewhere without a detour. Your question is less convenient than your official face.
You turn to the guard and ask what security reason actually requires that gate.
Ask the guard for the reason
You ask how long the separate entrance has existed. Several hands rise at once.
Ask how long it has been
You begin the written sentence. The workers wait without interrupting.
During a harbor visit, Fish-Man workers ask why they still have to use a separate entrance to the royal docks. Your escort hands you the prepared answer: “security reasons.”
event.family_royal_07_full_procession_em: You attend with fewer horses and less display. The rank remains visible without consuming everything it claims to represent.
The household misses part of the festival. The staff receive what they are owed before the title receives its display.
The procession is flawless. Wages wait again, and now you know who really finances perfection.
The treasurer warns that a royal branch disappearing from ceremonies loses political weight, which may cost even more later. The staff, however, need their wages this week.
You ask why horses come before wages. The treasurer half-closes his ledger.
You announce you will not take the carriage to the festival. The treasurer immediately calculates the difference.
You tell the two employees you heard them. Neither knows whether to apologize.
The treasurer says your household must fund its place in the royal festival despite its debts. In the corridor, you hear two employees discussing wages delayed again to pay for the procession horses.
The Procession and the Empty Purse
event.family_royal_07_household_fallback: The meeting moves. For once, powerful people's schedule adapts to work already done.
Food no longer needed for protocol goes to the staff on duty. Nothing is fixed, but nothing is wasted.
You eat without hunger and the room clears on time. You see how a small burden becomes invisible when everyone complies.
The meeting never asked the kitchen whether the hour worked. The kitchen never asked whether you were hungry. The decision came from above and everyone only passed it downward.
You ask to save your plate for later. The cook looks toward the coming meeting.
You sit and start eating because everyone already worked for this time.
You suggest someone else eat what was prepared if you cannot finish it.
Dinner is served an hour early because an unexpected meeting will take the room later. The staff rushed the whole kitchen; you are not hungry and nobody wants the food wasted.
event.family_royal_07_parents_on_steps_i: The procession waits. Your mother eventually comes down too, turning the delay into a family decision rather than one person's offense.
The ceremony leaves on time. Your father stays below for a few minutes and joins later, without pretending you all made the same choice.
The guard does not have to climb the steps: the first official greeting happens where he can stand.
The guard insists nobody should change the program for him. Your father replies that a rule demanding his discretion after an injury mainly protects everyone else's comfort.
event.family_royal_07_parents_on_steps.c: You call the guard up to you. He looks at his bandaged leg, then at the stairs.
You go down the steps toward the guard and your father, in front of the whole procession.
You stay beside your mother while the master of ceremonies counts the seconds.
event.family_royal_07_parents_on_steps.t: Before a ceremony, your father goes down to personally greet an injured guard. Your mother stays above: if she follows, the procession is officially late. If she does not, he faces the master of ceremonies alone.
event.family_royal_07_petitions_under_do: An hour later, the three residents enter through the official door. You have turned a shortcut into a public obligation.
You have each name entered in the ledger instead of letting the pages vanish. Procedure takes the complaints in without erasing them.
You return the pages after reading them. The office keeps control of the file, but not of what you know.
The clerk says answering directly would set a precedent. The three pages describe a broken well, a market tax, and a brutal guard; the problems already exist.
A Hearing That Followed You Home
You wedge your foot in the door and keep the petitions behind you.
Block the door with your foot
You call for your mother loudly enough that the clerk stops in the corridor.
You pick up the first sheet before the clerk reaches the door.
After seeing you at a hearing, townspeople slide three petitions under your door instead of using the official office. A clerk is already coming to take them back before you read them.
event.family_royal_07_tailor_before_cour: You get a comfortable outfit. The tailor puts away the other patterns, and you see exactly where privilege stops.
The council authorizes an adaptable pattern for service uniforms. Your privilege becomes a precedent others can use.
You refuse to be the only person the rule knows how to accommodate. The council must reopen the issue or return to the old problem.
The councillor calls it a personal favor. The tailor replies that a cut preventing pain and discomfort is craft knowledge, not a reward for rank.
You ask why the alteration should be royal when the clothing problem is not.
You ask the tailor to show the other designs he prepared.
You accept having the garment approved only for you.
The tailor presents a new design that fits your Mink ears while keeping the house colors. A councillor wants to approve it only for you, so other servants cannot use it to request adaptations.
event.family_royal_10_court_fallback_i01: You stay for one file and leave before a symbolic seat becomes fictional attendance.
Your seat remains in meetings. You learn that representation can exist long before participation.
The council agrees your nameplate appears only when you are actually present. Absence stops counting as decorative assent.
The council chair says your seat is mostly symbolic for now. Yet the symbol already creates the impression that your branch is represented in decisions you never hear.
event.family_royal_10_court_fallback.cho: You move your nameplate to the far end of the table where nobody prepared a chair.
You open the file placed on your name because nobody expected you to come.
You sit down in front of the pile. The official has to retrieve his files one by one.
event.family_royal_10_court_fallback.tex: An empty seat now bears your name in certain meetings even when you do not attend. Today an official piles files on it because he knows you are still too young to come.
event.family_royal_10_future_alliance_li: You agree only to revisit it later. The adviser gets a door left ajar; your mother makes sure he writes nothing more.
The file stays open but no house receives an answer. You keep the information without turning it into commitment.
Your name leaves the list. Any future alliance will have to begin with a real decision, not your childhood silence.
The adviser talks about ports, votes, and future treaties. Your mother says your existence is not a pending diplomatic promise. He asks whether she really wants to close options for the kingdom.
You ask your mother what she thinks of the list rather than what the adviser expects.
You ask what exactly your presence in that column is meant to gain for the house.
Ask what you are useful for
You take the file before the adviser closes it and read the names beside yours.
Your mother finds your name in a file of “future alliances”: several houses already suggest a later engagement. The adviser insists this is not a marriage arrangement, merely keeping doors open.
event.family_royal_10_guard_refuses_orde: The guard leaves the stall and records that you backed his reading of the permit. The dignitary can no longer call it simple disobedience.
The stall disappears before the procession. The guard obeys, the vendor loses her day, and the street looks perfectly orderly.
The vendor accepts a nearby spot and compensation. The procession gets its view without making her bear the whole cost of propriety.
The guard can obey the dignitary and contradict the permit, or respect the permit and risk discipline for insubordination. Your name is enough to change which risk looks more serious.
You ask which rule allows the stall to be removed. The dignitary first answers, “propriety.”
You ask to see the vendor's permit. It carries the market seal.
You stand beside the guard instead of moving on with the procession.
A dignitary orders a guard to remove an old vendor from the royal route. The guard hesitates: she has a market permit, but her stall “spoils the view” of the procession.
event.family_royal_10_household_fallback: You practice the signature, but only after reading each page. The habit forms with a question attached.
Learn the gesture and the reasons
You learn to write your name without letting practice blur into obedience to the documents in front of you.
The pen stays clean. The clerk notes that the first thing you learned about signing was that you could refuse.
The clerk says training starts early so you will not hesitate when it matters. He has no equivalent lesson prepared on the right not to sign.
You ask why they are training the gesture when it still decides nothing.
Ask why your seat is ready
You fill the practice sheet with your name without touching the official documents.
You ask for the pages before the pen. The clerk hands you the first document.

A clerk brings three documents for your household to countersign. Your place is already marked at the end of the table even though your signature has no legal force yet: they want you to learn the gesture.
event.family_royal_10_procession_invoice: You draw two columns: what was genuinely seized and what the family already owed.
You keep the letter as the main story. The decree was real; the debts become easier to forget.
You ask which current debts can be settled without recreating the old grandeur.
Neither story is enough alone: the house suffered a real political seizure, but it was already in debt. The family letter merges both into a fall caused entirely by enemies.
Two Truths in the Same Ledger
The treasurer separates property taken by decree from assets handed over to creditors.
You trace the accounts back to a loan signed before the political punishment. The fall does not have a single cause.
You line up the decree, the debts, and the letter. Some debts predate the seizure; other losses really did come from the punishment.

The treasurer opens the old file on your house's fall: a decree seized land after a political crisis, but older debts also bear the family seal. A letter from your great-uncle calls all of it “theft.”
event.family_royal_10_public_reform_with: The posters go out. You learn how much faster a symbol can move than the people it claims to represent.
Printing is suspended until a first dated measure is signed. Your image stops being free advance payment for the palace.
Condition your portrait on a real measure
The poster mentions the review and the still-separate entrance. The message becomes less polished and much harder to misuse.

The minister shows the poster where your royal name announces a port for everyone. Tomorrow, however, the affected workers must still use the separate entrance. The campaign sells an intention before any rule truly changes.
The Poster Promises Before the Reform
You ask when the study ends. The adviser searches for the line that does not exist.
You cross out “for everyone” on the poster. The printer stops before starting the run.
You refuse to let your face go to print with a change that has not happened yet.

After repeated complaints about access to the docks, the palace prepares a poster announcing “a harbor for everyone.” The main entrance will open more widely, but some separate controls remain. Your portrait is meant to prove the house is already moving forward.
event.family_royal_10_staff_pays_scandal: The penalties stand. You now understand that your privilege can operate even when you never ask it to.
Several penalties are reversed. You cannot erase the past humiliation, but you refuse to leave it as the price of your image.
An addendum to the apology acknowledges that your own choices caused the incident. The court loses part of its protective screen.
The palace explains that staff are responsible for royal appearances running smoothly. Nobody says you asked for these penalties; that did not stop them being imposed to protect your image.
An Image Repaired With Other Lives
You ask to see the decisions made after your apology. The clerk realizes you already know about the penalties.
You compare the posted apology with the internal sanctions. The two documents tell different stories.
Ask why the public record is silent
You leave the official corridor to find the people whose punishment appears in no speech.
After your earlier incident, the palace reassigned two servants and suspended a guard “to restore discipline.” Your public apology mentioned none of it; you learn by accident.
event.family_royal_10_subjects_at_gate_i: You have the demands recorded with names and numbers. Your role becomes a conduit rather than decoration.
You cross the courtyard and go back inside. The crowd saw you; it still has no answer about the tax.
A small delegation comes in with its accounts. The problem remains, but the gate stops being the palace's only answer.
Behind the gate, protesters demand a hearing and numbers. The council wanted an image of listening; the crowd now asks what happens after someone actually hears.
event.family_royal_10_subjects_at_gate.c: You refuse to appear until someone can tell you what the palace will do after your walk.
You go beyond the planned mark and get close enough to hear full sentences.
You stay in the corridor. The councillors lose the silhouette they wanted in the windows.
event.family_royal_10_subjects_at_gate.t: A protest forms at the palace gate after a new local tax. The council asks you to cross the courtyard in full view to show the house “hears the concern,” without announcing any measure.
event.family_royal_10_succession_chart_i: The discussion finally leaves your single box and reveals a whole family organized around possibilities no child chose.
Ask what is required of everyone else
You learn the obligations without pretending the throne is meant for you. Knowledge becomes preparation, not prophecy.
You reject schedule changes justified only by hypothetical accidents. The council keeps its chart, not your timetable.
Refuse a life built around the chart
The adviser says nobody is preparing you for the throne; he is preparing the institution for every possibility. Yet that caution already shapes what they teach you and where they want you kept.
event.family_royal_10_succession_chart.c: You ask who decides the scenarios written around living members of your family.
You count the people ahead of you in line. The clerk waits for you to reach your own name.
You fold away the section containing your name. The rest of the succession remains visible.
event.family_royal_10_succession_chart.t: A succession chart is unrolled before the council. Your name is nowhere near the top: it appears several branches down, surrounded by notes about what happens if other heirs die or renounce.
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback_i01: At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian with one rule: if your name opens a door, also look at who remains outside.
At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian and ask the court to stop scheduling your life. The name stays in your history, not your calendar.
At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian without cutting every family obligation. The inheritance remains pressure and access, not a career.
The clerk accepts the distinction: your family remains `royal_family`, but your Active entry will be civilian. Later Events may let you choose a personal affiliation without rewriting your origin.
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback.cho: You leave the space blank rather than invent a title the world does not recognize.
You write the only professional status that actually matches this departure.
You add that royal affiliation remains family origin, not a profession.
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback.tex: The family register opens a line reserved for “orientation at fifteen.” The clerk cannot enter any professional royal rank: he can only ask what relationship you want to keep with the family institution.
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback.tit: The Last Place in the Register
event.family_royal_13_family_not_institu: You accept a limited set of family obligations. At fifteen your career stays civilian, but that duty can still open future situations.
You keep your bond with your mother without keeping a court obligation. That boundary becomes a lasting part of your inheritance.
Keep the bond, leave the obligation
You ask for distance. A personal 5,000-Berry fund makes that autonomy concrete without erasing the family bond.
She does not promise it will be simple. She promises only not to turn affection into a signature. Tomorrow, the council may lose an obligation without you necessarily losing your family.
You ask the question no file contains: will she stay if you step away from court?
You ask what she would choose if her public role had no claim on you.
You sit beside her without speaking. For once, nobody takes notes.

Your mother waits alone after one last meeting about your future. She tells you she can remain your mother even if you refuse the obligations the court wants attached to your name. The council expects your answer tomorrow.
event.family_royal_13_household_fallback: You keep the key as family access. The old hound that slept outside your room leaves with you; returning remains a choice.
You return the key and ask to be invited like any relative. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian, with concrete distance from court.
You suggest the empty room serve visitors or staff on duty. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; an old privilege becomes at least a usable space.
Ask that the room serve another use
The steward reminds you that your name will always get you received here. You can accept that refuge, leave it behind, or treat it as a relationship rather than an automatic right.
A House That Remains Behind You
You ask what happens to the room and the work around it when you no longer live there.
Ask who will use the room
You close your hand around it. It opens a room, not a profession.
You place the key in the steward's palm. The room will remain, but not as an obligation.
A steward returns the key to your childhood rooms: the palace is already reassigning some spaces ahead of your fifteenth birthday. You must decide what the key still means to your family.
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name_i0: You refuse the podium without rejecting the petitioners. At fifteen, your Active entry will remain civilian; family duty does not automatically become a profession.
You open the hearing without pretending to govern. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; inherited access remains a tool, not a royal career.
Use the name to open access
You state your limits clearly. The hall gets fewer promises and more truth; At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian.
The hall waits. You hold neither throne nor profession at thirteen, but your name already opens a door many petitioners cannot push themselves.
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name.ch: You ask to see the files before deciding what to promise the people who wrote them.
You step down before the announcement. The master of ceremonies must choose someone else.
You take the sheet and read its three lines before the doors open.
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name.te: For the first time, you are offered the opening words at a public hearing in your own name. The prepared text promises only “attention and continuity”; beyond the doors wait the same kinds of petitions you have seen before.
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name.ti: Your Name Before the Open Hall
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost_i01_r: You abandon restoration. 5,000 Berrys from the last liquid assets become a fresh start instead of a payment toward the past.
The court recognizes a documented share of the seizure. 25,000 Berrys are restored without erasing debts the family genuinely owed.
You keep the name without turning former comfort into a debt the world owes you. That stance becomes publicly recognizable.
Keep the name, not the claim
You keep the names and the claim open. Your reputation now carries a demand you may pursue later.
You renounce the old claims. A cleanly liquidated 10,000 Berrys becomes a fund to rebuild without recreating former grandeur.
The file gives no single answer: some seizures are documented, some debts are real, and some privileges were never rights. You must decide what you want to carry forward from the fall.
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost.choic: You cross out acknowledged debts and set lost old privileges apart from the rest.
You close the file before the word “owed” becomes a personal obligation.
You mark only the land and property the decree actually took from the family.
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost.text: At thirteen, the treasurer gives you copies of the decree, the debts, and the family letter. The court asks what you still consider “owed” to your branch before another adult writes the answer for you.
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost.title: What Is Owed to You
event.family_royal_13_seal_without_thron: You keep the seal in the family archive as proof of origin, not professional authority.
Carry the history, not the power
You leave the seal with the council. Your origin remains true, but no physical symbol becomes necessary to prove it.
You accept archive access without pretending it makes you right. That privilege remains usable and contestable.
Use the name only to open doors
The clerk lists its limits: no professional authority, no new title, no automatic right over other people's lives. It still carries memory and access.
You first ask what this seal does not allow you to decide.
Ask what it does not grant
You leave the seal where the council placed it. Nobody makes you take it.
You take the seal without asking anyone to unroll the succession chart again.
The council gives you a copy of the family seal for your personal records. It announces no rank or succession: only proof that you belong to this history, whatever place you choose next.
The Seal Without a Promise of a Throne
event.family_royal_13_symbol_or_voice_i0: You refuse the campaign without rejecting the reform. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; your voice will not automatically serve as institutional proof.
You speak, but the campaign also names what remains unresolved. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; your voice no longer belongs automatically to palace messaging.
Support the progress and name its limits
Your portrait moves behind those living under the rule. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; your reputation already reflects that choice.

The measure genuinely improves access without ending every separation. You can support the step, criticize it, or refuse to become living proof of it. Your royal origin does not make your voice palace property.
event.family_royal_13_symbol_or_voice.ch: You refuse the photo session until affected dockworkers are in the room.
You read the exceptions before looking at the poster mock-up.
You push the portrait away without denying that the partial opening is a real improvement.
event.family_royal_13_symbol_or_voice.te: At thirteen, the palace is already preparing a new campaign about partial dock reform. Some restrictions will remain. They ask for your portrait and voice before the measure can speak entirely through its results.
event.family_royal_13_walk_beyond_gate_i: You accept a heavily supervised civilian start without mistaking it for a career. Distance from court will have to be negotiated later.
You pass through the gate without an official itinerary, wearing unmarked travel boots. Your origin stays real without becoming your schedule.
You keep a few useful visits and reject the rest. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian, with inherited access you will use case by case.
Nobody offers you a royal career: there is none. The real question is how much control the court keeps over your civilian life simply because it can open doors for you.
event.family_royal_13_walk_beyond_gate.c: You keep one visit that interests you and return the rest of the schedule.
You read the visits one by one: safe markets, allied institutions, not a single day left open.
You tear the sheet through the first month. The clerk does not move.
event.family_royal_13_walk_beyond_gate.t: The palace is already preparing a series of supervised civilian visits for when you turn fifteen, all chosen by the household. The gate is open; a clerk wants to know whether you accept that future program or will chart your own route.
event.origin_race.text: {{playerName}}, what people do you come from?
event.origin_to_childhood.title: Your Birth
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_depar: After living on the island long enough to understand its rhythms, you finally identify a viable window toward the New World. The exact destination will depend on the current available when you leave.
Check the current tables and be ready for the next departure window.

The current tables change. This time, Fish-Man Island no longer feels like a place you merely crossed through: you have had time to live, work, or help someone here. A new departure window is opening toward New World waters.
A Window to the New World
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_i01_d: The first drop throws you into a frame. A restraint snaps, several people panic, and the descent continues with injuries and a badly broken rhythm.
You read the first shift before it arrives and call the bracing change at exactly the right moment. The descent steadies almost at once.
You catch the line too late. The jolt knocks the breath from you and panic spreads before the craft is steadied.
You ride the drop instead of fighting it. The braces hold and the group quickly finds the rhythm of the descent.
Take the descent line and set the rhythm.
Sabaody’s light narrows above you. Pressure builds, the hull or cabin groans, and the current suddenly pitches everyone forward. The first seconds will decide whether the descent stays controlled.
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_i02_u: You correct at the wrong moment. The black current slams the side, tears grips loose, and drives you into the deck before the course is barely recovered.
You anticipate where the two currents converge and slip through their seam. The pressure turns into a clean acceleration toward the distant lights of the island.
The correction comes too wide. The transport cuts through a pressure pocket that batters everyone and costs long seconds before the course is recovered.
You follow the darkest vein until the pressure finally eases. The Red Line passes overhead without taking control of the course.
Read the seam in the current and correct at the last moment.

The last natural light disappears. Ahead, two bodies of water cross beneath the Red Line like invisible rivers. A bad correction can pin the transport into the pressure flow; the right one opens the route toward the underwater island.
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_i03_a: The bubble clears the last dark water and the island’s light fills the horizon. You disembark among the docks, still carrying the crossing in your legs.
Follow the harbor lights and disembark as soon as the passage opens.
You let the pressure equalize in stages. When the exit finally opens, the streets of Fish-Man Island lie ahead and everyone can step onto solid ground.
Take the slow berth and check everyone before disembarking.

After the darkness beneath the Red Line, colors appear in the distance: inhabited reefs, traffic bubbles, and sheltered docks. Only the pressure lock remains before everyone can get back onto solid ground.
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_local: You open the wrong pocket. The coating snaps, tears you from your footing, and the hull takes the hit before the workers can close the tear.
You also spot a second weakness before it starts flexing. The workers fix both areas at once and credit you with preventing a major repair.
You release the tension too quickly. The repair holds, but the pressure rebound strikes part of the hull.
You find the pocket loading the seam and bleed it in stages. The coating settles back into a clean curve.
Climb up with the crew and bleed the stressed pocket.
You pay for a full hull inspection. The yard returns the ship checked without asking you to take another risk.
Pay for a full inspection and let the specialists work.
Barely docked, a coating worker points out a long milky scar across the hull bubble. One section flexed during the descent and must be relieved before the next pressurization.
A Bubble Pulling Sideways
You mistake a backwash for the end of the sequence. The next surge catches you in the open and throws you against the slope before you can reach shelter.
You spot a weak pulse that signals the true cycle change. The survey becomes more precise than expected and the chartmaker increases your share.
You miss one pulse and have to stay for another cycle. The survey is saved, but the current catches you during the retreat.
You record the full sequence and leave before the next surge. The chartmaker pays you the promised share of the survey.
Read the markers and record the full sequence before the next heavy surge.

A local chartmaker is checking a current that strikes Coral Hill in irregular pulses. The markers are holding, but she needs a second set of eyes to record the sequence without staying exposed too long.
Survey of the Pulses
You reset the ribbons and the buyer realizes nobody will help him expand the cut. The harvesters finish without widening the patch.
Refuse the off-limit cut and reset markers shifted by the current.
You stay inside the markers and help sort what can be taken without ripping out young growth. The harvesters pay you for the work rather than for volume.
Help the harvesters finish the approved patch cleanly.
Harvesters tie ribbons around an approved coral patch while an impatient buyer urges them to cross the markers and fill his baskets faster.
The Marked Harvest
You take the wrong angle. The cable snaps tight, slams both of you into the reef, and the last loop has to be torn free in a panic.
You use the cable itself as a return line. The diver comes free and you climb back together without touching the sharp coral.
You free the diver, but the current throws both of you into the coral before you can climb back toward shelter.
You approach from the sheltered side, loosen the loop, and guide the diver out of the current. They come out with only a few scrapes.
Reach the loop and free it before the current pins the diver against the reef.
At the edge of a Coral Hill drop, a harvester is caught in an old marker cable. Every movement tightens the loop while a side-current pulls them toward sharp coral.
The Diver in the Cable
You repeat their cadence aloud. The group crosses in the right window, and the guides appreciate that you relayed their instructions instead of arguing with them.
Follow the guides’ count and help other travelers leave at the right moment.
The movement of the water feels familiar. You translate what you feel into simple landmarks for the visitors, and the tunnel clears without incident.
Read the water yourself and explain the change to the travelers.
You give up a few minutes. When the push finally weakens, you cross safely without adding to the guides’ workload.
Wait for the current to ease instead of forcing the passage.
At the mouth of a transit tunnel, local guides stop travelers: a cross-current has shifted since morning. Surface visitors hesitate over directions that seem to contradict the signs.
Guides of the Cross-Current
You grab the wrong bale at the wrong angle. Two more slam into you and the ring widens before the handlers can stop it.
You use the current to bring the bales back one behind another. The last one nearly settles itself against the anchor and the plaza applauds the maneuver.
You break the rhythm of the ring, but a bale catches you in the shoulder before the last one is secured.
You work against the pattern instead of meeting it head-on. The bales return to the anchor without hitting a bystander.
Enter the ring and bring the bales back to the anchor one by one.
A bubble cart loses its restraint at the edge of the plaza. Heavy bales drift in a circle around the vehicle, accelerated by a traffic current, and threaten passersby.
The Ring of Cargo Bales
You remove obsolete schedules and group the warnings still in force. The board becomes readable again before the next convoy crowd arrives.
Sort the notices by seal and date before putting them back.
You spend a long while sending groups toward the correct tunnels. When the attendant returns, nobody has followed the old dangerous detour.
Stay at the junction and redirect travelers until an attendant returns.
A traffic bubble bursts against the plaza notice board. Work notices, schedules, and current warnings scatter while travelers are already following outdated directions.
Notices Adrift
You declare the scale rigged too quickly. A second test proves you wrong, the crowd turns, and you have to pay for some of the goods spilled in the argument.
You run three cross-checks using weights from neighboring stalls. The crowd sees exactly where the discrepancy comes from and the merchants adopt the check for the rest of the day.
You restore the weighing but leave everyone to interpret the result. The argument continues and you pay to replace a basket knocked over near you.
You test the counterweight and then the goods. The fault is identified without humiliating either seller or customers, and trading resumes.
Reweigh the goods in front of everyone and force a verifiable result.
Familiar local cues
Two customers accuse a dried-shell vendor of rigging his scale. The vendor swears pressure shifted the counterweight; the crowd starts taking sides before anyone has tested it.
The Vendor’s Scale
You take the map literally and lead the group into a current loop. You have to pay for local transport to get everyone out before someone collapses.
You reconstruct the whole route from the current pulses and show the crew how to read the changes. They leave with a reliable method, not just an escort.
You notice the reversal too late. The detour costs time, energy, and a paid passage to get back onto the correct route.
You correct the arrows against the real flow and find a junction marked from the opposite direction. The crew reaches the docks without another detour.
Re-read the map against the current flow and guide them to the right junction.
A small surface crew missed its guide and no longer knows which tunnel leads back to the docks. Their map shows arrows for the rising flow, but the current has already reversed.
The Crew Without a Current
You cover the disputed handling fee to move the lot immediately. The berth starts flowing again, but your wallet carries the cost of the quick solution.
Front the handling fee to get the crates out of the way.
You match seals, weights, and destinations until the list makes sense again. The handlers clear the queue and thank you for preventing a blanket seizure.
Rebuild the manifest from the marks still visible on the crates.
A surface convoy dropped its crates at the wrong berth after the crossing. Two handlers argue over a soaked manifest while the queue blocks the passage.
Crates Without a Berth
You mistake a real emergency for a panic attack. Trying to recover the mistake leaves you exhausted and hurt in the scramble.
You spot a subtle reaction before it turns dangerous. The clinic reorganizes triage around your observation and several travelers avoid getting worse.
You let a serious case wait a few minutes too long. The medic stabilizes the patient, but the mistake shakes you and takes a physical toll.
You quickly separate emergencies from travelers who are mostly panicking. The medic can focus treatment where it matters.
Help triage the patients and identify signs that need immediate treatment.
In a small harbor clinic, several surface travelers are still shaking after the descent. A medic is short-handed and needs help separating panic from dangerous pressure reactions.
Depth Sickness
You give the loudest people the floor and both lines collapse together. The guards have to push everyone back; you take a hit in the crush and become the target of the complaints.
You turn the crowd into two workable lines and pass information group to group. The gallery starts moving again before the new barrier is fully secured.
You convince part of the group, but not its ringleaders. The gallery stays closed longer and the argument leaves you drained.
You separate the genuinely urgent cases and get everyone else to step back. The guards reopen a narrow lane without another surge.
Calm both lines and secure an orderly passage for urgent cases.
A public gallery is closed after a traffic barrier breaks. Guards are trying to keep two lines apart while a group of travelers insists they will miss their convoy.
The Closed Corridor
The host shows where to leave shoes, bags, and cumbersome weapons. The group stops guessing and the entrance resumes with visible relief.
Simply ask the host what is expected before entering.
You wait a moment, then follow the motions without turning them into a performance. The travelers behind you understand as well and the doorway clears.
Watch local residents enter and follow their sequence.
At the entrance to a meeting house, a group of travelers blocks the way while trying to guess the local etiquette. The hosts wait, somewhere between amusement and impatience.
Sandals at the Entrance
You refuse to turn harbor rumors into official evidence. The clerk grumbles, removes your name from the record, and continues with direct witnesses.
Refuse to sign an account you cannot confirm.
Your testimony narrows the dispute to a few verifiable lots. The clerk redraws the allotment without blaming an entire group for diverting the shipment.
Describe only the cargo and timings you actually saw at the harbor.
Outside a kingdom supply office, cooks and carriers dispute how to divide a shipment delayed by the currents. A clerk asks for precise testimony before redrawing the allotments.
The Supply Hearing
You jam the collar at an angle. The conduit lashes when flow returns, strikes you, and forces the workers to shut the whole section again.
You use the lull to realign the coral support as well. The conduit comes back stable and the workers can reopen the pools immediately.
The collar slips on the first try and the jet hits you before you can reset it. The repair finally holds, but not before a hard blow.
You lock both fasteners during the lull. Flow returns without a leak and the district avoids a longer shutdown.
Help fit the collar during the pressure lull.
A public conduit feeding several pools has split along a coral support. Workers shut the main flow, but residual pressure keeps them from fitting the repair collar.
The Coral Conduit
events.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.c: You force one last inspection of the fastenings and coating bubbles. The descent begins with an extra safety margin.
Inspect every seam before the descent.
You refuse to lose the current window. The lines come free and Sabaody vanishes above the bubble.
Commit to the current now, before it turns.
You shift passengers, bags, and crates until everyone knows where to brace when the sea drops away beneath the hull.
Rebalance people and cargo before casting off.
events.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.t: Preparations are ending on Sabaody. Beneath the mangrove roots, the coating shimmers around the transport that must dive ten thousand meters down. The next current leads under the Red Line; once taken, there will be no dock left to correct a mistake.

npcStat.calm.description: Measures the ability to keep a cool head under pressure. Useful when an Admiral decides your day was going too well.
npcStat.loyalty.description: Measures how attached a crewmate is and how willing they are to stay when everything goes wrong. Songs around a barrel help.
originNarrative.household.bandit: {{familyReference}} hides supplies, watches the roads and rarely asks where a sack came from.
originNarrative.household.celestial_drag: {{familyReference}} lives surrounded by servants and privileges almost nobody dares challenge.
originNarrative.household.civilian_modes: {{familyReference}} works, pays what must be paid and knows the neighbors by name.
originNarrative.household.civilian_poor: {{familyReference}} counts berrys, keeps anything still useful and knows the price of a meal.
originNarrative.household.civilian_wealt: {{familyReference}} shields you from need, but not from expectations already attached to your name.
originNarrative.household.generic: {{familyReference}} becomes your first fixed point in the world.
originNarrative.household.marine: {{familyReference}} lives by Marine orders and the timing of returning from duty.
originNarrative.household.orphan: No stable home is waiting for you; you depend early on which doors open and which stay shut.
originNarrative.household.pirate: {{familyReference}} lives among stained maps, passing crews and objects nobody explains.
originNarrative.household.prisoner: {{familyReference}} shares with you a life ruled by locks, guards and imposed hours.
originNarrative.household.revolutionary: {{familyReference}} knows names that are never spoken loudly and papers hidden before a door is opened.
originNarrative.household.royal_family: {{familyReference}} lives behind guards, court rules and a name others recognize before you do.
originNarrative.household.slave: {{familyReference}} teaches you early that meals, gestures and even time can belong to someone else.
originNarrative.location.coastal: The sea is close enough to dictate schedules, trades and departures.
originNarrative.location.entertainment: The streets live on music, crowds and travelers who change every week.
originNarrative.location.generic: Everyone eventually learns the same faces and the same rumors.
originNarrative.location.isolated: Here, every sail on the horizon becomes news for everyone.
originNarrative.location.military: Marine boots and barracks calls already set the rhythm of the streets.
originNarrative.location.nature: Forest, remedies and drying herbs begin almost at the doors of the houses.
originNarrative.location.outlaw: Merchants meet enough smugglers here to learn not to ask every question.
originNarrative.location.port: The quays mix cargo, dockworkers' shouts and crews that never stay long.
originNarrative.location.royal: Guards, clean walls and fine clothes remind everyone who rules.
originNarrative.location.rural: Houses spread out between dirt roads, fields and the smell of the sea.
originNarrative.location.snow: Cold wind presses salt and snow against the shutters.
originNarrative.location.urban: The alleys are full of shops, shouted orders and neighbors who know everything.
originNarrative.race.buccaneer: Your unusual build quickly draws looks your family learns to recognize.
originNarrative.race.fishman: Your Fish-Man body marks you out immediately in most Blue Sea streets.
originNarrative.race.giant: Even as an infant, your size makes it impossible to mistake you for the other children.
originNarrative.race.longarm: Your long arms already force adults to adapt clothes, beds and gestures.
originNarrative.race.mink: Your fur and Mink features draw looks anywhere your people are rare.

stat.agility.description: Used to dodge, chase and escape situations that require functioning legs. Running on water is still reserved for absurdly trained people.
stat.charisma.description: Helps persuade, recruit and impose your presence. Shouting that you will become Pirate King works surprisingly often, but not on everyone.
stat.health.description: How much punishment you can take before collapsing. Bandages are not a strategy, even if some crews seem convinced otherwise…
stat.intelligence.description: Used to understand, plan and solve problems that do not surrender after three punches. Yes, those exist.
stat.luck.description: Matters when the plan is terrible but the universe has not decided to punish you yet. Does not replace a navigator or a brain.
stat.morale.description: Helps you endure fear, defeats and extremely bad news. A proper banquet fixes many things. Not everything.
stat.navigation.description: Used to read seas, currents and Grand Line's impossible routes. Without it, even a Log Pose mostly looks decorative.
stat.observation.description: Helps you spot danger, read opponents and develop Observation Haki. Seeing the hit coming does not guarantee you can dodge it.
stat.strength.description: Used for close combat and developing Armament Haki. You will still lose to the Kung-Fu Dugongs…

event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.title: Before Dawn
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.text: A recall order hits the door before dawn. Your father pulls his boots back on under the lamp. There is nobody else to stay with you when he leaves.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.choic: You clutch his sleeve. Your father stops in the middle of the motion.
You push his boots toward him. He realizes you saw the recall order.
You do not move. Your eyes follow every buckle, button, and movement.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i01_t: Your father pauses at the threshold, the folded order in one hand. Outside, the Marine waiting for him avoids looking in.
You tighten your grip. He has to gently pry your fingers loose before leaving.
You hand him what he forgot. He thanks you before stepping outside.
He meets your eyes, then looks down at the order as if he owes an explanation.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i02_a: The door closes. His footsteps fade before the room stops feeling too large.
You refuse to forget that he left despite you.
You put away the rest of his things as if it were already your responsibility.
You remember the door, the lamp, and the sound of his boots.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.te: A Marine from the neighborhood brings a small blue pennant for the household window. He sets it within reach while speaking with the adult beside you.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.ch: You grab the blue cloth before the Marine finishes his sentence.
You immediately hand the pennant back to its owner.
Your finger traces the emblem's lines without leaving the cloth.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant_i0: The Marine crouches to take the pennant back, then pauses when he sees what you are doing.
He laughs and says you already seem to recognize Marine colors.
He nods, surprised by your seriousness.
He names the emblem and shows you where it will be visible from the street.
The pennant is fixed to the window. Passing Marines recognize it at a glance; everyone else looks a little longer.
The symbol quickly becomes something familiar in the household.
You watch the pennant as something that belongs to the adults first.
You memorize the emblem well enough to recognize it elsewhere.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.te: At the base family check, the clerk stops at a form designed for a Human child. Its chair, ruler, or boxes simply do not match your body.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.ch: You stay put while he rearranges his equipment around you.
You push away the tool that keeps trying to force you into a measure that does not fit.
You watch the form while the clerk crosses out one box and searches for another.
You deliberately stretch your arm beyond the end of the ruler. The clerk calls someone else over.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form_i0: They Improvise
The clerk gives up on the standard setup. He fetches string, a second stool, and a blank sheet while the line waits behind you.
Show what works
You show him where to place things so they stop getting in your way.
Keep the tool away
You refuse to let him use the old method again, even to save time.
Follow his new notes
You watch the words he invents to replace the crossed-out box.
Ask how far the string goes
The clerk unrolls the entire string. A quartermaster at the far desk turns around.
The Corrected Record
The clerk finally writes something that fits you instead of forcing the old box. The record goes back toward the base archives.
Look at the new entry
For once, the form changes around you.
Turn away from the desk
You leave after forcing the adults to respect a clear boundary.
Remember the correction
You mostly remember the moment the adult had to invent another way to do it.
Watch the quartermaster note your name
The quartermaster writes your name separately before handing the form back.
event.family_marine_04_behind_office_doo: Behind the Office Door
You wait in a base corridor. Behind the door, your father flatly refuses a patrol order. His superior reminds him that a Marine does not choose his missions.
Press your ear to the door
The handle turns while your ear is still against the wood.
You catch a few words, then footsteps approach.
You understand the order concerns civilians your father believes would be endangered.
You hear the order, the refusal, and each man's reason before anyone approaches.
Call your father
You call him before hearing more. The argument stops behind the door.
Back away quietly
Your heel knocks over a bucket in the corridor.
You leave too late: your father spots you at the end of the corridor.
You leave the corridor unseen.
You leave silently and even memorize the route back.
A Few Words Too Many
The word “civilians” carries through the door, then “risk.” Your father answers that an order can be lawful and still be wrong.
Stay to the end
You stay long enough to understand the dispute is about specific people, not your father's pride.
Call him again
Your father finally opens the door. His superior immediately sees you were right outside.
Keep walking
You walk away knowing he said no, but not fully knowing why.
The Door Opens
A few minutes later, your father finds you. He knows you were close enough to understand that he defied a superior.
Ask him why
You ask him directly why he refused.
Pretend you heard nothing
You give him the chance to keep the argument to himself.
Say he was right
You take his side before he has fully explained himself.
Why Did You Say No?
Your father finally chooses what to tell you: the order, the danger he saw, and what a Marine is supposed to do when the two no longer align.
Believe him
You discover that an uniform can contain refusal.
Ask what he risked
You understand his refusal could cost him something real.
Keep your doubt
You mainly remember that the same mission can have two different versions.
event.family_marine_04_dinner_interrupte: Dinner Interrupted
A Marine messenger knocks during dinner. Your father already reaches for his coat; your mother keeps a hand on his bowl and reminds him he promised to stay.
Pull him back to the table
You pull your father toward his chair. Your mother keeps her hand on the bowl.
Push his plate toward him
You push his plate toward his coat as if the choice were already made.
Say “Stay”
Your voice triggers the argument both adults were holding back.
Your father avoids your eyes and keeps hold of his coat.
Your father stops long enough for your mother to speak again.
Your father puts his coat back on the chair. Even the messenger waits for a different answer.
Two Duties
Your father says the patrol is short-handed. Your mother answers that the household is too. The messenger remains at the threshold holding the order.
Stay beside your mother
Your father understands the cost of leaving before he even exits the room.
Hand him his coat
You hand him the coat. Your mother's silence grows heavier.
Ask who is right
The question forces them to explain what each had been demanding from the other.
The Messenger Waits
Nobody can pretend the decision is automatic: the messenger is still waiting, and dinner is getting cold.
Accept that he goes
Your father leaves. Your mother stays beside you until his footsteps fade.
Ask him to stay tonight
Your father returns the order to the messenger and stays, at the cost of an explanation he will owe tomorrow.
Ask him to leave after dinner
The messenger agrees to wait a few minutes. For once, duty and family are not treated as an instant either-or choice.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.title: The Empty Chair
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.text: Your father promised to be there for the neighborhood celebration. The benches fill, the second shift call sounds, and his chair stays empty.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.choic: You push away the adult's hand when they try to take the chair.
You fold the chair yourself before the celebration ends.
Your voice breaks and several adults stare without knowing what to say.
They tell you a Marine cannot always choose. The chair stays empty.
The neighbor about to move the chair leaves it alone.
The small row around you agrees to keep the seat empty until the end.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i01_w: The celebration begins. Music covers the shift bell, but not the empty chair beside you.
You watch every uniform that passes at the end of the street.
You move the chair away so you no longer have to look at it.
Repeat it to anyone who asks
Every time someone asks, you give the same answer: he promised.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i02_t: Your father arrives as the benches are already emptying. He immediately sees the place you kept for him — or the one you put away.
You make him look at the ending celebration before accepting his excuse.
You are still angry, but you refuse to let his lateness erase the rest of the evening.
You head home before he can explain the mission.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_adaptati: In the base mess, the table reserved for families does not fit your body. An adult offers to carry you or move everyone else for you.
You gather what is nearby to make a place that fits you.
You let the adults move what is needed.
You refuse to be carried and stay standing beside the table.
Benches scrape, trays shift, and every eye turns toward the solution you chose.
Nobody had to give up their place, and you did not need to be carried.
The adaptation becomes a shared task instead of a spectacle.
You keep your decision to the end despite the stares.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.tex: Rain slips under the threshold while your father's service coat is already catching drops. The basin overflows and nobody tells you what to save first.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.cho: You pull down the coat before it is soaked.
You deal with the overflow first.
You push the water back toward the door with whatever you can find.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home_i01: When the rain eases, the result of your first choice is obvious in the room.
The coat is dry, but some floorboards are soaked.
You limited the damage by handling the most urgent source first.
Your arms tire before the rain does, but you kept the household afloat.
At pay distribution, a Marine places two nearly identical tokens on the counter: one belongs to your household, the other to an absent family. He asks which one to take.
You invent a difference and choose with far too much confidence.
You hesitate until the Marine takes both tokens back.
You spot a familiar scratch on the right token.
You spot the scratch and a wear mark the Marine had missed.
You immediately choose the wrong token.
You guess wrong and the Marine corrects you before the token leaves the counter.
You guess right without being able to explain why.
You guess right and the Marine laughs at your confidence.
You refuse to choose without proof.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_service_: The Marine finally opens the pay ledger. Small notes beside the numbers explain why the two tokens look alike.
You leave with the right token and a better idea of how the base keeps its accounts.
You accept the written check over your intuition.
You memorize the detail that will let you rely less on someone else next time.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.title: Made to Fit
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.text: A base seamstress opens the seams of a small practice jacket to adapt it to your body. She asks you to show her what gets in the way.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.choic: Show what gets in the way
You point out where the fabric pulls or blocks.
You test the fastenings one by one instead of making her guess.
You stand as still as you can while she works.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i01_f: The first version holds for a few seconds, then a seam pulls, a sleeve catches, or a fastening pops as soon as you move.
You show her the exact movement that makes the jacket fail.
You suggest a different fastening instead of repeating the same setup.
You hold still a few more seconds before admitting it does not work.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i02_f: The seamstress places the chalk in your hand and asks you to mark what she should change.
The second version works because you helped shape it.
You move until you find the last weak spots, then she fixes them.
You let her apply what she just learned about your body.
Children of Marines chalk out a drill square. When you approach, one blocks the entrance with a stick: “Not with this equipment.”
You take another piece of chalk and start a space beside theirs.
You force your way in and fall in front of everyone.
You step in, but the game stops around you.
You step in and refuse to leave. Eventually the game resumes.
You step in, move two markers, and show everyone another way to continue.
You stay outside the square and memorize their movements.
event.family_marine_04_off_drill_square_: The other children turn toward you. The problem is no longer the equipment: they now have to decide what to do with your presence.
Two children hesitate, then cross the chalk line toward you.
You stay there until someone agrees to resume the game.
From the edge, you copy a drill they just failed.
A Marine stops in front of the two chalk squares. He asks why the group is split before the other children can invent an excuse.
You describe the stick, the equipment, and the refusal. The adult has to answer something concrete.
You point to your own square instead of waiting for the adult to decide for you.
You give him no explanation. The group resumes, but the scene remains entirely between the children.
event.family_marine_04_quartermaster_mea: The Quartermaster's Measure
A quartermaster unrolls his measuring rope to the end, checks your reach, then writes your name in a notebook. At four, he already wants to know how large you will grow.
Stretch out both arms
You deliberately hold the pose and let him record everything.
Ask why
The officer cuts off your question and keeps measuring as if your opinion does not belong in the notebook.
He only says a Giant is “worth tracking.”
He admits some officers track Giant growth for military potential.
You keep asking until he explains what he records, for whom, and why your name matters.
Pull your arm back
You pull your arm back before the final measurement.
The Notebook
When the officer turns the page, you see other large measurements, ages, and notes about expected strength. Your name is not alone.
Look at the other entries
You realize this tracking existed before you and will continue after today.
Close the notebook
You place your hand on the page. The officer has to stop for the first time.
Point at your name
You make it clear you want to know why your name is there.
“Worth Tracking”
The officer finally says it plainly: some superiors want to identify Giants early who might one day serve in Marine forces.
Accept testing, not deciding
You accept being tested, but not having your future decided for you.
Ask who decides for you
You refuse to let the notebook answer for you.
Refuse the tracking
You ask that your name not be used to prepare a career you never chose.
In Front of Your Father
The officer finally asks your father whether he agrees to bring you back. This time, the question is asked in front of you.
Answer before your father
You answer for yourself. The officer writes that down too.
Let your father answer
You watch your father decide what he allows on your behalf.
Refuse yourself
You refuse clearly. Military tracking may continue elsewhere, but not with your consent.
